Interactive module

JPA & Hibernate

Persistence done properly — entity mapping, the persistence context, relationships and fetching, JPQL and the Criteria API, transactions and locking, inheritance, batching and caching, schema management — with the warehouse's products, orders and stock finally stored in a real database, and every SQL statement on the page emitted by Hibernate itself at build time.

Applied Java 21 · Hibernate 7.4 · JPA 3.2 · H2 9–11 hours Updated October 2026

Start here

How to use this module

Work through it at your own pace. Your section checkmarks, quiz answers, flashcard marks and notes are saved in this browser under a key scoped to this file, so closing the tab loses nothing and the earlier modules cannot overwrite it. Nothing is sent anywhere — this page makes no network requests at all. Press ? at any time for the keyboard shortcuts, and use Reset progress in the sidebar to start over.

Every program in this module was compiled and executed as part of the build, against a pinned stack: Hibernate ORM 7.4.1, Jakarta Persistence 3.2 and an in-memory H2 database, on JDK 21. That matters more here than in the earlier modules, because most of what you will read is not program output at all — it is SQL. Every line that begins Hibernate: in an Expected output block is a statement Hibernate actually sent to the database when the page was built, captured with hibernate.show_sql. The prose reads those statements line by line, and when a section claims that a mapping produces two queries instead of one, the count was checked by the build, not asserted by the author. Where a widget animates something — a persistence context filling up, a lock being lost — it carries the Simulated badge: nothing in a browser talks to a database.

The warehouse, finally persisted

Three modules of Product, Order and InventoryService have lived entirely in memory. This module puts them in a database and keeps the same vocabulary, so the mapping decisions are about types you already know:

  • Product becomes the first entity: a generated id, a unique sku, an enum stored as text, a price stored as cents, and value objects for money and dimensions (§1, §2).
  • Order and OrderLine become the first association, and the place where the owning side, cascades and lazy loading are learned the hard way (§3–§5).
  • StockLevel is the row two pickers fight over: it carries the @Version column that turns a lost update into an exception (§7).
  • Supplier is the many-to-many; Discount is the sealed hierarchy from Intermediate, mapped three different ways so you can compare the tables (§4, §8).
  • The reports from Intermediate are rewritten as JPQL, the Criteria API and projections, and then made fast with batching (§6, §9).
Your notes

Before you begin

Prerequisites

This module assumes Java Fundamentals and Java Intermediate, or the equivalent. Java Advanced is not required, though §7 on locking reads more easily if you have met the lost-update problem there. Each item below is leaned on directly, with the section that taught it:

Prerequisite skills, where they were taught, and what depends on them here
You should already be able to…Taught inBecause this module…
Implement equals and hashCode as a matched pair, and say what breaks a HashSetFundamentals §10puts entities whose id is assigned after they enter a Set into exactly that trap (§11)
Choose a collection for an access pattern and explain the costFundamentals §12, Intermediate §11maps a Set and a List to the same table and shows why Hibernate treats them differently (§4)
Read a generic signature such as TypedQuery<Product> or CriteriaQuery<Long>Intermediate §1uses the typed query APIs throughout, and the Criteria API is generics all the way down (§6)
Write a lambda and trace a stream pipelineIntermediate §4, §5projects query results into records and streams them, and streams a Query result lazily (§6, §9)
Say when a record is the wrong choiceIntermediate §8needs mutable, identity-bearing, non-final classes for entities — and records for everything that is not one (§2, §11)
Use try-with-resources and distinguish checked from unchecked exceptionsFundamentals §11opens and closes an EntityManager per unit of work and treats every PersistenceException as unchecked (§3, §12)

You also need basic SQL, stated plainly: you can read a select with a join and a where, you know what a primary key, a foreign key and an index are, and you know that a transaction either commits or rolls back. This module reads a great deal of SQL; it does not teach it.

What you need installed

A JDK 21 or newer, plus the library jars — this is the first module whose programs do not run on the JDK alone. If you are working from the course repository, one command resolves the exact versions the pages were built with into build/lib/java-jpa/:

node tools/fetch-deps.mjs java-jpa          # Hibernate 7.4.1, Jakarta Persistence 3.2, H2 2.4 and their runtime deps
javac -cp "build/lib/java-jpa/*" FirstEntity.java
java  -cp ".;build/lib/java-jpa/*" FirstEntity      # on Linux/macOS the separator is : not ;

With Maven or Gradle you need two coordinates; everything else arrives transitively:

<dependency><groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId><artifactId>hibernate-core</artifactId><version>7.4.1.Final</version></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>com.h2database</groupId><artifactId>h2</artifactId><version>2.4.240</version></dependency>

H2 is used because it needs no installation and starts in milliseconds. Every mapping here works unchanged on PostgreSQL or MySQL; where the generated SQL would differ, the text says so.

Three habits to unlearn

An ORM is convenient enough that it invites three assumptions, each of which works in a demo and fails in production:

  • "An entity is just a data holder." It is not. A managed entity is watched: change a field and the change is written at commit whether you meant it or not, and hand it to a view layer and the view can trigger queries. Entities are a persistence tool; records are for carrying data around (§3, §11).
  • "A collection on an entity is a collection." It is a promise to load one later, valid only while the session that made the promise is open. Touch it afterwards and you get LazyInitializationException; touch it in a loop and you get the N+1 problem (§5).
  • "hbm2ddl.auto=update keeps the schema in sync." It adds what is missing and never removes, renames or narrows anything, and it has no idea what your data means. It is a development convenience; a deployment is a migration script (§10).

The contract

Learning objectives

By the end of this module you will be able to do each of the following without reaching for a reference. The final quiz tests exactly these twelve.

  1. Explain the object–relational impedance mismatch, what JPA standardises and what Hibernate adds, and read the SQL Hibernate emits for a simple persist and load.
  2. Map an entity with @Id, a generation strategy chosen for the database, @Column constraints, enums as strings, java.time columns and @Embeddable value objects, and say what each generation strategy costs.
  3. Trace an entity through transient, managed, detached and removed states, predict when the first-level cache serves a load, and explain dirty checking and flush timing.
  4. Model many-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many and one-to-one associations, identify the owning side, and keep both sides in sync with cascade and orphan removal chosen deliberately.
  5. Diagnose the N+1 problem from statement counts and fix it with join fetch, an entity graph or batch fetching; explain LazyInitializationException and why open-session-in-view hides rather than solves it.
  6. Write JPQL with joins, parameters, aggregates, constructor projections and pagination; build the same query with the Criteria API; know when native SQL is the right choice.
  7. Control transaction boundaries and flushing, and implement optimistic locking with @Version and pessimistic locking with LockModeType, naming the failure each prevents.
  8. Choose an inheritance strategy (single table, joined, table per class, mapped superclass) from the DDL and query shape each produces.
  9. Tune writes with JDBC batching and ordered inserts, reads with DTO projections and read-only sessions, and explain what the second-level and query caches can and cannot do.
  10. Manage schema with generation modes for development, validate for safety, and a migration tool for production; explain why update is never a deployment strategy.
  11. Design entities that behave in collections (identity, equals/hashCode on a business key or a stable id), use lifecycle callbacks and entity listeners for auditing, and model soft deletes.
  12. Read show_sql output and statistics to explain a slow page, and map the common exceptions to their causes and fixes.
Deliberately out of scope

Spring Data JPA and Spring Boot get one paragraph, in §12, on how they wrap what this module teaches — a JpaRepository is an EntityManager with the boilerplate generated, and every problem here surfaces there with a Spring stack trace on top. Hibernate Envers (audit history), multi-tenancy, Hibernate Reactive and jOOQ are each mentioned once where they fit. Connection pools are used (Hibernate's built-in one, which is not for production) but not tuned; HikariCP is named as the one to use.

Section 1

Why an ORM, and what it costs

A relational database stores rows in tables and relates them by values in columns. A Java program holds objects on a heap and relates them by references. Neither model is wrong, but they disagree about almost everything that matters, and the disagreement has a name: the object–relational impedance mismatch. An object-relational mapper exists to translate across it — and like every translator, it is only trustworthy once you know what it says on your behalf.

The five places objects and rows disagree
DisagreementObjectsRowsWhere it bites
IdentityTwo things are the same if they are the same reference; equals is a separate, optional notionA row is identified by its primary key; two rows with equal columns are two rows§3 (the identity guarantee), §11 (equals for entities)
AssociationsDirectional references; a Product may hold a Supplier without the supplier knowingA foreign key column in one table, navigable from either side by a join§4 (the owning side)
GranularityA Product holds a Dimensions object holds three intsOne table, three extra columns; there is no "small object" in SQL§2 (embeddables)
InheritancePercentOff extends Discount, dispatched at runtimeNo such thing; you choose between one wide table, several joined tables, or one table per class§8
NavigationFollow references one at a time: order.lines().get(0).product().supplier()Declare the whole shape up front in one query and get a single result set back§5 (lazy loading and N+1)

Worked example, part 1: the baseline without an ORM

Before reading a line of Hibernate, see what it replaces. This is plain JDBC against the same in-memory H2 database every other program in this module uses. Note everything you have to write yourself: the table, the parameter indices, the column names repeated in the select and again in the ResultSet reads, the row-to-object code, and the update statement for a change to one field.

javaJdbcBaseline.java
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
 
public class JdbcBaseline {
 
    record Product(long id, String sku, int priceInCents) {}
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
        String url = "jdbc:h2:mem:JdbcBaseline;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1";
        try (Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(url, "sa", "")) {
            c.setAutoCommit(false);                         // a transaction starts here
 
            try (Statement s = c.createStatement()) {
                s.execute("create table product (" +
                          "id bigint generated always as identity primary key, " +
                          "sku varchar(16) not null unique, " +
                          "price_in_cents int not null)");
            }
 
            try (PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(
                    "insert into product (sku, price_in_cents) values (?, ?)")) {
                ps.setString(1, "BOLT-7"); ps.setInt(2, 80); ps.executeUpdate();
                ps.setString(1, "NUT-3");  ps.setInt(2, 25); ps.executeUpdate();
            }
            c.commit();
 
            List<Product> cheap = new ArrayList<>();
            try (PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(
                    "select id, sku, price_in_cents from product where price_in_cents < ? order by sku")) {
                ps.setInt(1, 100);
                try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
                    while (rs.next()) {                      // row -> object, by hand, column by column
                        cheap.add(new Product(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("sku"), rs.getInt("price_in_cents")));
                    }
                }
            }
            System.out.println("mapped by hand = " + cheap);
 
            try (PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement(
                    "update product set price_in_cents = ? where sku = ?")) {
                ps.setInt(1, 90); ps.setString(2, "BOLT-7");
                System.out.println("rows updated   = " + ps.executeUpdate());
            }
            c.commit();
        }
    }
}
Expected output
mapped by hand = [Product[id=1, sku=BOLT-7, priceInCents=80], Product[id=2, sku=NUT-3, priceInCents=25]]
rows updated   = 1

Nothing here is wrong. JDBC is explicit, fast, and every statement is one you wrote. The cost is repetition that must agree: the column list appears in the DDL, the insert, the select and the mapping loop, and a renamed column breaks all four at runtime, not at compile time. Multiply by forty tables and two hundred queries and the mapping code is the largest, dullest, most bug-prone part of the application. That is the problem an ORM solves — not "writing SQL", which it cannot spare you from reading, but writing the same SQL and the same mapping over and over.

Worked example, part 2: the same thing as an entity

Now the ORM version. The class is annotated instead of mapped by hand; the table is generated from it; the insert, the select and the update are all written by Hibernate. Read the program, then read the SQL it produced — every Hibernate: line below was captured from the real run.

javaFirstEntity.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.util.List;
 
public class FirstEntity {
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")              // the name JPQL uses; for a nested class it would otherwise be FirstEntity$Product
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16)
        private String sku;
        private int priceInCents;
 
        protected Product() {}             // JPA instantiates entities reflectively
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
 
        Long id() { return id; }
        String sku() { return sku; }
        int priceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
        void reprice(int cents) { this.priceInCents = cents; }
        @Override public String toString() { return "Product[" + id + ", " + sku + ", " + priceInCents + "c]"; }
    }
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf(Class<?>... entities) {
        var cfg = new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:FirstEntity;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true");
        for (Class<?> c : entities) cfg.managedClass(c);
        return cfg.createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf(Product.class)) {
 
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                em.persist(new Product("BOLT-7", 80));
                em.persist(new Product("NUT-3", 25));
                em.getTransaction().commit();           // the inserts happen here, not at persist()
            }
 
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                List<Product> all = em.createQuery(
                        "select p from Product p order by p.sku", Product.class).getResultList();
                System.out.println("loaded " + all);
            }
 
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product bolt = em.find(Product.class, 1L);
                bolt.reprice(90);                        // no SQL written by you: dirty checking does it
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                System.out.println("after reprice " + bolt);
            }
        }
    }
}
Expected output
Hibernate: create global temporary table HTE_product(priceInCents integer, rn_ integer not null, id bigint, sku varchar(16), primary key (rn_)) transactional
Hibernate: drop table if exists product cascade
Hibernate: drop sequence if exists product_SEQ
Hibernate: create sequence product_SEQ start with 1 increment by 50
Hibernate: create table product (priceInCents integer not null, id bigint not null, sku varchar(16) not null unique, primary key (id))
Hibernate: select next value for product_SEQ
Hibernate: select next value for product_SEQ
Hibernate: insert into product (priceInCents,sku,id) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: insert into product (priceInCents,sku,id) values (?,?,?)
Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.priceInCents,p1_0.sku from product p1_0 order by p1_0.sku
loaded [Product[1, BOLT-7, 80c], Product[2, NUT-3, 25c]]
Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.priceInCents,p1_0.sku from product p1_0 where p1_0.id=?
Hibernate: update product set priceInCents=?,sku=? where id=?
after reprice Product[1, BOLT-7, 90c]

Read the output as a transcript of what Hibernate did on your behalf, in order:

  1. create global temporary table HTE_product … — a scratch table Hibernate 7 prepares on H2 for bulk JPQL update and delete statements that touch several tables (§6). It appears at the top of every program in this module; it is harmless, and from here on the text will not mention it again.
  2. drop … / create sequence / create table — schema generation, because the configuration asked for drop-and-create. The column list came from the fields of Product: @Column supplied not null unique and varchar(16); the primitive int became not null on its own, because a primitive cannot hold null. Hibernate orders columns its own way; you did not write this DDL and should not rely on its shape (§10).
  3. create sequence product_SEQ start with 1 increment by 50 — the default for GenerationType.SEQUENCE is an allocation size of 50: Hibernate asks the database for one value and hands out fifty ids from it before asking again. That is why two persist calls produced only two select next value lines here — and why a thousand would produce twenty, not a thousand. §2 compares this with the other strategies.
  4. Two inserts, after both persist calls — persist does not write. It assigns the id, registers the object with the persistence context, and queues the insert; the queue is flushed at commit. §3 is entirely about that gap, and almost every surprise in Hibernate lives in it.
  5. select p1_0.id, … from product p1_0 order by p1_0.sku — the JPQL select p from Product p became SQL with Hibernate's own aliases. JPQL names entities and fields; the SQL names tables and columns. That translation is the whole job (§6).
  6. select … where p1_0.id=? then update product set priceInCents=?,sku=? where id=? — find loaded the row; reprice changed a field in memory; nothing in the program said "update". At commit Hibernate compared the entity's current state with a snapshot taken at load, found a difference, and wrote the row back. That is dirty checking. Note that it updated every column, not only the changed one — the default, and tunable (§9, §11).

What Hibernate holds
SQL sent

What JPA specifies, what Hibernate adds

Jakarta Persistence (JPA) is a specification: the annotations (@Entity, @Id, @OneToMany …), the EntityManager API, the query language JPQL, the Criteria API, the lifecycle rules and the exception hierarchy. Hibernate is the implementation almost everyone uses, and it has existed longer than the specification it implements; JPA was largely written by standardising what Hibernate already did. In practice you program against the JPA API and reach into Hibernate's own API when you need something the spec does not offer:

The JPA standard versus Hibernate-specific capabilities
Standard JPAHibernate-only (unwrap or annotate)
EntityManagerFactory, EntityManagerSessionFactory, Session — the same objects; em.unwrap(Session.class) gets the richer one
JPQLHQL — a superset: more functions, insert … select, with clauses, window functions
@GeneratedValue strategies@UuidGenerator styles, custom generators, @NaturalId with its own cache
@Version, LockModeType@OptimisticLocking(type = ALL), @DynamicUpdate, @SQLDelete, @SQLRestriction (§7, §11)
Entity graphs, FetchType@BatchSize, @Fetch(SUBSELECT), the Statistics API that counts statements (§5, §9)
Schema generation propertiesJDBC batching, ordered inserts/updates, StatelessSession, second-level cache integration (§9)

This module uses the JPA API wherever it exists and names every Hibernate-specific feature as such, so you know which parts would survive a switch to another provider — and which parts you would miss.

The architecture, in three objects

  • One EntityManagerFactory per application. Expensive to build (the stepper above), thread-safe, holds the metamodel, the dialect, the connection pool and the second-level cache. In a Spring application it is the bean behind every repository.
  • One EntityManager per unit of work. Cheap, not thread-safe, and the owner of a persistence context: the set of entities it currently manages. A web request, a message handler, a batch chunk — each gets its own, and closes it.
  • One transaction per unit of work, usually. Begun and committed explicitly here with EntityTransaction; in a container, declared with @Transactional and begun for you. Reads outside a transaction are allowed; writes without one are silently never flushed (§7).

When not to use an ORM

Hibernate is a tool for an object model that is persisted: a domain with identity, invariants and associations, where the same objects are loaded, changed and saved many times. It is the wrong tool when there is no such model:

  • Reporting and analytics. A query that joins six tables and groups by three columns does not want to become entities. Use a projection (§6), or skip the ORM and use a query builder such as jOOQ, which gives you type-safe SQL without pretending the result is an object graph.
  • Bulk operations. Updating a million rows through managed entities loads a million objects. Use a JPQL or native bulk statement (§6), or a StatelessSession (§9).
  • Very small applications. Three tables and ten queries are less code with Spring's JdbcClient than with an entity model, and far easier to reason about.

Most applications are a mixture: an ORM for the transactional core, plain SQL for the reports. Knowing where the line falls is a large part of what this module teaches.

The cost model: what you pay for not writing the SQL
  • SQL you did not write still runs. The update above wrote every column. A lazy collection you touched in a loop ran a query per iteration. Nothing is free because it is implicit; it is merely hidden. Keep show_sql on in development and read it, every time (§12).
  • The N+1 problem is the default outcome, not an edge case. Loading twenty orders and printing each one's lines is twenty-one queries unless you say otherwise (§5).
  • Flushes happen when Hibernate decides. Before a query that might see stale data, and at commit. An unexpected update in the middle of a read is usually a flush you did not plan for (§3).
  • The factory is slow to build and the first query is slow to run — metamodel, dialect probing, schema checks, query plan compilation. Measure a warm application, never the first request.
  • The database still has the last word. Constraints, indexes, isolation levels and locks are database facts. An ORM that lets you forget them has not made them go away.

Check yourself

1.In FirstEntity, two persist calls produced two insert statements — but only after both calls, at commit. Why?

C. This is the persistence context's write-behind behaviour: operations are collected in an action queue and flushed as late as possible so they can be ordered and batched. §3 shows exactly when a flush happens.

A confuses the database transaction with Hibernate's queue; the database executes each statement as it arrives. B is backwards — the sequence was consulted at each persist (two select next value lines appear before the inserts). D is invented: show_sql prints at execution time, which is exactly how you can tell that execution was deferred.

2.The program never contains the word update, yet an update product set … statement ran. Which mechanism produced it?

B. The snapshot comparison is why a managed entity needs no "save" call — and why it is dangerous to hand managed entities to code that mutates them casually: every change is a pending update.

A would mean a round trip per field assignment; nothing in the output shows that. C: Hibernate uses proxies for lazy loading, not for intercepting setters on an entity you constructed with new. D is false — unchanged entities produce no SQL at all, which is what makes loading a thousand products for a read cheap.

3.Which of these are good reasons to bypass the ORM for a particular piece of code? Select all that apply.

A and D. A read-only aggregate has no object model to manage, and a bulk move has no business passing through two million managed entities; both are SQL jobs (or a projection / bulk JPQL statement, §6).

B is the ORM's home ground: load, mutate, let dirty checking write the change, with optimistic locking for free (§7). C is far too broad — JPQL and the Criteria API join entities perfectly well, and join fetch is the standard fix for N+1 (§5).

Section 2

Mapping entities to tables

An entity is a class whose instances correspond to rows. The mapping says which class, which table, which field goes in which column with which type, and — the decision with the longest consequences — where the primary key comes from. Every annotation in this section is a sentence in that contract, and the generated DDL is the database's reading of it. The rules an entity class must obey come first, because Hibernate enforces them at bootstrap and the error messages assume you know them:

  • A no-argument constructor, at least protected. Hibernate instantiates the class reflectively when it loads a row, then sets the fields. The constructor you actually use can take whatever it likes.
  • Not final, and ideally no final methods: lazy loading (§5) works by subclassing the entity at runtime to make a proxy, and a final class cannot be subclassed.
  • Exactly one identifier — an @Id field (or an @EmbeddedId) — and it must not change once the row exists.
  • A top-level or static nested class. An inner class carries a hidden reference to its outer instance and cannot be instantiated without one.
  • Not a record. Records are final and immutable; an entity is neither, because Hibernate needs to set its id after insert and track changes to its fields. Records are the right type for everything an entity is not: projections, value objects passed around the application, API payloads (Intermediate §8, §11 here).

Worked example

One factory, three entities, three id strategies, and most of the column mappings you will ever need. Read the DDL Hibernate generated against the annotations that produced it — and watch where the inserts happen, because one of the three strategies changes when rows are written.

javaMapping.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.annotations.NaturalId;
 
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.UUID;
 
public class Mapping {
 
    enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, TOOLING }
 
    /** A value object stored inline in the owner's row: three columns, no identity, no table. */
    @Embeddable
    public static class Dimensions {
        private int widthMm, heightMm, depthMm;
        protected Dimensions() {}
        Dimensions(int w, int h, int d) { widthMm = w; heightMm = h; depthMm = d; }
        long volumeMm3() { return (long) widthMm * heightMm * depthMm; }
        @Override public String toString() { return widthMm + "x" + heightMm + "x" + depthMm + " mm"; }
    }
 
    /** A domain type the database never sees: the converter stores it as one bigint of cents. */
    record Money(long cents) {
        @Override public String toString() { return String.format("%d.%02d", cents / 100, cents % 100); }
    }
    @Converter(autoApply = true)
    public static class MoneyConverter implements AttributeConverter<Money, Long> {
        @Override public Long convertToDatabaseColumn(Money m) { return m == null ? null : m.cents(); }
        @Override public Money convertToEntityAttribute(Long cents) { return cents == null ? null : new Money(cents); }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    @Access(AccessType.FIELD)                                   // map fields, not getters
    public static class Product {
        @Id
        @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "product_seq")
        @SequenceGenerator(name = "product_seq", sequenceName = "product_seq", allocationSize = 10)
        private Long id;
 
        @NaturalId                                              // Hibernate: a business key with its own lookup
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16)
        private String sku;
 
        @Basic(optional = false)
        @Column(length = 80)
        private String name;
 
        @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)                            // never ORDINAL
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
        private Category category;
 
        @Column(name = "unit_price")
        private Money unitPrice;                                // MoneyConverter applies automatically
 
        @Column(precision = 8, scale = 3)
        private BigDecimal weightKg;
 
        @Embedded
        @AttributeOverride(name = "widthMm",  column = @Column(name = "dim_w_mm"))
        @AttributeOverride(name = "heightMm", column = @Column(name = "dim_h_mm"))
        @AttributeOverride(name = "depthMm",  column = @Column(name = "dim_d_mm"))
        private Dimensions dimensions;
 
        private LocalDate introducedOn;                         // java.time maps directly: no @Temporal
        private Instant createdAt;
 
        @Transient
        private String label;                                   // derived, never a column
 
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, String name, Category category, Money unitPrice, BigDecimal weightKg,
                Dimensions dimensions, LocalDate introducedOn, Instant createdAt) {
            this.sku = sku; this.name = name; this.category = category; this.unitPrice = unitPrice;
            this.weightKg = weightKg; this.dimensions = dimensions; this.introducedOn = introducedOn; this.createdAt = createdAt;
        }
        Long id() { return id; }
        String sku() { return sku; }
        Category category() { return category; }
        Money unitPrice() { return unitPrice; }
        BigDecimal weightKg() { return weightKg; }
        Dimensions dimensions() { return dimensions; }
        LocalDate introducedOn() { return introducedOn; }
        Instant createdAt() { return createdAt; }
        String label() {
            if (label == null) label = sku + " / " + name;      // computed on demand, cached in the object only
            return label;
        }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "Warehouse")
    @Table(name = "warehouse")
    public static class Warehouse {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)   // the database assigns the id at insert
        private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 40)
        private String name;
        protected Warehouse() {}
        Warehouse(String name) { this.name = name; }
        Long id() { return id; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "AuditEvent")
    @Table(name = "audit_event")
    public static class AuditEvent {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID)       // generated in the JVM, random
        private UUID id;
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 120)
        private String message;
        protected AuditEvent() {}
        AuditEvent(String message) { this.message = message; }
        UUID id() { return id; }
    }
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf(Class<?>... managed) {
        var cfg = new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:Mapping;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true");
        for (Class<?> c : managed) cfg.managedClass(c);
        return cfg.createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf(Product.class, Warehouse.class, AuditEvent.class, MoneyConverter.class)) {
 
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product bolt = new Product("BOLT-7", "M8 hex bolt", Category.FASTENER, new Money(80),
                        new BigDecimal("0.012"), new Dimensions(8, 8, 40),
                        LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 1), Instant.parse("2026-10-15T08:30:00Z"));
                Warehouse main = new Warehouse("Main");
                AuditEvent event = new AuditEvent("catalogue seeded");
                em.persist(bolt);
                em.persist(main);
                em.persist(event);
                System.out.println("ids before commit: product=" + bolt.id() + " warehouse=" + main.id()
                        + " audit assigned=" + (event.id() != null));
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
 
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                Product p = em.find(Product.class, 1L);
                System.out.println("category   = " + p.category());
                System.out.println("unitPrice  = " + p.unitPrice());
                System.out.println("weightKg   = " + p.weightKg());
                System.out.println("dimensions = " + p.dimensions() + " -> " + p.dimensions().volumeMm3() + " mm3");
                System.out.println("introduced = " + p.introducedOn() + ", createdAt kept = "
                        + p.createdAt().equals(Instant.parse("2026-10-15T08:30:00Z")));
                System.out.println("label      = " + p.label());
 
                Object[] raw = (Object[]) em.createNativeQuery(
                        "select category, unit_price, dim_w_mm from product where id = 1").getSingleResult();
                System.out.println("raw row    = " + raw[0] + " | " + raw[1] + " | " + raw[2]);
 
                Product bySku = em.createQuery("select p from Product p where p.sku = :sku", Product.class)
                        .setParameter("sku", "BOLT-7").getSingleResult();
                System.out.println("by sku     = same instance: " + (bySku == p));
            }
        }
    }
}

Reading the DDL against the annotations:

  • create table product (dim_d_mm integer, dim_h_mm integer, dim_w_mm integer, …) — the @Embeddable Dimensions became three columns in the owner's table, renamed by @AttributeOverride. There is no dimensions table; a value object has no identity and no row of its own. (The scratch HTE_ table ignores the overrides — it is internal, never yours.)
  • weightKg numeric(8,3) from @Column(precision = 8, scale = 3); createdAt timestamp(6) with time zone from a plain Instant field and introducedOn date from a LocalDate. The java.time types need no @Temporal; that annotation exists for the legacy java.util.Date, which is ambiguous about what it stores.
  • category enum ('FASTENER','STRUCTURAL','TOOLING') not null — H2 and PostgreSQL have native enum types and Hibernate 7 uses them; on MySQL this is also enum, on Oracle a varchar2 with a check constraint. Either way the name is stored, because of EnumType.STRING. The gotcha callout below explains why the alternative is a trap.
  • unit_price bigint — the Money record exists only in Java. The @Converter(autoApply = true) turns it into a long on the way out and back on the way in, for every entity that has a Money field, with no annotation at the field. The native query confirms the column really holds 80.
  • name varchar(80) not null came from @Basic(optional = false); sku … not null unique from @Column. Both are hints that become real constraints only because schema generation ran. In production the constraints must exist in the migration script too (§10): Hibernate never checks them on read, and a null in a not null column from some other writer is still a bug on its way to you.
  • No label column. @Transient fields are invisible to the mapping; the field is recomputed lazily in each loaded instance.

Now the three id strategies, which is where the output stops being a transcript of DDL and becomes a transcript of timing:

  • Product: SEQUENCE. create sequence product_seq … increment by 10, then one select next value at persist. The id is known immediately — product=1 prints before commit — but the insert can wait, so it would be batched with others (§9).
  • Warehouse: IDENTITY. The column is generated by default as identity and the insert sends default for the id. The database assigns it, and Hibernate must read it back before it can register the entity — so the insert runs at persist, not at commit. Look at the order of the output: the product insert, which was queued, was forced out before the warehouse insert to keep the two in program order. IDENTITY makes write-behind impossible for that entity, and makes insert batching impossible with it (§9).
  • AuditEvent: UUID. Generated in the JVM, random, assigned at persist with no database call at all; its insert waits for commit like the sequence-backed one. The value is random, so the program prints only audit assigned=true. Random UUIDs are convenient and terrible for index locality on large tables, as the sandbox explains.

Two last lines. The native query shows the raw row: the enum as text, the money as an integer, the embedded width as its own column. And the JPQL lookup by sku returned the same instance as find had — not an equal object, the same reference. That is the persistence context's identity guarantee, and §3 is about it.

What each id strategy costs

The identifier strategy is the mapping decision you cannot cheaply change later, because the key is in every foreign key. Pick the strategy and the database, and read the consequences.

How 100 inserts reach the database

The rest of the mapping vocabulary

Mapping annotations, what they do, and the default when omitted
AnnotationSaysIf you leave it out
@Table(name, schema, uniqueConstraints, indexes)Which table, and constraints/indexes for schema generationTable named after the entity, by the naming strategy
@Column(name, nullable, unique, length, precision, scale, insertable, updatable)Column name and DDL hints; updatable = false makes a field write-onceColumn named after the field; varchar(255) for strings
@Basic(optional, fetch)A plain column; optional = false → not null; fetch = LAZY is only honoured for large columns with bytecode enhancementImplied on every non-annotated field
@Enumerated(STRING)Store the constant's nameORDINAL — the position; see the gotcha
@LobLarge object: clob for String, blob for byte[]A bounded varchar/varbinary
@Embedded / @EmbeddableInline a value object's fields into this tableHibernate treats an unannotated class-typed field as an error
@Convert(converter = …)Apply an AttributeConverter to this field; autoApply = true on the converter makes it global for the typeOnly JDBC-known types map
@TransientNot persistent at allEvery field is a column
@Access(FIELD | PROPERTY)Read/write fields directly, or go through getters/settersDecided by where @Id sits — put it on the field
@NaturalId (Hibernate)A unique, immutable business key; gets its own cache region and lookup APIJust a unique column
@Formula("…") (Hibernate)A read-only attribute computed by a SQL expression in every selectCompute it in Java, or in a projection
@VersionThe optimistic-locking column (§7)Lost updates are silent

Naming. With no naming strategy configured, a field priceInCents becomes a column priceInCents, which most databases fold to PRICEINCENTS or quote awkwardly. Set hibernate.physical_naming_strategy to CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy and it becomes price_in_cents everywhere, with no @Column(name = …) on every field. Spring Boot does this by default, which is why Spring projects' tables look different from these.

Mapping gotchas
  • EnumType.ORDINAL is a time bomb. It stores 0, 1, 2. Insert a constant in the middle of the enum and every existing row silently means something else. STRING costs a few bytes and survives any reordering; renaming a constant is then a one-line migration you can see.
  • IDENTITY forces an early insert and disables batching. It is the right choice only when the database offers nothing else, or when writes are rare. On MySQL, where sequences do not exist, know that SEQUENCE silently becomes a table generator — check the DDL.
  • A random UUID key scatters the index. Each insert lands on a random page of the primary-key B-tree. Fine at thousands of rows, painful at hundreds of millions; time-ordered UUIDs fix it.
  • @Column hints are not validation. length = 16 becomes varchar(16) in generated DDL and nothing else: a longer string is rejected by the database, not by Hibernate, and only if the constraint actually exists. Validate in Java (Bean Validation integrates) and constrain in the schema.
  • Default varchar(255). Every unannotated String. Set a length deliberately, or use @Lob/columnDefinition = "text" for real text.
  • java.util.Date and Calendar need @Temporal and still lose the zone. Use Instant for a point in time, LocalDate for a calendar date, and store instants in UTC (Intermediate §12). Hibernate 7's hibernate.timezone.default_storage defaults to normalising to UTC.

Check yourself

1.In the worked example the insert into product ran before ids before commit was printed, even though the product uses SEQUENCE and inserts are normally deferred to commit. What forced it out early?

B. persist(main) on the IDENTITY-keyed Warehouse cannot complete without the database-generated id, so its insert executes at once — and Hibernate executes earlier queued inserts first rather than reorder them. The AuditEvent, persisted last, waited for commit as usual.

A: one id was used out of a block of ten. C: reading a field is plain Java; Hibernate does not intercept it. D: @NaturalId affects lookups and caching, not insert timing — uniqueness is checked by the database constraint whenever the insert runs.

2.A team stored Category with the default @Enumerated, then added PACKAGING between FASTENER and STRUCTURAL in the enum. What happens to existing rows?

C. The default is ORDINAL: the column holds a position, and positions shifted. No error anywhere — the data just means something different now. This is why EnumType.STRING is the rule.

A describes what you might wish ordinals did. B: Hibernate has no way to know what the numbers meant before. D is what STRING mapping does when a stored name no longer exists — loud, and therefore safe.

3.Which statements about @Embeddable are true? Select all that apply.

A and C. An embeddable is a value object: the Dimensions columns live in product, and the object is compared by its fields, never by a key. It is the ORM's answer to the granularity mismatch.

B describes a @OneToOne entity (§4). D is the opposite of the point: an embeddable with an @Id is a mapping error — if it needs identity it is an entity.

Section 3

The persistence context and the entity lifecycle

Everything surprising about JPA — the update you never wrote, the second find that hits no database, the change that silently vanished — comes from one object: the persistence context. An EntityManager owns one. It is two things at once: an identity map (for each primary key, at most one Java instance) and a snapshot store (a copy of every managed entity's state as it was loaded). Hibernate uses the first to answer loads from memory and the second to work out, at flush time, which rows changed and what SQL to emit for them. That second mechanism is called dirty checking, and it is why you never call an update method: there is none.

An entity instance is always in exactly one of four states relative to a context. Transient: a plain Java object the context has never seen, no row behind it. Managed: tracked by a context; changes to it will be written at flush. Detached: it has a row, but no context is watching it any more — the context was closed or the instance was evicted. Removed: scheduled for deletion at flush. Every EntityManager method you call is a transition between those states, and the worked example walks all of them.

Worked example: one entity, nine transitions

Read the Hibernate: lines as closely as the prose. Where SQL appears, and where it does not, is the lesson.

javaLifecycle.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
 
public class Lifecycle {
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16)
        private String sku;
        private int priceInCents;
 
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        String sku() { return sku; }
        int priceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
        void setPriceInCents(int p) { this.priceInCents = p; }
        @Override public String toString() { return "Product[" + id + ", " + sku + ", " + priceInCents + "c]"; }
    }
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf() {
        return new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(Product.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:Lifecycle;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true")
            .createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf()) {
 
            System.out.println("-- 1. persist: transient -> managed, insert deferred to commit --");
            Long id;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                Product bolt = new Product("BOLT-7", 80);
                System.out.println("managed before persist: " + em.contains(bolt));
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                em.persist(bolt);
                System.out.println("managed after persist:  " + em.contains(bolt) + ", id already assigned: " + (bolt.id() != null));
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                id = bolt.id();
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 2. find twice in one context: one select, one instance --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                Product a = em.find(Product.class, id);
                Product b = em.find(Product.class, id);
                System.out.println("same instance: " + (a == b));
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 3. dirty checking: a plain setter becomes an update at commit --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product p = em.find(Product.class, id);
                p.setPriceInCents(85);
                System.out.println("no SQL yet; committing...");
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 4. detach, then modify: nothing is written --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product p = em.find(Product.class, id);
                em.detach(p);
                p.setPriceInCents(999);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                System.out.println("managed after detach: " + em.contains(p));
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 5. merge a detached copy: select, then update; a different instance comes back --");
            Product detached;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                detached = em.find(Product.class, id);     // loaded, then the context closes
            }
            detached.setPriceInCents(90);                       // modified outside any context
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product merged = em.merge(detached);
                System.out.println("merged == detached: " + (merged == detached)
                        + ", detached managed: " + em.contains(detached) + ", merged managed: " + em.contains(merged));
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 6. refresh discards an in-memory change --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product p = em.find(Product.class, id);
                p.setPriceInCents(1);
                em.refresh(p);
                System.out.println("after refresh: " + p.priceInCents() + "c");
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 7. flush: SQL now, visible inside the same transaction --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                em.persist(new Product("NUT-3", 25));
                em.flush();
                Number rows = (Number) em.createNativeQuery("select count(*) from product").getSingleResult();
                System.out.println("rows visible after flush: " + rows);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 8. getReference: a proxy, no select until a field is read --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                Product ref = em.getReference(Product.class, id);
                System.out.println("is a proxy subclass: " + (ref.getClass() != Product.class));
                System.out.println("reading sku forces the load...");
                System.out.println("sku = " + ref.sku());
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 9. remove: delete at commit --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product p = em.find(Product.class, id);
                em.remove(p);
                System.out.println("still managed? " + em.contains(p));
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                System.out.println("find after remove: " + em.find(Product.class, id));
            }
        }
    }
}

Nine blocks, nine lessons:

  1. persist is not insert. The only SQL at persist time is select next value for product_SEQ — Hibernate must know the id to register the instance in the identity map, and a SEQUENCE strategy lets it get one without inserting. The insert itself waits for the flush at commit. (With IDENTITY the insert would have to happen immediately — §2 explains why that disables batching.)
  2. The identity map answers the second find. One select, two calls, a == b. Inside one context an entity is loaded at most once; this is the first-level cache, and it is scoped to the EntityManager, not the application.
  3. Dirty checking. A plain setter on a managed instance, no further API call, and an update appears at commit. Hibernate compared the instance against the snapshot it took at load time. Note that the update sets every column (priceInCents=?,sku=?), not just the changed one — §9 shows @DynamicUpdate for the cases where that matters.
  4. Detached means invisible. After detach, the setter runs on a plain object as far as the context is concerned. Commit writes nothing. This is the state every entity is in once its EntityManager closes — which is most of the time in a web application.
  5. merge copies, it does not adopt. Hibernate loads the current row (the first select; the second comes from find inside the previous block), copies the detached object's state onto the managed instance, and returns that managed instance. The object you passed in is still detached: merged == detached: false. Keep using the return value, never the argument.
  6. refresh is the opposite of flush. It overwrites the in-memory state from the database; the 1c is gone and 90c is back.
  7. flush forces the SQL now, but not the commit. The native count(*) runs in the same transaction and sees the new row. Hibernate would in fact have flushed automatically before that query: in FlushModeType.AUTO any JPQL or native query triggers a flush first, so queries never miss pending writes. The explicit call just makes the order visible.
  8. getReference returns a proxy. No select runs until sku() is called. Use it to set an association (line.setOrder(em.getReference(Order.class, id))) without loading the target. The class is a runtime subclass generated by ByteBuddy — which is why entity classes and their accessors must not be final.
  9. remove is deferred too. The instance leaves the context immediately (still managed? false) but the delete runs at commit. The find afterwards goes to the database — the context no longer holds the instance — and returns null.

Watch the context

Identity map, snapshot and action queue Simulated ← → to step
Source
Product bolt = new Product("BOLT-7", 80);   // transient
em.getTransaction().begin();
em.persist(bolt);                            // managed
bolt.setPriceInCents(85);                    // still managed, now dirty
Product again = em.find(Product.class, 1L);  // identity map hit
em.flush();                                  // SQL runs
em.detach(bolt);                             // detached
bolt.setPriceInCents(999);                   // nobody is watching
Product managed = em.merge(bolt);            // copy onto a managed instance
em.remove(managed);                          // removed
em.getTransaction().commit();                // flush + commit
Persistence context
SQL sent to the database

Which call moves an entity where?

Drag an operation onto the transition it causes, or click one then the other

All six correct. The two that trip people up are merge, which never changes the state of its argument, and remove, which takes the instance out of the context immediately even though the delete waits for the flush. clear() is detach for every managed instance at once — and it also discards the action queue, so un-flushed changes are lost.

Flushing: when the SQL actually runs

The context is write-behind: operations are queued and run together at flush. A flush happens at commit, when you call flush(), and — in the default FlushModeType.AUTO — just before any JPQL, Criteria or native query that might otherwise read stale data. (Hibernate is clever about JPQL: it flushes only if the query touches a table with pending changes. For native SQL it cannot know, so it flushes every time.) FlushModeType.COMMIT switches the automatic pre-query flush off; a query can then return rows that your own pending writes contradict, which is occasionally what a bulk job wants and usually a bug.

At flush, Hibernate does not replay your calls in order. It sorts the queue: all inserts, then updates, then collection removals and additions, then deletes. That order keeps foreign keys satisfied in the common cases, and it is why "I removed the old row and persisted a new one with the same unique key" fails with a constraint violation — the insert runs first. The fix is flush() between the two, or a different key design.

  • Takes a transient instance and makes that instance managed. Returns void; keep using your reference.
  • Passing a detached instance throws: PersistentObjectException: detached entity passed to persist. Hibernate knows it is detached because the id is already set (or, with @Version, the version is).
  • Passing an instance whose id already exists in the context throws EntityExistsException; if the row exists only in the database, the duplicate surfaces at flush as a constraint violation.
  • Cascades along CascadeType.PERSIST associations (§4).
  • Takes a detached (or transient) instance, loads the current row if it is not already in the context, copies the state across, and returns the managed copy. Your argument is untouched.
  • Because it copies every field, a detached object with a stale or missing field overwrites the database with that stale value. A form that binds only three columns of a ten-column entity and merges it is the classic data-loss bug. Load, then set the three fields, instead.
  • With a transient instance (no id) it behaves like persist but still returns a copy.
  • Cascades along CascadeType.MERGE.
Lifecycle exceptions, their cause and the fix
ExceptionYou didDo instead
PersistentObjectException "detached entity passed to persist"persist on an object that already has an idmerge, or load it and modify the managed instance
NonUniqueObjectExceptionTried to make a second instance with the same id managed (often via merge after a find of the same row)Use the instance the context already holds
TransientPropertyValueExceptionFlushed an entity that references a transient one with no cascadepersist the referenced object first, or add CascadeType.PERSIST
LazyInitializationExceptionTouched a lazy association on a detached instance§5: fetch it while the context is open, or project a DTO
IllegalStateException "EntityManager is closed"Used an EntityManager after its close() (or from another thread after it was closed there)One EntityManager per unit of work, per thread
Persistence-context gotchas
  • The context grows until you clear it. A loop that persists a million rows keeps a million managed instances and a million snapshots in memory, and every auto-flush dirty-checks all of them. Batch jobs flush() then clear() every few hundred rows (§9).
  • An EntityManager is not thread-safe. It is a unit-of-work object, not a connection pool. Share the EntityManagerFactory; create an EntityManager per request or job and close it.
  • The first-level cache can lie to you — within a transaction. If another transaction updates a row after you loaded it, your find keeps returning the old state. That is correct repeatable-read behaviour, and refresh is the way out when you need the latest.
  • "No SQL ran" is not "nothing happened". Changes sit in the queue. A test that asserts on a native query without flushing first reads stale data — or, with native SQL, triggers a flush you did not expect.
  • Modifying an entity outside a transaction on a managed instance in an open context queues an update that may never run (no commit) — or runs at the next transaction's flush, long after the line that caused it. Keep modifications inside transaction boundaries.

Check yourself

1.Inside one transaction you call em.find(Product.class, 1L), then em.find(Product.class, 1L) again. Meanwhile another transaction committed a price change to that row. What does the second find return?

C. The identity map already holds key 1, so find returns that instance without touching the database. The context gives you repeatable reads for free, and it has no idea the row changed.

A and B would both need a select, which the first-level cache exists to avoid; refresh is how you ask for it. D only happens at write time, and only with a @Version column (§7) — a read never checks versions.

2.A controller receives a detached Product from a form, calls Product m = em.merge(product);, then product.setPriceInCents(200); and commits. What is in the database?

B. merge copies state onto a managed instance and returns it; the argument stays detached (merged == detached: false in the worked example). The setter on product is invisible to the context, so the merged state — the form's price — is what gets flushed.

A is the mistake the question is about: use m. C is backwards — merge does queue an update of the copied state. D is what persist would throw for a detached instance; merge accepts them by design.

3.Which of these cause SQL to be sent before commit(), in the default FlushModeType.AUTO? Select all that apply.

A and D. flush() runs the queue on demand, and a JPQL query over a table with pending changes triggers an automatic flush so the query cannot miss them.

B: with SEQUENCE only select next value runs at persist; the insert waits (it would run immediately with IDENTITY, which is one reason to avoid that strategy). C: a setter changes a Java field; the context notices at flush, not at the call.

Section 4

Relationships and the owning side

A relational database stores a relationship in exactly one place: a foreign-key column, or a row in a join table. An object graph stores it in two — order.getLines() and line.getOrder() are both references, and nothing forces them to agree. JPA bridges that gap with a rule that explains most relationship bugs: one side owns the column, and only writes to the owning side reach the database. The other side, marked mappedBy, is the inverse side: Hibernate loads it, iterates it, cascades through it, but never consults it when deciding what to write.

For @ManyToOne / @OneToMany the owning side is always the many side, because that is the table holding the foreign key — an order_line row has one order_id; an orders row has nowhere to put a list. For @ManyToMany neither table has the key; the side that declares @JoinTable owns the join table. For @OneToOne you choose: the side with @JoinColumn owns the key, and @MapsId lets the dependent row reuse the parent's primary key instead of adding a second column.

Worked example: five associations, and the bug in block 1

Block 1 does what every beginner does — adds the line to the order's list and persists both — and the database quietly stores a line that belongs to nobody. Block 2 fixes it with a two-line helper. The rest of the program maps a many-to-many, a shared-key one-to-one, orphan removal and cascading delete, and shows the SQL each one costs.

javaRelationships.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;
 
public class Relationships {
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16)
        private String sku;
 
        // many-to-many: THIS side owns the join table because it declares @JoinTable
        @ManyToMany
        @JoinTable(name = "product_supplier",
                   joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "product_id"),
                   inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "supplier_id"))
        private Set<Supplier> suppliers = new HashSet<>();
 
        // one-to-one, inverse side: the FK (shared primary key) lives in product_details
        @OneToOne(mappedBy = "product", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
        private ProductDetails details;
 
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        String sku() { return sku; }
        Set<Supplier> suppliers() { return suppliers; }
        void addSupplier(Supplier s) { suppliers.add(s); s.products.add(this); }
        void setDetails(ProductDetails d) { this.details = d; d.product = this; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "Supplier")
    @Table(name = "supplier")
    public static class Supplier {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true)
        private String name;
        @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "suppliers")                // inverse: never written from here
        private Set<Product> products = new HashSet<>();
        protected Supplier() {}
        Supplier(String name) { this.name = name; }
        String name() { return name; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "ProductDetails")
    @Table(name = "product_details")
    public static class ProductDetails {
        @Id
        private Long id;                                   // no @GeneratedValue: copied from product
        @OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
        @MapsId                                            // "my primary key IS the product's primary key"
        @JoinColumn(name = "product_id")
        private Product product;
        private String description;
        protected ProductDetails() {}
        ProductDetails(String description) { this.description = description; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        String description() { return description; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "Order")
    @Table(name = "orders")                                // ORDER is a reserved word in SQL
    public static class Order {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        private String reference;
 
        // inverse side: the FK order_id lives in order_line, so this side is mappedBy
        @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
        private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
 
        protected Order() {}
        Order(String reference) { this.reference = reference; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        List<OrderLine> lines() { return lines; }
 
        // the sync helper: sets BOTH sides, so the owning side gets written
        void addLine(OrderLine line) { lines.add(line); line.order = this; }
        void removeLine(OrderLine line) { lines.remove(line); line.order = null; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "OrderLine")
    @Table(name = "order_line")
    public static class OrderLine {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)                 // optional by default, so a line CAN exist with no order
        @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")                     // owning side: this column IS the relationship
        private Order order;
        private String sku;
        private int qty;
        protected OrderLine() {}
        OrderLine(String sku, int qty) { this.sku = sku; this.qty = qty; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        String sku() { return sku; }
    }
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf() {
        return new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(Product.class).managedClass(Supplier.class).managedClass(ProductDetails.class)
            .managedClass(Order.class).managedClass(OrderLine.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:Relationships;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true")
            .createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    static long count(EntityManager em, String sql) {
        return ((Number) em.createNativeQuery(sql).getSingleResult()).longValue();
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf()) {
 
            System.out.println("-- 1. setting only the inverse side: the FK is never written --");
            Long orphanOrderId;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Order o = new Order("WRONG-1");
                OrderLine line = new OrderLine("BOLT-7", 10);
                o.lines().add(line);                       // inverse side only: line.order stays null
                em.persist(o);
                em.persist(line);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                orphanOrderId = o.id();
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                System.out.println("order_line rows with order_id null: " + count(em, "select count(*) from order_line where order_id is null"));
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 2. the sync helper sets the owning side: FK written, lines cascaded --");
            Long orderId;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Order o = new Order("ORD-1");
                o.addLine(new OrderLine("BOLT-7", 10));
                o.addLine(new OrderLine("NUT-3", 40));
                o.addLine(new OrderLine("CAM-9", 1));
                em.persist(o);                             // cascade = ALL persists the lines too
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                orderId = o.id();
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                System.out.println("order_line rows for ORD-1: " + count(em, "select count(*) from order_line where order_id = " + orderId));
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 3. orphanRemoval: dropping a line from the collection deletes the row --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Order o = em.find(Order.class, orderId);
                OrderLine cam = o.lines().stream().filter(l -> l.sku().equals("CAM-9")).findFirst().orElseThrow();
                o.removeLine(cam);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                System.out.println("lines left: " + count(em, "select count(*) from order_line where order_id = " + orderId));
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 4. many-to-many: the @JoinTable side writes the join rows --");
            Long boltId;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Supplier acme = new Supplier("Acme Fasteners");
                Supplier zeta = new Supplier("Zeta Metals");
                Product bolt = new Product("BOLT-7");
                bolt.addSupplier(acme);
                bolt.addSupplier(zeta);
                em.persist(acme); em.persist(zeta); em.persist(bolt);   // no cascade on many-to-many
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                boltId = bolt.id();
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                Product bolt = em.find(Product.class, boltId);
                Set<String> names = new TreeSet<>();
                for (Supplier s : bolt.suppliers()) names.add(s.name());
                System.out.println("suppliers of BOLT-7: " + names);
                System.out.println("join rows: " + count(em, "select count(*) from product_supplier"));
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 5. one-to-one with @MapsId: the details row reuses the product's id --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product bolt = em.find(Product.class, boltId);
                bolt.setDetails(new ProductDetails("M8 hex bolt, zinc plated"));
                em.getTransaction().commit();              // cascade ALL on the one-to-one persists it
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                ProductDetails d = em.find(ProductDetails.class, boltId);
                System.out.println("details id == product id: " + d.id().equals(boltId) + ", " + d.description());
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- 6. cascade REMOVE: deleting the order deletes its lines first --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                em.remove(em.find(Order.class, orderId));
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                System.out.println("order_line rows left: " + count(em, "select count(*) from order_line"));
            }
        }
    }
}
