Reading the schema first: order_line.order_id is nullable because the @ManyToOne is optional by default — that is what lets block 1 store an orphan instead of failing. Add optional = false and the column becomes not null, block 1 fails at flush with PropertyValueException, and every join Hibernate generates for the association becomes an inner join instead of a left join. Prefer that whenever the business rule really is "a line always belongs to an order". Then the six blocks:

  1. The inverse side is ignored for writes. o.lines().add(line) changes the Java object only. Hibernate inserts the line from its state — and line.order is null — so the foreign key is null. No error, no warning: a row that no order will ever find.
  2. The helper sets both sides. addLine writes line.order = this, the owning side, and the FK is populated. cascade = ALL also means em.persist(o) reaches the three lines; the three inserts follow the order's. Note order_id = 2: block 1's order took id 1.
  3. orphanRemoval turns "no longer in the collection" into delete. Removing CAM-9 from the list produces exactly one delete from order_line where id=?. Without orphanRemoval, the same code would leave the row in place with order_id nulled — because a List element disappearing is not, by itself, a deletion.
  4. Many-to-many rows come from the @JoinTable side. addSupplier adds to Product.suppliers (owning) and Supplier.products (inverse); only the first matters for the two product_supplier inserts. Look at the find(Product) afterwards: it also runs a select … from product_details. That lazy @OneToOne(mappedBy) on the inverse side cannot be lazy — Hibernate must know whether to put null or a proxy in the field, and the only way to know is to query. The gotcha callout covers the fix.
  5. @MapsId shares the primary key. product_details has no id of its own; its product_id is both primary key and foreign key, so d.id().equals(boltId). Hibernate copied the parent's id when it persisted the dependent entity through the cascade.
  6. Cascade REMOVE orders the deletes correctly. Lines first, then the order, so the foreign key constraint never complains. The surviving row is block 1's orphan — the database kept it because nothing references it.

Which side did you set?

What Hibernate writes for the sides you set

Cascade and orphan removal, chosen deliberately

Cascade types and when each is appropriate
SettingWhat propagatesUse it forNever for
CascadeType.PERSISTpersist reaches the associated entitiesChildren that exist only as part of the parent (order lines, address of a customer)Shared references — a Product referenced by many lines must be persisted once, on its own
CascadeType.MERGEmerge copies the whole graphDetached aggregates edited as a unitGraphs containing entities the user did not load — stale copies overwrite fresh rows
CascadeType.REMOVEremove deletes the associated entities tooComposition: the child has no meaning without the parent@ManyToMany — it deletes the other side's entity, not just the join row; and @ManyToOne, which would delete the shared parent
CascadeType.ALLAll of the above plus REFRESH and DETACHParent-owned children, which is where orphanRemoval usually joins itAnything that is not strictly owned
orphanRemoval = trueRemoving an element from the collection, or setting a one-to-one to null, deletes the rowCollections that are the parent's state — the same cases as REMOVEReassigning a child to a different parent (it gets deleted, then re-inserted; with a List you may get a constraint violation in between)

A List without @OrderColumn is what Hibernate calls a bag: unordered, duplicates allowed, and — because the database cannot tell two equal rows apart — some changes are implemented by deleting every row and re-inserting the survivors. Removing one element from a 500-element bag on the owning side of a @ManyToMany is 1 delete-all plus 499 inserts. A Set can address rows individually and emits one delete. Two bags also cannot be join fetched together (§5).

  • Set for @ManyToMany and for any collection you will join fetch alongside another.
  • List + @OrderColumn(name = "position") when order is part of the data (steps in a recipe). Hibernate maintains the column — at the cost of updating every later row on an insert in the middle.
  • List with @OrderBy("sku") only sorts on load; it is still a bag for writes. Fine for a mappedBy side with cascaded children, which is the case in the worked example.

A @OneToMany with no @ManyToOne on the other side and no @JoinColumn has nowhere to put the foreign key, so Hibernate invents a join table (orders_order_line) and maintains it with extra inserts and deletes — a surprise in the DDL and a tax on every write. Add @JoinColumn(name = "order_id") to the collection to put the key where you expected it; better, make the association bidirectional and let the many side own it, which is the mapping the database actually wants.

Default fetch type per association kind
AssociationDefaultRecommended
@ManyToOneEAGERLAZY, always — the default is the single most common cause of accidental joins
@OneToOneEAGERLAZY on the owning (@JoinColumn / @MapsId) side; the mappedBy side cannot be lazy without bytecode enhancement
@OneToManyLAZYKeep it
@ManyToManyLAZYKeep it
Relationship gotchas
  • The inverse @OneToOne is eager whatever you write. Block 4 proves it: find(Product) also selected product_details. Hibernate cannot create a proxy for a field that might legitimately be null without querying. Fixes: map the association only from the dependent side (drop Product.details), use @MapsId on the owning side so the parent's id is the key (then Hibernate can proxy), or enable bytecode enhancement.
  • Never put a @ManyToOne entity in equals/hashCode of the child — a lazy proxy's class is not the entity's class, and comparing it loads it. And never add an entity to a HashSet before its id is generated if hashCode uses the id: the hash changes after persist and the set can no longer find it (§11).
  • Cascading REMOVE through a @ManyToMany deletes the supplier when you delete the product. Nothing in the mapping warns you.
  • Bidirectional sync is your job. Forgetting the inverse side will not corrupt the database (only the owning side is written) but it will give you an in-memory order that does not list its own lines until reloaded — and a test that passes against the database while the object graph is wrong.
  • @JoinColumn names default to field_referencedId. Without it the column is order_id only because the field is order; rename the field and the schema changes. Always name the column.

Check yourself

1.In a bidirectional Order – OrderLine mapping, which side is the owning side, and why?

B. The owning side is the side that maps the physical column. A one-row-per-line foreign key can only live in order_line, so OrderLine.order owns the relationship and Order.lines must be mappedBy.

A and D confuse ownership with cascade — cascade decides which operations propagate, not which side is written. C is invented; ownership is fixed in the mapping, not by call order.

2.Product has @ManyToMany(cascade = CascadeType.ALL) Set<Supplier> suppliers. You call em.remove(product). What happens to Acme Fasteners, a supplier that also supplies forty other products?

C. REMOVE cascades to the entity on the other side, not to the join rows. Hibernate queues delete from supplier; whether that succeeds depends only on the database's constraints. Either outcome is wrong, which is why cascade REMOVE (and therefore ALL) has no place on a many-to-many.

A is what happens without cascade — Hibernate always cleans this product's join rows. B: Hibernate does not check for other references; the database might. D: cascade applies to every association type.

3.Which statements about orphanRemoval = true on Order.lines are correct? Select all that apply.

A and C. Orphan removal watches the collection: an element that leaves it is deleted. That is also why re-parenting is risky — the removal schedules a delete even though another order now references the line.

B: REMOVE cascades a remove call on the parent; it does nothing when an element merely leaves the collection. The two are complementary, not equal. D: without orphan removal, and with the many side owning the key, removing from the inverse collection changes nothing in the database — the line's own order field still points at the order. Only the sync helper's line.order = null would null the column.

Section 5

Fetching: lazy, eager and the N+1 problem

When Hibernate loads an Order, what happens to its lines? The mapping says LAZY for collections by default, so Hibernate puts a proxy collection in the field: an object that knows which order it belongs to and nothing else. The first time you call size(), iterator() or get(0) on it, it runs a select … where order_id = ? and fills itself. That is exactly right for one order. For a list of five hundred orders in a loop it is one query for the list and five hundred more for the lines — the N+1 problem, the single most common performance bug in JPA applications, and one you cannot see in the code because every line of it looks innocent.

The cure is never "make it eager". fetch = EAGER on the mapping changes how every load behaves, forever, including the loads that did not need the lines, and (as the sandbox shows) does not even remove the extra statements for JPQL queries. The cure is to decide per query what the query needs and fetch that in one or two statements: join fetch, an entity graph, or batch fetching. This section measures all three against the problem with Hibernate's own statistics, so the numbers are facts rather than folklore.

Worked example: counting statements

Five orders, three lines each. The report in totalQty is the same every time; only the fetch plan changes. hibernate.generate_statistics lets the program count prepared statements, and the Hibernate: lines show what they were.

javaNPlusOne.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.stat.Statistics;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
 
public class NPlusOne {
 
    @Entity(name = "Order")
    @Table(name = "orders")
    public static class Order {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        private String reference;
        @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL)   // lazy by default
        private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
        protected Order() {}
        Order(String reference) { this.reference = reference; }
        List<OrderLine> lines() { return lines; }
        void addLine(OrderLine l) { lines.add(l); l.order = this; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "OrderLine")
    @Table(name = "order_line")
    public static class OrderLine {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
        @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")
        private Order order;
        private String sku;
        private int qty;
        protected OrderLine() {}
        OrderLine(String sku, int qty) { this.sku = sku; this.qty = qty; }
        int qty() { return qty; }
    }
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf() {
        return new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(Order.class).managedClass(OrderLine.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:NPlusOne;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true")
            .property("hibernate.generate_statistics", "true")
            .createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    // the "report": walks every order's lines — touching lines() initialises the collection
    static int totalQty(List<Order> orders) {
        int total = 0;
        for (Order o : orders) for (OrderLine l : o.lines()) total += l.qty();
        return total;
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf()) {
            Statistics stats = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
 
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
                    Order o = new Order("ORD-" + i);
                    o.addLine(new OrderLine("BOLT-7", i));
                    o.addLine(new OrderLine("NUT-3", i * 2));
                    o.addLine(new OrderLine("CAM-9", 1));
                    em.persist(o);
                }
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- A. lazy default: 1 query for the orders, then 1 per order for its lines --");
            stats.clear();
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                List<Order> orders = em.createQuery("select o from Order o order by o.id", Order.class).getResultList();
                System.out.println("total qty: " + totalQty(orders) + ", statements: " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- B. join fetch: one query, lines arrive with their orders --");
            stats.clear();
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                List<Order> orders = em.createQuery(
                        "select o from Order o join fetch o.lines order by o.id", Order.class).getResultList();
                System.out.println("orders: " + orders.size() + " (no duplicates: Hibernate 6+ de-duplicates root entities)");
                System.out.println("total qty: " + totalQty(orders) + ", statements: " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- C. entity graph: the same plan, declared instead of written into the query --");
            stats.clear();
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                EntityGraph<Order> graph = em.createEntityGraph(Order.class);
                graph.addAttributeNodes("lines");
                List<Order> orders = em.createQuery("select o from Order o order by o.id", Order.class)
                                       .setHint("jakarta.persistence.fetchgraph", graph)
                                       .getResultList();
                System.out.println("total qty: " + totalQty(orders) + ", statements: " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
            }
 
            System.out.println("-- D. batch fetching (size 10): 1 + ceil(5/10) queries --");
            stats.clear();
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.unwrap(Session.class).setFetchBatchSize(10);   // same effect as @BatchSize(size = 10) on the mapping
                List<Order> orders = em.createQuery("select o from Order o order by o.id", Order.class).getResultList();
                System.out.println("total qty: " + totalQty(orders) + ", statements: " + stats.getPrepareStatementCount());
            }
        }
    }
}

total qty: 50, statements: 2

Before the four phases, notice the seeding: fifteen separate insert statements, each its own round trip. §9 turns those into two batched statements. Now the phases, same report, same answer of 50 every time:

  • A — six statements. One for the orders, then the loop touches o.lines() five times and the proxy collection runs its select … where order_id=? each time. With 500 orders it would be 501. The cost is round trips, not rows: each query is tiny, and that is what makes N+1 invisible in a local test and ruinous over a network.
  • B — one statement. join fetch o.lines tells Hibernate to pull the lines in the same query. Fifteen result rows come back (each order repeated per line) and Hibernate assembles five Order objects with their collections already initialised. Since Hibernate 6 the duplicates are removed automatically; the old select distinct idiom is unnecessary and would only push a pointless DISTINCT to the database.
  • C — one statement, as a plan rather than a query. An entity graph says "when you run this query, also fetch lines". The query text stays reusable and the SQL is the same join — a left join this time, because a fetch graph must not drop orders that have no lines, whereas join fetch is an inner join unless you write left join fetch.
  • D — two statements. Batch fetching leaves the collection lazy but, when the first one is touched, loads it for up to ten orders at once with where order_id in (?, …). For 500 orders that is 1 + 50 statements, no cartesian product, and no change to the query. The ten placeholders are padded (Hibernate rounds the batch to a fixed size so the database can cache the plan) even though only five ids exist.

The exception you will meet first

A lazy collection needs its context to load itself. Close the EntityManager, keep the entity, touch the collection:

javaLazyInit.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
 
public class LazyInit {
 
    @Entity(name = "Order")
    @Table(name = "orders")
    public static class Order {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        private String reference;
        @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL)
        private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
        protected Order() {}
        Order(String reference) { this.reference = reference; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        List<OrderLine> lines() { return lines; }
        void addLine(OrderLine l) { lines.add(l); l.order = this; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "OrderLine")
    @Table(name = "order_line")
    public static class OrderLine {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
        @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")
        private Order order;
        private String sku;
        protected OrderLine() {}
        OrderLine(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        EntityManagerFactory emf = new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(Order.class).managedClass(OrderLine.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:LazyInit;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true")
            .createEntityManagerFactory();
 
        Long id;
        try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
            em.getTransaction().begin();
            Order o = new Order("ORD-1");
            o.addLine(new OrderLine("BOLT-7"));
            em.persist(o);
            em.getTransaction().commit();
            id = o.id();
        }
 
        Order detached;
        try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
            detached = em.find(Order.class, id);          // lines is an uninitialised proxy collection
        }                                                 // the context that owned it is now closed
 
        System.out.println("order loaded, context closed; touching lines() ...");
        System.out.println("lines: " + detached.lines().size());   // LazyInitializationException escapes here
        emf.close();
    }
}

Standard error
Exception in thread "main" org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException: Cannot lazily initialize collection of role 'LazyInit$Order.lines' with key '1' (no session)

The message names the collection role and the key, and the cause is always the same: the entity outlived its context. In a web application that context is usually the service method's transaction, and the touch happens later, in the view. The tempting fix is open session in view — keep the EntityManager open until the response is written — and it is a trap: it hides the exception while leaving every one of those lazy loads in place, now running N+1 from the template with a database connection pinned for the whole request. The real fixes are to fetch what the view needs inside the service (join fetch, entity graph) or to return a DTO that already contains it (§6, §9).

Plan a fetch

How many statements will this plan cost?

Choosing between the fixes

Fetch strategies compared
StrategyStatementsWhere it is declaredBest forWatch out
join fetch1The JPQL queryLoading one aggregate (an order and its lines) or a small list with one collectionTwo List collections → MultipleBagFetchException; two Sets → cartesian product. Pagination (setMaxResults) with a fetched collection is done in memory, with a warning.
Entity graph1@NamedEntityGraph on the entity, or built at runtime; applied as a query hint or a find optionThe same query used by several screens that need different parts of the graphfetchgraph treats everything not listed as lazy (even EAGER mappings); loadgraph adds to the mapping's defaults. Same cartesian caveat as join fetch.
@BatchSize / setFetchBatchSize1 + ⌈N / size⌉ per collectionThe mapping, the class, or the sessionLists where every row shows a collection; several collections at once (no cartesian product)Loads whole batches of collections even when the loop stops early. Padded in (…) lists.
@Fetch(SUBSELECT)1 + 1 per collectionThe mapping (Hibernate-specific)A query whose result's collections are always all neededLoads every collection of the original result the moment one is touched; re-runs the original query as a subquery.
DTO projection1The query's select new … or TupleRead-only screens — most of themNo entities, so no dirty checking and no lazy anything; that is the point (§6).
Fetching gotchas
  • EAGER is a mapping-level decision you cannot undo per query. A @ManyToOne left at its EAGER default drags the parent into every load of the child, and a chain of them (line → order → customer → account) loads half the schema for a find. Mark every @ManyToOne and @OneToOne LAZY and fetch deliberately.
  • EAGER does not even help JPQL. Only em.find turns an eager association into a join; a JPQL query runs the extra selects immediately after the main query instead — the same N+1, just without the loop.
  • A proxy is not the entity. ref.getClass() is a generated subclass, instanceof works but a pattern match on the concrete class fails, and Hibernate.unproxy(ref) or Hibernate.isInitialized(ref) are the tools when you must know. Also: accessing the proxy's id does not trigger a load — Hibernate knows the key — but any other getter does.
  • Pagination plus join fetch = in-memory paging. Hibernate cannot apply LIMIT to a joined result without truncating a collection, so it fetches everything and pages in Java, logging HHH90003004. Page the parents first, then batch-fetch the collections.
  • Lazy loading in toString, equals or a JSON serialiser is how N+1 and LazyInitializationException arrive from code you did not write. Keep associations out of toString, and never hand an entity to a serialiser; serialise a DTO.

Check yourself

1.A page lists 200 orders and shows each order's line count. The service runs select o from Order o and the template calls order.getLines().size() inside a transaction. How many SQL statements run?

C. The textbook N+1: size() initialises the proxy collection, which selects the lines for that one order. The worked example's phase A is this at N = 5.

A would need join fetch or an entity graph. B is what batch fetching with a size ≥ 200, or @Fetch(SUBSELECT), would give. D: size() loads the whole collection, not a count (Hibernate's @LazyCollection(EXTRA) once did a count and is deprecated); and the orders still cost one query.

2.You add fetch = FetchType.EAGER to Order.lines to fix that page. The page now runs select o from Order o again. What changed?

B. For a JPQL query, an eager collection is honoured by issuing the secondary selects immediately — the statement count does not drop. And because the setting lives on the mapping, a find(Order.class, id) on a checkout page that never shows lines now joins them in as well.

A is only what em.find does for eager associations. C: the query is legal. D: subselect fetching is an explicit Hibernate annotation, never a default.

3.An Order has List<OrderLine> lines and List<Note> notes, both lazy. A screen needs both for 50 orders. Which approaches work without an exception and without a cartesian product? Select all that apply.

B and D. Batch fetching loads each collection in in (…) chunks — three statements for 50 orders — with no joins to multiply. Two queries in one context also work: the second query's fetched notes attach to the Order instances the identity map already holds.

A throws MultipleBagFetchException: cannot simultaneously fetch multiple bags — two Lists cannot be joined in one result. C runs, but every order row is repeated lines × notes times: 50 orders with 10 of each is 5,000 rows for 1,050 useful ones, and it gets worse quadratically.

Section 6

JPQL, the Criteria API and native SQL

find() gets you one row by primary key. Everything else — a filtered list, a report, a page of results, a bulk price change — needs a query, and JPA gives you three ways to write one. JPQL is a query language over entities and their attributes: you name Product and p.priceInCents, never the table or the column, and Hibernate translates to the SQL of whatever database it is talking to. The Criteria API builds the same query from Java objects, which is the right tool when the shape of the query depends on which filters a user filled in. Native SQL is the escape hatch for the one query per project that genuinely needs a database-specific feature.

The mental model that keeps JPQL from feeling like "SQL with the keywords moved": a JPQL query walks the object graph. l.product.sku is a path through a @ManyToOne, and Hibernate turns the path into a join for you. o.lines is empty is a predicate on a collection, and Hibernate turns it into a not exists subquery. You describe what you want in terms of the model from §2 and §4; the SQL below each query in the worked example is what that description became.

Worked example

One factory, three entities, eleven queries. The order with no lines (initech) is there on purpose: it is what makes left join and is empty show their difference from their inner-join cousins. Every Hibernate: line is the SQL this program actually sent to H2.

javaQueries.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
 
public class Queries {
 
    public enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, MOTION }
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    @NamedQuery(name = "Product.bySku", query = "select p from Product p where p.sku = :sku")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16)
        private String sku;
        @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) @Column(nullable = false, length = 16)
        private Category category;
        private int priceInCents;
 
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, Category category, int priceInCents) {
            this.sku = sku; this.category = category; this.priceInCents = priceInCents;
        }
        String sku() { return sku; }
        int priceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "@" + priceInCents + "c"; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "PurchaseOrder")                 // "Order" is an SQL keyword; name the entity and table safely
    @Table(name = "purchase_order")
    public static class PurchaseOrder {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 32)
        private String customer;
        @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL)
        private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
 
        protected PurchaseOrder() {}
        PurchaseOrder(String customer) { this.customer = customer; }
        PurchaseOrder add(Product p, int qty) { lines.add(new OrderLine(this, p, qty)); return this; }
        String customer() { return customer; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "OrderLine")
    @Table(name = "order_line")
    public static class OrderLine {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false) @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")
        private PurchaseOrder order;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false) @JoinColumn(name = "product_id")
        private Product product;
        private int qty;
 
        protected OrderLine() {}
        OrderLine(PurchaseOrder order, Product product, int qty) { this.order = order; this.product = product; this.qty = qty; }
    }
 
    /** A DTO for projections: the query instantiates it directly, no entity is hydrated. */
    public record SkuRevenue(String sku, long cents) {}
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf() {
        return new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(Product.class).managedClass(PurchaseOrder.class).managedClass(OrderLine.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:Queries;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true")
            .createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    static void seed(EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
            em.getTransaction().begin();
            Product bolt = new Product("BOLT-7", Category.FASTENER, 80);
            Product nut  = new Product("NUT-3",  Category.FASTENER, 25);
            Product gird = new Product("GIRD-1", Category.STRUCTURAL, 120_000);
            Product cam  = new Product("CAM-9",  Category.MOTION, 2_300);
            for (Product p : List.of(bolt, nut, gird, cam)) em.persist(p);
            em.persist(new PurchaseOrder("acme").add(bolt, 100).add(nut, 400));
            em.persist(new PurchaseOrder("globex").add(bolt, 50).add(gird, 1));
            em.persist(new PurchaseOrder("initech"));                       // an order with no lines
            em.getTransaction().commit();
        }
    }
 
    static void section(String title) { System.out.println("-- " + title + " --"); }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf()) {
            seed(emf);
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
 
                section("named parameter");
                List<Product> dear = em.createQuery(
                        "select p from Product p where p.priceInCents > :min order by p.sku", Product.class)
                    .setParameter("min", 1_000).getResultList();
                System.out.println(dear);
 
                section("join + aggregate + having + DTO projection");
                List<SkuRevenue> revenue = em.createQuery(
                        "select new Queries$SkuRevenue(p.sku, sum(l.qty * p.priceInCents)) " +
                        "from OrderLine l join l.product p " +
                        "group by p.sku having sum(l.qty) >= :minQty order by p.sku", SkuRevenue.class)
                    .setParameter("minQty", 100L).getResultList();
                System.out.println(revenue);
 
                section("left join: products that were never ordered still appear");
                List<Object[]> counts = em.createQuery(
                        "select p.sku, count(l) from Product p left join OrderLine l on l.product = p " +
                        "group by p.sku order by p.sku", Object[].class).getResultList();
                for (Object[] row : counts) System.out.println(row[0] + " ordered on " + row[1] + " line(s)");
 
                section("pagination");
                List<Product> page2 = em.createQuery("select p from Product p order by p.sku", Product.class)
                    .setFirstResult(2).setMaxResults(2).getResultList();
                System.out.println(page2);
 
                section("in with a list parameter");
                System.out.println(em.createQuery(
                        "select p from Product p where p.sku in :skus order by p.sku", Product.class)
                    .setParameter("skus", List.of("NUT-3", "CAM-9")).getResultList());
 
                section("collection predicates: is empty, size()");
                System.out.println(em.createQuery(
                        "select o.customer from PurchaseOrder o where o.lines is empty", String.class).getResultList());
                System.out.println(em.createQuery(
                        "select o.customer from PurchaseOrder o where size(o.lines) = 2 order by o.customer", String.class).getResultList());
 
                section("named query, single result, result stream");
                Product bolt = em.createNamedQuery("Product.bySku", Product.class)
                    .setParameter("sku", "BOLT-7").getSingleResult();
                System.out.println("single = " + bolt);
                long cheap = em.createQuery("select p from Product p", Product.class)
                    .getResultStream().filter(p -> p.priceInCents() < 100).count();
                System.out.println("cheap via stream = " + cheap);
 
                section("bulk update bypasses the persistence context");
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                int changed = em.createQuery(
                        "update Product p set p.priceInCents = p.priceInCents + 5 where p.category = :c")
                    .setParameter("c", Category.FASTENER).executeUpdate();
                System.out.println("rows updated = " + changed);
                System.out.println("managed copy still says " + bolt.priceInCents() + "c");
                em.refresh(bolt);
                System.out.println("after refresh " + bolt.priceInCents() + "c");
                em.getTransaction().commit();
 
                section("native SQL");
                List<Object[]> raw = em.createNativeQuery(
                        "select sku, priceInCents from product where category = 'FASTENER' order by sku", Object[].class)
                    .getResultList();
                for (Object[] row : raw) System.out.println(row[0] + " " + row[1]);
 
                section("Criteria API: a dynamic filter");
                System.out.println(find(em, Category.FASTENER, null));
                System.out.println(find(em, null, 2_000));
 
                section("Criteria API: construct projection");
                CriteriaBuilder cb = em.getCriteriaBuilder();
                CriteriaQuery<SkuRevenue> cq = cb.createQuery(SkuRevenue.class);
                Root<OrderLine> l = cq.from(OrderLine.class);
                Join<OrderLine, Product> p = l.join("product");
                cq.select(cb.construct(SkuRevenue.class, p.get("sku"), cb.sum(cb.prod(l.<Integer>get("qty"), p.<Integer>get("priceInCents")))))
                  .groupBy(p.get("sku"))
                  .orderBy(cb.asc(p.get("sku")));
                System.out.println(em.createQuery(cq).getResultList());
            }
        }
    }
 
    /** Predicates are added only for the filters the caller supplied — no string concatenation. */
    static List<Product> find(EntityManager em, Category category, Integer minPrice) {
        CriteriaBuilder cb = em.getCriteriaBuilder();
        CriteriaQuery<Product> cq = cb.createQuery(Product.class);
        Root<Product> p = cq.from(Product.class);
        List<Predicate> where = new ArrayList<>();
        if (category != null) where.add(cb.equal(p.get("category"), category));
        if (minPrice != null) where.add(cb.ge(p.get("priceInCents"), minPrice));
        cq.select(p).where(where.toArray(new Predicate[0])).orderBy(cb.asc(p.get("sku")));
        return em.createQuery(cq).getResultList();
    }
}

Reading the SQL, query by query

  • Named parameter. :min became a JDBC ?. The value travels separately from the SQL text, so the database can cache one plan for every price, and a value that happens to contain a quote cannot change the query. Never build a JPQL string with + sku + "'"; that is the SQL-injection bug with an extra layer of paint.
  • Join, aggregate, having, DTO. join l.product p became join product p1_0 on p1_0.id=ol1_0.product_id — Hibernate knew the foreign key from the @ManyToOne mapping. select new Queries$SkuRevenue(…) handed each row straight to the record's constructor: no Product entity was loaded, nothing became managed, and the result is a plain immutable value you can return from a service without a lazy-loading worry. The class name in select new is the binary name, hence the $ for a nested record.
  • Left join with on. count(l) became count(ol1_0.id), which counts 0 for CAM-9 because its joined columns are all null. An inner join would have dropped the row; a path like p.lines would have required a mapped collection. The explicit on clause (JPA 2.1) lets you join two entities that have no mapped association between them.
  • Pagination. setFirstResult(2).setMaxResults(2) became offset ? rows fetch first ? rows only — the SQL:2008 form, chosen by the H2 dialect; MySQL would get limit ?,?. Pagination without an order by is a bug: the database is free to return pages in any order, and the same row can appear on two pages.
  • in :skus. The list was expanded to in (?,?) — one placeholder per element, bound in order. A list of a different length is a different SQL string, which matters for the database's plan cache when callers pass lists of wildly varying sizes.
  • Collection predicates. o.lines is empty became not exists(select 1 …) and size(o.lines) = 2 became a correlated (select count(*) …) = 2. Neither loaded a single OrderLine; the database answered the question about the collection.
  • Named query, single result, stream. @NamedQuery is parsed and validated once, at factory start-up, so a typo fails at boot rather than at 3 a.m. getSingleResult() throws NoResultException on zero rows and NonUniqueResultException on two; for a lookup that may miss, prefer getResultList() or Hibernate's uniqueResultOptional(). The stream example is a trap shown deliberately: filter(p -> p.priceInCents() < 100) ran in Java after every product had been loaded — look at the SQL, it has no where. Filter in the query, not in the stream.
  • Bulk update. One update product … where category=? changed two rows without loading either. The price is the point of the next three lines: bolt was loaded earlier in this same persistence context, and it still says 80c, because a bulk statement talks to the database directly and the first-level cache (§3) is never told. refresh() re-reads the row. In the Criteria filter further down, NUT-3 prints as 25c for the same reason: the query returned the row, but the identity guarantee handed back the already-managed instance with its stale field. Bulk operations belong at the start of a transaction, or in one of their own.
  • Native SQL. Tables and columns, verbatim, sent as written. The default column name for priceInCents is priceInCents — Hibernate's default naming strategy copies the field name; a CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy would make it price_in_cents, and a native query is the first thing that breaks when someone changes the strategy.
  • Criteria, dynamic filter. find(em, FASTENER, null) and find(em, null, 2_000) produced two different where clauses from one method and zero string concatenation. That is what the Criteria API is for. The second query, construct(…), is the typed twin of select new; note Hibernate aliased the columns c0, c1 and ordered by position.

What a fragment of JPQL turns into

Drag a JPQL fragment onto the SQL it produces, or click one then the other

All four correct. The first is a fetch join: it changes what is loaded, not what is returned, and §5 shows why it is the standard cure for N+1. The middle two push a question about a collection down to the database. The last avoids the persistence context entirely.

Projections, pages, native SQL and hints

Kinds of query result
You selectYou getManaged?Use when
select p from Product pList<Product>yesyou will modify the rows, or need lazy associations later
select p.sku, p.priceInCents …List<Object[]>noquick scalar reads; brittle — a reordered select list changes the indexes
the same, with Tuple.classList<Tuple>, access by aliasnoscalar reads with names instead of indexes
select new pkg.Dto(…) or Criteria constructList<Dto>noread-only views, API responses, reports — the default for anything you do not update

Hibernate 6+ also instantiates a record or a class with a matching constructor when you pass it as the result type without select new: createQuery("select p.sku, p.priceInCents from Product p", SkuPrice.class). It is convenient and non-standard; select new is the portable spelling.

setFirstResult / setMaxResults become the dialect's offset and limit syntax, and they are the only correct way to page: loading everything and calling subList is a memory bomb with a delay fuse.

The trap is paginating a fetch join. select o from PurchaseOrder o join fetch o.lines returns one SQL row per line, so a database-side limit of 10 rows is not 10 orders. Hibernate refuses to guess: it loads the whole result set and pages in memory, logging HHH90003004: firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory. Page the parent ids first, then fetch the collections for that page in a second query, or use @BatchSize (§5).

Keyset pagination — where (placedOn, id) > (:lastDate, :lastId) order by placedOn, id — is what large tables need; offset pagination re-reads every skipped row.

A native query is sent verbatim, so it can use anything the database has: window functions, jsonb operators, recursive CTEs, vendor hints. The cost is portability and the fact that Hibernate cannot validate it at start-up.

// scalars: List<Object[]>
em.createNativeQuery("select sku, priceInCents from product where category = :c", Object[].class)
  .setParameter("c", "FASTENER").getResultList();
 
// entities: Hibernate maps the columns by name onto the entity — they ARE managed
em.createNativeQuery("select * from product where priceInCents > 1000", Product.class).getResultList();
 
// a DTO via @SqlResultSetMapping(name = "skuRevenue",
//     classes = @ConstructorResult(targetClass = SkuRevenue.class,
//               columns = { @ColumnResult(name = "sku"), @ColumnResult(name = "cents", type = Long.class) }))
em.createNativeQuery("select p.sku as sku, sum(l.qty * p.priceInCents) as cents from order_line l " +
                     "join product p on p.id = l.product_id group by p.sku", "skuRevenue").getResultList();

Parameters work exactly as in JPQL; never concatenate. A native update bypasses the persistence context just like a JPQL bulk update, with the same staleness consequence.

  • setHint("org.hibernate.readOnly", true) — Hibernate skips the dirty-checking snapshot for the loaded entities: less memory, no accidental UPDATE. §9 uses it for reports.
  • setHint("org.hibernate.fetchSize", 500) — the JDBC fetch size for getResultStream(), so a million-row export does not load a million rows at once (driver-dependent; PostgreSQL also needs a transaction).
  • setHint("jakarta.persistence.query.timeout", 5000) — milliseconds before the driver cancels the statement.
  • setHint("jakarta.persistence.fetchgraph", graph) — an entity graph (§5) decides what to fetch eagerly for this one query.

The static metamodel (Product_.sku, Product_.priceInCents), generated at compile time by hibernate-jpamodelgen, replaces the string p.get("sku") in Criteria queries with a typed, refactoring-safe reference. Any Criteria query longer than a few lines should use it; this module's examples use strings only because they must compile from a single file.

Query mistakes that pass code review
  • Filtering in Java. getResultList().stream().filter(…) loads every row to throw most away. If the predicate can be said in JPQL, say it there.
  • Implicit joins in the where clause. where l.product.category = :c is fine; select l.product from OrderLine l is an implicit inner join that silently drops lines whose product is null. Write the join you mean.
  • Bulk update, then trusting managed entities. Shown above: the entities are stale until refresh() or clear(). Hibernate's Statistics will not warn you.
  • Pagination without order by. Pages overlap and skip. Order by something unique — add the id as a tiebreaker.
  • Building JPQL with string concatenation for optional filters. It works until the day two filters are both null and you ship where and. The Criteria API exists for exactly this.
  • getSingleResult() for a lookup that may miss. NoResultException is an unchecked exception that also marks the transaction for rollback in a container. Use getResultList() and check isEmpty(), or getResultStream().findFirst().

Check yourself

1.A colleague writes em.createQuery("select p from Product p where p.sku = '" + sku + "'"). What is wrong with it?

B. JPQL is translated to SQL and sent to the database, so a value containing ' or '1'='1 rewrites the query exactly as it would in raw SQL. Even with trusted input, each distinct string is a distinct statement that must be parsed and planned; a :sku parameter gives one plan for every value.

A is the dangerous belief that makes this bug common. C is false: literals are legal, which is why the code compiles and runs. D misses that a quote, not a space, is the problem — and that the plan-cache cost applies to every value.

2.Inside a transaction, bolt is a managed Product at 80c. You run em.createQuery("update Product p set p.priceInCents = p.priceInCents + 5").executeUpdate(). What does bolt.priceInCents() return immediately afterwards?

B. The worked example printed exactly this: managed copy still says 80c. A bulk JPQL or native update is executed as one SQL statement; Hibernate does not know which managed objects it touched and does not try to find out. refresh(bolt) or clear() is on you.

A describes what people expect and is why the bug is subtle. C is wrong: nothing throws, which is the whole problem. D is wrong too: commit flushes dirty entities to the database, it never pulls database changes into entities — and if bolt were dirty, its stale 80 would overwrite the 85.

3.Which of these produce no managed entities? Select all that apply.

A and C. A constructor projection and a scalar projection both return values that are not entities; the persistence context is neither consulted nor populated, and nothing will be dirty-checked at flush.

B returns entities, which are managed. D is the one people miss: a native query whose result type is an entity class maps the columns onto managed entities exactly like a JPQL query would — it is only the text that bypasses Hibernate, not the result handling.

Section 7

Transactions, flushing and locking

§3 said that a managed entity's changes reach the database "at flush". This section is about when that is, what a transaction has to do with it, and what happens when two users change the same row. The short version: a transaction is a unit of work — a set of changes that either all become visible to other users or none do — and the persistence context queues your writes until the latest safe moment inside it. Locking is how you decide what "safe" means when a second transaction is editing the same stock level at the same time.

Worked example 1: when SQL is actually sent

Four small transactions. Read the SQL interleaved with the printed lines: the position of each insert and update relative to the println around it is the point.

javaFlushing.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
 
public class Flushing {
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16)
        private String sku;
        private int priceInCents;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        void setPriceInCents(int c) { priceInCents = c; }
        @Override public String toString() { return "Product[" + id + ", " + sku + ", " + priceInCents + "c]"; }
    }
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf() {
        return new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(Product.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:Flushing;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true")
            .createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    static long rowsInDatabase(EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {          // a fresh context: sees only committed rows
            return ((Number) em.createNativeQuery("select count(*) from product").getSingleResult()).longValue();
        }
    }
 
    static void section(String title) { System.out.println("-- " + title + " --"); }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf()) {
 
            section("1. a query flushes pending writes first, then rollback undoes them");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                EntityTransaction tx = em.getTransaction();
                tx.begin();
                Product bolt = new Product("BOLT-7", 80);
                em.persist(bolt);                                            // no SQL yet: only scheduled
                System.out.println("persisted, id already assigned = " + bolt.id());
                long seen = em.createQuery("select count(p) from Product p", Long.class).getSingleResult();
                System.out.println("count inside the transaction = " + seen);
                tx.rollback();
                System.out.println("after rollback, em.contains(bolt) = " + em.contains(bolt));
            }
            System.out.println("rows committed = " + rowsInDatabase(emf));
 
            section("2. FlushModeType.COMMIT: the query does NOT see the pending insert");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.setFlushMode(FlushModeType.COMMIT);
                EntityTransaction tx = em.getTransaction();
                tx.begin();
                em.persist(new Product("NUT-3", 25));
                long seen = em.createQuery("select count(p) from Product p", Long.class).getSingleResult();
                System.out.println("count inside the transaction = " + seen);
                tx.commit();                                                 // the insert happens here
            }
            System.out.println("rows committed = " + rowsInDatabase(emf));
 
            section("3. dirty checking: a changed field becomes an UPDATE at flush");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                EntityTransaction tx = em.getTransaction();
                tx.begin();
                Product nut = em.createQuery("select p from Product p where p.sku = 'NUT-3'", Product.class).getSingleResult();
                nut.setPriceInCents(30);                                     // no em call at all
                System.out.println("field changed, nothing written yet");
                tx.commit();                                                 // flush compares snapshot → UPDATE
                System.out.println("committed " + nut);
            }
 
            section("4. a failure marks the transaction rollback-only");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                EntityTransaction tx = em.getTransaction();
                tx.begin();
                em.persist(new Product("CAM-9", 2_300));
                try {
                    if (true) throw new IllegalStateException("price feed unavailable");
                } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
                    tx.setRollbackOnly();
                    System.out.println("caught '" + e.getMessage() + "', rollbackOnly = " + tx.getRollbackOnly());
                }
                try {
                    tx.commit();
                    System.out.println("commit() returned normally: Hibernate rolled back instead of committing");
                } catch (RollbackException e) {
                    System.out.println("commit refused: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
                }
                System.out.println("tx.isActive() = " + tx.isActive());
            }
            System.out.println("rows committed = " + rowsInDatabase(emf));
        }
    }
}
Expected output

-- 2. FlushModeType.COMMIT: the query does NOT see the pending insert --

count inside the transaction = 0
Hibernate: insert into product (priceInCents,sku,id) values (?,?,?)

rows committed = 1
-- 3. dirty checking: a changed field becomes an UPDATE at flush --
Hibernate: select p1_0.id,p1_0.priceInCents,p1_0.sku from product p1_0 where p1_0.sku='NUT-3'
field changed, nothing written yet
Hibernate: update product set priceInCents=?,sku=? where id=?
committed Product[2, NUT-3, 30c]
-- 4. a failure marks the transaction rollback-only --
caught 'price feed unavailable', rollbackOnly = true

Hibernate: select count(*) from product
rows committed = 1
  1. A query flushes first. persist() obtained an id from the sequence immediately (ids are assigned at persist, not at flush) but sent no insert. The count query did: Hibernate's default FlushModeType.AUTO flushes pending changes before any query that might see them, so your own transaction never reads a stale answer. Then rollback() undid the insert at the database and evicted bolt from the context — a rolled-back entity is detached, and reusing it is a bug.
  2. FlushModeType.COMMIT defers everything. The same query now counts 0: the insert waited for commit(). Use this mode for a transaction that does many reads and one write at the end, when you can prove the reads do not depend on the write; it saves flush-time dirty checks on every query.
  3. Dirty checking. No em call touched nut, yet an update went out at commit. Hibernate kept a snapshot of the row when it loaded it and compared field by field at flush. Notice the SQL: set priceInCents=?,sku=? — every column, not just the changed one, because Hibernate caches one UPDATE statement per entity. @DynamicUpdate changes that at the cost of a statement per distinct change set.
  4. Rollback-only. After setRollbackOnly(), commit() did not commit — CAM-9 never reached the database — but it also did not throw. That is Hibernate's historical behaviour; the JPA specification says commit() on a rollback-only transaction throws RollbackException, and you get that by setting hibernate.jpa.compliance.transaction=true. In a container (Spring, Jakarta EE) the container does the equivalent and throws. Either way, never assume a returned commit() means "written" without checking the flag.

Flush order and the transaction boundary

At flush, Hibernate does not replay your calls in order. It sorts: all inserts (in persist order, respecting foreign-key dependencies), then all updates, then collection changes, then all deletes. This is why a remove() followed by a persist() of a row with the same unique key can fail with a constraint violation — the insert runs first. hibernate.order_inserts and hibernate.order_updates go further and group statements by entity type, which §9 needs for JDBC batching.

The boundary matters as much as the order. Code that runs after commit() but still uses the entities — sending an email with order.getLines(), say — works until the first lazy association, which throws LazyInitializationException because the context is closed (§5). And code that does side effects inside the transaction — calling a payment gateway before commit — can charge the card and then roll back the order. Do external calls after a successful commit, driven by what was committed.

Isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent
Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom readTypical default
READ_UNCOMMITTEDpossiblepossiblepossible—
READ_COMMITTEDpreventedpossiblepossiblePostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, H2
REPEATABLE_READpreventedpreventedpossible*MySQL/InnoDB
SERIALIZABLEpreventedpreventedprevented— (opt in, expect retries)

JPA sets no isolation level; you get the connection's default (hibernate.connection.isolation overrides it). Within one persistence context you have repeatable reads anyway, because a second find() of the same id is served from the first-level cache without touching the database. *InnoDB's gap locks prevent most phantoms.

Worked example 2: two pickers, one row

The classic lost update: two users read stock of 10, one picks 1 and writes 9, the other picks 2 and writes 8. The first pick has vanished. @Version is the JPA cure, and the SQL shows exactly how it works.

javaOptimisticLock.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
 
public class OptimisticLock {
 
    @Entity(name = "StockLevel")
    @Table(name = "stock_level")
    public static class StockLevel {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16)
        private String sku;
        private int onHand;
        @Version
        private long version;                    // Hibernate owns this field: never set it yourself
 
        protected StockLevel() {}
        StockLevel(String sku, int onHand) { this.sku = sku; this.onHand = onHand; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        int onHand() { return onHand; }
        long version() { return version; }
        void pick(int qty) { onHand -= qty; }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + " onHand=" + onHand + " v" + version; }
    }
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf() {
        return new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(StockLevel.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:OptimisticLock;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true")
            .createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    static void section(String title) { System.out.println("-- " + title + " --"); }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf()) {
            Long id;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                StockLevel s = new StockLevel("BOLT-7", 10);
                em.persist(s);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                id = s.id();
                System.out.println("seeded " + s);
            }
 
            section("two pickers load the same row");
            EntityManager picker1 = emf.createEntityManager();
            EntityManager picker2 = emf.createEntityManager();
            picker1.getTransaction().begin();
            picker2.getTransaction().begin();
            StockLevel copy1 = picker1.find(StockLevel.class, id);
            StockLevel copy2 = picker2.find(StockLevel.class, id);
            System.out.println("picker1 sees " + copy1);
            System.out.println("picker2 sees " + copy2);
 
            section("picker1 commits first: UPDATE ... where id=? and version=?");
            copy1.pick(1);
            picker1.getTransaction().commit();
            System.out.println("picker1 committed " + copy1);
 
            section("picker2 commits on a stale version");
            copy2.pick(2);
            try {
                picker2.getTransaction().commit();
                System.out.println("(unreachable)");
            } catch (RollbackException e) {
                System.out.println("commit failed: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()
                    + " caused by " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
            }
            picker1.close();
            picker2.close();
 
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                System.out.println("database row is " + em.find(StockLevel.class, id)
                    + " (picker1's write survived, picker2's was refused, nothing was lost)");
            }
 
            section("OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT: bump the version on a read");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                StockLevel s = em.find(StockLevel.class, id, LockModeType.OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                System.out.println("after commit " + s);
            }
 
            section("PESSIMISTIC_WRITE: the database locks the row until commit");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                StockLevel s = em.find(StockLevel.class, id, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE);
                s.pick(3);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                System.out.println("after commit " + s);
            }
        }
    }
}
Expected output

Hibernate: drop table if exists stock_level cascade

Hibernate: create sequence stock_level_SEQ start with 1 increment by 50
Hibernate: create table stock_level (onHand integer not null, id bigint not null, version bigint not null, sku varchar(16) not null unique, primary key (id))
Hibernate: select next value for stock_level_SEQ
Hibernate: insert into stock_level (onHand,sku,version,id) values (?,?,?,?)

-- two pickers load the same row --
Hibernate: select sl1_0.id,sl1_0.onHand,sl1_0.sku,sl1_0.version from stock_level sl1_0 where sl1_0.id=?
Hibernate: select sl1_0.id,sl1_0.onHand,sl1_0.sku,sl1_0.version from stock_level sl1_0 where sl1_0.id=?
picker1 sees BOLT-7 onHand=10 v0
picker2 sees BOLT-7 onHand=10 v0
-- picker1 commits first: UPDATE ... where id=? and version=? --
Hibernate: update stock_level set onHand=?,sku=?,version=? where id=? and version=?
picker1 committed BOLT-7 onHand=9 v1
-- picker2 commits on a stale version --
Hibernate: update stock_level set onHand=?,sku=?,version=? where id=? and version=?
commit failed: RollbackException caused by OptimisticLockException
Hibernate: select sl1_0.id,sl1_0.onHand,sl1_0.sku,sl1_0.version from stock_level sl1_0 where sl1_0.id=?
database row is BOLT-7 onHand=9 v1 (picker1's write survived, picker2's was refused, nothing was lost)
-- OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT: bump the version on a read --
Hibernate: select sl1_0.id,sl1_0.onHand,sl1_0.sku,sl1_0.version from stock_level sl1_0 where sl1_0.id=?
Hibernate: update stock_level set version=? where id=? and version=?
after commit BOLT-7 onHand=9 v2
-- PESSIMISTIC_WRITE: the database locks the row until commit --
Hibernate: select sl1_0.id,sl1_0.onHand,sl1_0.sku,sl1_0.version from stock_level sl1_0 where sl1_0.id=? for update
Hibernate: update stock_level set onHand=?,sku=?,version=? where id=? and version=?
after commit BOLT-7 onHand=6 v3
  • The version column is just a column (version bigint not null) that Hibernate includes in every UPDATE's where: where id=? and version=?, with set version=? incrementing it. Picker 1's update matched 1 row (version 0 → 1). Picker 2's update, sent with the stale version=0, matched 0 rows, and Hibernate turned "0 rows updated" into OptimisticLockException, wrapped in RollbackException because it happened during commit. The database row shows picker 1's write; no update was silently overwritten.
  • What to do with the exception is a business decision, not a technical one. Re-read the row and retry the pick (stock is now 9, so picking 2 still works), or tell the user "someone else just changed this". What you cannot do is catch it and carry on with the same EntityManager: after the exception the context is in an undefined state and must be closed.
  • OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT bumped the version with an update … set version=? even though nothing else changed. Use it when reading a parent while editing its children, so that two users editing different lines of the same order still conflict — the version on the parent becomes the version of the aggregate.
  • PESSIMISTIC_WRITE appended for update to the select: the database locked the row until commit, so a second transaction's find with the same lock would wait instead of fail. This program could not show the waiting (a blocked second transaction would stall the build); the behaviour is that jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout milliseconds later the waiter gets PessimisticLockException (or LockTimeoutException, which does not roll back the transaction).

Watch the version check

a.pick(1);
