Choosing a locking strategy

  • The field may be int, long, their wrappers, or a timestamp (Instant, LocalDateTime). Prefer an integer: timestamps have clock resolution and clock-skew problems.
  • Never set, increment or expose a setter for it. Hibernate manages it; a mapped version that your code changes defeats the check.
  • Cost: one extra column and an extra predicate on each update. No locks, no waiting, no deadlocks — conflicts are detected, not prevented. Right for web applications where conflicts are rare and users can retry.
  • Hibernate-only alternative for legacy tables without a version column: @OptimisticLocking(type = OptimisticLockType.DIRTY) with @DynamicUpdate puts every changed column's old value in the where clause.
  • OPTIMISTIC lock mode (without FORCE_INCREMENT) re-checks the version at commit even if you did not modify the entity — for reads that must not have been overtaken.
  • PESSIMISTIC_WRITE → select … for update: exclusive row lock until commit. Readers using plain selects are not blocked on MVCC databases (PostgreSQL, Oracle, MySQL/InnoDB), only other lockers.
  • PESSIMISTIC_READ → for share where the dialect has it: others may read and share-lock, none may write.
  • PESSIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT → locks and bumps @Version, for combining both schemes.
  • Set jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout (ms) as a hint or property; 0 means nowait on databases that support it. Without a timeout, a forgotten lock holder stalls everyone.
  • Lock rows in a consistent order (by id, by SKU — Advanced §3's rule in SQL clothing) or the database will detect a deadlock and kill one transaction with an exception you must handle.
  • Right for short, high-contention operations where a retry would be worse than a short wait: decrementing stock at checkout, allocating the next invoice number.

A user opens an edit form, goes to lunch, and saves at 2 p.m. No database transaction can span that — a connection held open for an hour is a connection the pool has lost. The pattern is detached entities with versions: load the entity in one short transaction, close the context, let the user edit the detached object (or a DTO carrying the version), and in a second short transaction merge() it back. Because the detached object still carries version=0, the merge's UPDATE … where version=0 fails if anyone else saved in between — the lost update is caught across an hour and two transactions. Hidden form fields carrying the version are not a hack; they are the mechanism.

What does not work: an EntityManager kept open across requests ("extended persistence context") outside a very controlled container-managed setup, and copying the version into a fresh entity by hand.

Transaction mistakes that cost real money
  • Side effects before commit. Charging a card, sending an email, calling another service inside the transaction: if the commit then fails, the side effect is already done. Do them after commit, from a record of what committed.
  • Catching an exception and continuing with the same context. Any exception from flush, commit or a query leaves the persistence context undefined. Roll back, close it, start again.
  • Reading the entity after rollback(). It is detached; its ids may refer to rows that were never committed.
  • Assuming commit() throws. Shown above: with Hibernate's defaults a rollback-only transaction rolls back quietly. Check getRollbackOnly() or turn on hibernate.jpa.compliance.transaction.
  • Pessimistic locks without timeouts, or in inconsistent order. A hung request becomes a hung system.
  • A @Version field with a setter. The first "helpful" refactoring that copies all fields from a DTO will write it and silently disable the check.

Check yourself

1.In worked example 1, why does an insert appear before the select count SQL in the first transaction, when the code called persist and then ran the query?

A. FlushModeType.AUTO (the default) flushes before executing a query whose result could be affected by pending changes. Section 2 of the same program proves the other half: with FlushModeType.COMMIT the same query counted 0 and the insert moved to commit().

B is false for SEQUENCE ids — the program printed the assigned id with no insert yet; only IDENTITY ids force an immediate insert (§2). C confuses the database with the ORM; H2 counts whatever is there. D is wrong: the transaction stayed open and was rolled back afterwards, undoing the insert.

2.Two transactions load the same StockLevel (version 3). The first changes it and commits. The second changes it and commits. With @Version mapped, what happens to the second commit?

B. That is the mechanism in worked example 2: the second session's where id=? and version=? carries the stale version, matches nothing, and Hibernate converts the unexpected row count into an exception. Nothing is overwritten.

A is what happens without @Version at the common isolation levels. C describes pessimistic locking (for update), which was not requested. D does not exist: Hibernate has no idea which of two conflicting values is right, and does not guess.

3.Which of these prevent the lost-update problem on a stock row? Select all that apply.

A and B. Optimistic locking detects the conflict at commit; pessimistic locking prevents it by making the second reader wait for the first writer. They solve the same problem with opposite trade-offs — retries versus waiting.

C only changes when within the transaction the write is sent; both transactions still write unconditionally. D concerns id generation and has nothing to do with concurrent updates of an existing row.

Section 8

Inheritance mapping

Tables do not inherit. A relational schema has no way to say "a CardPayment is a Payment with two extra columns", so when your Java model has a hierarchy — Intermediate §9's sealed Discount family, a Payment with card and bank-transfer variants — something has to decide how the hierarchy is laid out as rows. JPA offers three layouts, plus a fourth option that is not a layout at all. Each one is a real trade-off between normalisation, query cost and constraints, and the choice is visible in every statement Hibernate generates afterwards.

Worked example

Three small hierarchies, one per strategy, in a single factory so that the DDL for all of them appears together. Read the create table lines first, then the polymorphic queries.

javaInheritanceMapping.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.List;
 
public class InheritanceMapping {
 
    /** Not an entity: its columns are copied into every entity table that extends it. */
    @MappedSuperclass
    public static abstract class Auditable {
        @Column(nullable = false)
        protected LocalDate createdOn = LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 15);
    }
 
    // ── SINGLE_TABLE: one table, a discriminator column, nullable subclass columns ──
    @Entity(name = "Discount")
    @Table(name = "discount")
    @Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.SINGLE_TABLE)
    @DiscriminatorColumn(name = "kind", length = 8)
    public static abstract class Discount extends Auditable {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        protected Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 16)
        protected String code;
        protected Discount() {}
        Discount(String code) { this.code = code; }
        abstract long apply(long cents);
        @Override public String toString() { return getClass().getSimpleName() + "(" + code + ")"; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "PercentOff") @DiscriminatorValue("PCT")
    public static class PercentOff extends Discount {
        private Integer percent;                 // Integer, not int: the column must be nullable for other kinds
        protected PercentOff() {}
        PercentOff(String code, int percent) { super(code); this.percent = percent; }
        int percent() { return percent; }
        @Override long apply(long cents) { return cents - cents * percent / 100; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "FixedOff") @DiscriminatorValue("FIX")
    public static class FixedOff extends Discount {
        private Integer offCents;
        protected FixedOff() {}
        FixedOff(String code, int offCents) { super(code); this.offCents = offCents; }
        @Override long apply(long cents) { return Math.max(0, cents - offCents); }
    }
 
    // ── JOINED: one table per class, subclass tables share the parent's primary key ──
    @Entity(name = "Payment")
    @Table(name = "payment")
    @Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.JOINED)
    public static abstract class Payment {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        protected Long id;
        protected long amountCents;
        protected Payment() {}
        Payment(long amountCents) { this.amountCents = amountCents; }
        @Override public String toString() { return getClass().getSimpleName() + "(" + amountCents + "c)"; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "CardPayment") @Table(name = "card_payment")
    public static class CardPayment extends Payment {
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 4)
        private String last4;                    // NOT NULL is possible: the column lives in its own table
        protected CardPayment() {}
        CardPayment(long amountCents, String last4) { super(amountCents); this.last4 = last4; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "BankTransfer") @Table(name = "bank_transfer")
    public static class BankTransfer extends Payment {
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 34)
        private String iban;
        protected BankTransfer() {}
        BankTransfer(long amountCents, String iban) { super(amountCents); this.iban = iban; }
    }
 
    // ── TABLE_PER_CLASS: one complete table per concrete class, polymorphic reads are a UNION ──
    @Entity(name = "Shipment")
    @Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.TABLE_PER_CLASS)
    public static abstract class Shipment {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)   // IDENTITY is impossible here: ids must be unique ACROSS tables
        protected Long id;
        protected int weightKg;
        protected Shipment() {}
        Shipment(int weightKg) { this.weightKg = weightKg; }
        @Override public String toString() { return getClass().getSimpleName() + "(" + weightKg + "kg)"; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "ParcelShipment") @Table(name = "parcel_shipment")
    public static class ParcelShipment extends Shipment {
        private String carrier;
        protected ParcelShipment() {}
        ParcelShipment(int weightKg, String carrier) { super(weightKg); this.carrier = carrier; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "FreightShipment") @Table(name = "freight_shipment")
    public static class FreightShipment extends Shipment {
        private int pallets;
        protected FreightShipment() {}
        FreightShipment(int weightKg, int pallets) { super(weightKg); this.pallets = pallets; }
    }
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf() {
        return new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(Discount.class).managedClass(PercentOff.class).managedClass(FixedOff.class)
            .managedClass(Payment.class).managedClass(CardPayment.class).managedClass(BankTransfer.class)
            .managedClass(Shipment.class).managedClass(ParcelShipment.class).managedClass(FreightShipment.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:InheritanceMapping;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true")
            .createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    static void section(String title) { System.out.println("-- " + title + " --"); }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf()) {
            section("insert one of each");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                em.persist(new PercentOff("SPRING10", 10));
                em.persist(new FixedOff("WELCOME5", 500));
                em.persist(new CardPayment(12_000, "4242"));
                em.persist(new BankTransfer(250_000, "GB33BUKB20201555555555"));
                em.persist(new ParcelShipment(2, "DHL"));
                em.persist(new FreightShipment(900, 3));
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
 
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                section("SINGLE_TABLE polymorphic query: one select, filtered by the discriminator");
                List<Discount> discounts = em.createQuery("select d from Discount d order by d.id", Discount.class).getResultList();
                for (Discount d : discounts) System.out.println(d + " applied to 10000c = " + d.apply(10_000));
 
                section("type() and treat(): asking for one subtype");
                System.out.println(em.createQuery("select d from Discount d where type(d) = PercentOff", Discount.class).getResultList());
                System.out.println(em.createQuery("select treat(d as PercentOff).percent from Discount d where type(d) = PercentOff", Integer.class).getResultList());
 
                section("JOINED polymorphic query: the parent table left-joins every subclass table");
                System.out.println(em.createQuery("select p from Payment p order by p.id", Payment.class).getResultList());
 
                section("JOINED subtype query: an inner join to the parent");
                System.out.println(em.createQuery("select c from CardPayment c", CardPayment.class).getResultList());
 
                section("TABLE_PER_CLASS polymorphic query: a UNION of every concrete table");
                System.out.println(em.createQuery("select s from Shipment s order by s.id", Shipment.class).getResultList());
 
                section("find() by id works for every strategy");
                System.out.println(em.find(Payment.class, 1L) + ", " + em.find(Shipment.class, 2L));
            }
        }
    }
}

Reading the schema

  • SINGLE_TABLE — discount. One table holds both subtypes; kind is the discriminator, with a check constraint Hibernate derived from the two @DiscriminatorValues. percent and offCents are nullable, and must be: a FIX row has no percent. That is the strategy's defining weakness — a subclass field can never be NOT NULL at the database level. It is also the fastest: a polymorphic read is one select … from discount, a subtype read is the same with where kind='PCT', and an insert is one row.
  • JOINED — payment, card_payment, bank_transfer. The parent table has the shared columns; each subclass table has its own columns plus the same primary key, enforced by a foreign key back to payment. last4 and iban are NOT NULL, because each lives in a table where every row has it. The price is in the queries: a polymorphic read is the parent left joined to every subclass table with a case when … then 1 … then 2 expression deciding the type per row, a subtype read is an inner join, and an insert is two statements.
  • TABLE_PER_CLASS — parcel_shipment, freight_shipment. No shipment table exists; each concrete class gets a complete table with the inherited columns copied in. A polymorphic read is a union all over every concrete table with a synthetic clazz_ column, which no index can help. Ids must be unique across the tables — hence one shared Shipment_SEQ — so IDENTITY generation is impossible here. Subtype reads and inserts are as cheap as they get, which is the only argument for it.
  • @MappedSuperclass — Auditable. Not an entity: no table, no discriminator, no polymorphic query. Its createdOn column simply appears in the discount table because Discount extends it. It is the right tool for "every entity has these audit columns" and the wrong tool for "I want to query all Auditable things".
  • type() and treat(). where type(d) = PercentOff became where d1_0.kind='PCT'; treat(d as PercentOff).percent let the query reach a subclass attribute. Under JOINED the same predicate becomes a test on which subclass table has a matching row.
  • The last line printed no SQL. Both find() calls were served from the persistence context — the earlier polymorphic queries had already loaded those rows. §3's first-level cache applies to subclasses exactly as it does to any entity.

See each strategy's tables and queries

What a hierarchy becomes on disk
Operation

Choosing

Inheritance strategies compared
StrategyTablesPolymorphic readInsertNOT NULL on subclass columnsReach for it when
SINGLE_TABLE1one select, discriminator filterone rowno (use a @Check constraint)the default: few subclass-specific fields, polymorphic queries common
JOINED1 + one per subclassleft joins + caseone row per levelyesmany mandatory subclass fields, normalised schema matters, hierarchy is shallow
TABLE_PER_CLASSone per concrete classunion all, unindexableone rowyesyou never query the base type and cannot share a table — rare; many teams ban it
@MappedSuperclassnone of its ownimpossible—yesshared columns and behaviour without a shared type: audit fields, ids

Two rules cover most decisions. Start with SINGLE_TABLE; move to JOINED when the nullable columns become embarrassing or the subclass-specific columns outnumber the shared ones. And model the hierarchy for the data, not for code reuse: if two kinds of thing share behaviour but no identity — a Product and a ServicePlan are both priced — give them an interface in Java and separate tables, not a Priceable entity hierarchy.

Polymorphic associations follow the strategy: @ManyToOne Discount applied on an Order works for any of the three, and loads whichever subtype the row is. Only the root carries @Inheritance; writing it on a subclass is ignored. Hibernate 6+ also allows @ManyToOne to an interface implemented by several unrelated entities via @Any, which is a different, discriminator-plus-id mapping and best left for when nothing else fits.

Where hierarchies go wrong
  • Discriminator values are data. Rename the class PercentOff and nothing changes; rename the value PCT and every existing row is unreadable. Set @DiscriminatorValue explicitly rather than relying on the default (the entity name), and never change it without a migration.
  • SINGLE_TABLE plus a NOT NULL requirement. The column cannot be NOT NULL; add @Check(constraints = "kind <> 'PCT' or percent is not null") on the root so the database still refuses a broken row.
  • JOINED with a deep hierarchy. Each level is another join on every read and another insert on every write. Three levels is the practical ceiling.
  • TABLE_PER_CLASS with IDENTITY. Fails at start-up: ids must be unique across the union, so a sequence or table generator is mandatory.
  • Associations to a @MappedSuperclass. @ManyToOne Auditable x is a mapping error; the target of an association must be an entity.
  • Querying the root when you meant a subtype. select p from Payment p under JOINED left-joins every subclass table even if your code immediately checks instanceof CardPayment. Ask for CardPayment.

Check yourself

1.In the worked example, PercentOff.percent is declared Integer and the column is created nullable, while CardPayment.last4 is NOT NULL. Why the difference?

C. The strategy decides it. A single shared table must tolerate every subtype's absent fields, which is the one hard limitation of SINGLE_TABLE; the @Check constraint in the gotcha callout is the workaround. In JOINED (and TABLE_PER_CLASS) the subclass column lives where every row has a value, so the constraint is honest.

A is false — nullable is set by annotation, not by Java type, and a primitive int percent would have produced not null and then failed on the first FixedOff insert. B misses that adding nullable = false to percent would make the program fail. D is invented; the discriminator column itself carries a check constraint in the DDL.

2.Which strategy cannot use GenerationType.IDENTITY, and why?

B. A polymorphic read is a union all over the concrete tables, and find(Shipment.class, 2L) only makes sense if id 2 exists in exactly one of them. Identity columns are per table, so two tables would both hand out 2. The worked example therefore shares one Shipment_SEQ sequence, and Hibernate rejects IDENTITY here at start-up.

A is backwards: under JOINED the parent row is inserted first and its generated id is reused for the subclass row — IDENTITY works fine. C is invented. D is the belief that fails at boot.

3.Which statements about a @MappedSuperclass are true? Select all that apply.

A and C. A mapped superclass contributes mappings, not identity: its fields are copied into each subclass's table as if declared there, and no table or discriminator exists for it. That is exactly why audit columns and shared id fields are its natural use.

B fails — it is not an entity, so it has no name in JPQL and no polymorphic query. D is a mapping error for the same reason: associations target entities, and a foreign key needs a table to point at.

Section 9

Batching, projections and caching

Everything Hibernate does ends as a round trip to the database, and round trips are what you pay for. A persistence layer that is "slow" is almost never slow because Hibernate is slow; it is slow because it makes ten thousand trips where twenty would do, hydrates ten thousand entities to read two columns, or drags a persistence context the size of the table through a loop. This section is about seeing those trips — with Statistics, not guesswork — and removing them.

The tool matters, because show_sql misleads here: it prints one line per logical statement, so a hundred batched inserts and a hundred unbatched ones look identical on the console. Only the statistics tell you how many statements were actually prepared and sent.

Worked example: counting the trips

Three phases on one in-memory database. Phases A and B insert a hundred products each with the SQL echo off and the statistics on, so the numbers are the whole story; phase C turns the echo back on for the read paths, where the SQL itself is the lesson.

javaBatching.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.StatelessSession;
import org.hibernate.stat.Statistics;
 
import java.util.List;
 
public class Batching {
 
    /* Phase A: IDENTITY ids — the database assigns the id when the row is inserted,
       so Hibernate must execute every INSERT immediately to learn it. */
    @Entity(name = "IdProduct")
    @Table(name = "id_product")
    public static class IdProduct {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) private String sku;
        private int priceInCents;
        protected IdProduct() {}
        IdProduct(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
    }
 
    /* Phase B: SEQUENCE ids — the id is known before the INSERT, so inserts can be
       queued and sent in batches. */
    @Entity(name = "SeqProduct")
    @Table(name = "seq_product")
    public static class SeqProduct {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) private String sku;
        private int priceInCents;
        protected SeqProduct() {}
        SeqProduct(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
    }
 
    /* Phase C: the read paths, on a tiny table, with the SQL echoed. */
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) private String sku;
        private int priceInCents;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        String sku() { return sku; }
        int priceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
        void setPriceInCents(int p) { this.priceInCents = p; }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + "=" + priceInCents + "c"; }
    }
 
    /* A projection: no identity, no dirty checking, no persistence context entry. */
    public record ProductView(String sku, int priceInCents) {}
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf(boolean showSql, boolean batching, Class<?>... entities) {
        var cfg = new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:Batching;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", String.valueOf(showSql))
            .property("hibernate.generate_statistics", "true");
        if (batching) {
            cfg.property("hibernate.jdbc.batch_size", "20")
               .property("hibernate.order_inserts", "true")
               .property("hibernate.order_updates", "true");
        }
        for (Class<?> c : entities) cfg.managedClass(c);
        return cfg.createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    static Statistics stats(EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        return emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("-- phase A: 100 inserts, IDENTITY ids, batch_size=20 --");
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf(false, true, IdProduct.class)) {
            Statistics st = stats(emf);
            st.clear();
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                for (int i = 1; i <= 100; i++) em.persist(new IdProduct("ID-" + i, i));
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
            System.out.println("statements prepared = " + st.getPrepareStatementCount());
            System.out.println("entities inserted   = " + st.getEntityInsertCount());
        }
 
        System.out.println("-- phase B: 100 inserts, SEQUENCE ids, batch_size=20, flush+clear every 20 --");
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf(false, true, SeqProduct.class)) {
            Statistics st = stats(emf);
            st.clear();
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                for (int i = 1; i <= 100; i++) {
                    em.persist(new SeqProduct("SEQ-" + i, i));
                    if (i % 20 == 0) { em.flush(); em.clear(); }   // bound the persistence context
                }
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
            System.out.println("statements prepared = " + st.getPrepareStatementCount());
            System.out.println("entities inserted   = " + st.getEntityInsertCount());
        }
 
        System.out.println("-- phase C: read paths --");
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf(true, false, Product.class)) {
            Statistics st = stats(emf);
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                em.persist(new Product("BOLT-7", 80));
                em.persist(new Product("NUT-3", 25));
                em.persist(new Product("CAM-9", 2300));
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
 
            System.out.println("- entity query -");
            st.clear();
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                List<Product> all = em.createQuery("select p from Product p order by p.sku", Product.class).getResultList();
                System.out.println("rows = " + all + ", entities hydrated = " + st.getEntityLoadCount());
            }
 
            System.out.println("- DTO projection -");
            st.clear();
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                List<ProductView> views = em.createQuery(
                        "select p.sku, p.priceInCents from Product p order by p.sku", ProductView.class).getResultList();
                System.out.println("rows = " + views + ", entities hydrated = " + st.getEntityLoadCount());
            }
 
            System.out.println("- read-only session: a change is not written -");
            st.clear();
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.unwrap(Session.class).setDefaultReadOnly(true);
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product bolt = em.createQuery("select p from Product p where p.sku = 'BOLT-7'", Product.class).getSingleResult();
                bolt.setPriceInCents(999);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
            System.out.println("entity updates = " + st.getEntityUpdateCount());
 
            System.out.println("- StatelessSession: no persistence context at all -");
            try (StatelessSession ss = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).openStatelessSession()) {
                ss.getTransaction().begin();
                ss.insert(new Product("PIN-2", 15));
                ss.getTransaction().commit();
            }
 
            System.out.println("- bulk update in one statement -");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                int changed = em.createQuery("update Product p set p.priceInCents = p.priceInCents + 5").executeUpdate();
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                System.out.println("rows changed = " + changed);
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                System.out.println("after = " + em.createQuery("select p from Product p order by p.sku", Product.class).getResultList());
            }
        }
    }
}

Read the two counts first. Phase A prepared 100 statements for 100 rows even though batch_size was set: with IDENTITY the database invents the id during the INSERT, and Hibernate must have an id for every managed entity, so each persist runs immediately and there is never anything to batch. Phase B prepared 8: three round trips to the sequence (the pooled optimiser fetches a value per block of 50, plus one call to establish its first block) and five batched INSERT executions carrying 20 rows each. Same rows, same table shape, twelve times fewer trips — and the flush(); clear() every twenty rows means the persistence context never holds more than twenty entities and their snapshots.

Phase C is about what a read costs after the SQL returns. The entity query hydrated three managed objects — each with a snapshot for dirty checking, a place in the identity map, and the obligation to be scanned at flush. The projection into ProductView selected only the two columns it needed and hydrated zero entities: Hibernate 6 and later build a record straight from the row when you pass the record class as the result type. The read-only session proves the other half: the price was changed to 999 and committed, and entity updates = 0 — no snapshot, no dirty check, no UPDATE. The StatelessSession skips the persistence context entirely (one INSERT, nothing cached, no cascades, no lazy loading), and the bulk update changed four rows in one statement instead of loading four entities to change them one by one.

Plan a bulk write

How many round trips will this insert cost?

The write side: rules that decide the trip count

Settings that affect batching and what each does
LeverEffectWatch out
hibernate.jdbc.batch_sizeQueues up to N inserts/updates/deletes for the same table and sends them as one JDBC batch at flush.Off by default. Pointless with IDENTITY ids.
hibernate.order_inserts / order_updatesSorts queued statements by entity type so a batch is not broken every time the loop alternates between Order and OrderLine.Without it, interleaved types yield batches of size 1.
hibernate.jdbc.batch_versioned_dataAllows batching of UPDATEs on @Versioned entities (§7); on by default since 5.x for drivers that report correct update counts.An old driver that returns SUCCESS_NO_INFO silently disables optimistic-lock checks in batches.
SEQUENCE allocation sizeOne sequence call per block of ids (50 by default). The id is known before the insert, which is what makes batching possible.Ids have gaps after a restart. That is fine; ids are identifiers, not counters.
flush() + clear()Sends the queued batch and empties the context, so memory stays flat and each flush scans only the current chunk.After clear() every previously loaded entity is detached; keep nothing from before the clear.
StatelessSessionDirect JDBC-ish operations: insert, update, delete, get. No context, no dirty checking, no cascades, no lazy loading, no first-level cache.Callbacks and listeners do not fire. Batches still apply if batch_size is set.
Bulk JPQL update / deleteOne statement for the whole set. The persistence context is not updated: entities already loaded keep their old values.Clear or refresh after a bulk statement if you continue in the same context.

The read side: fetch what the screen needs

// 1. a record, instantiated by Hibernate from the selected columns
record StockRow(String sku, int onHand) {}
List<StockRow> rows = em.createQuery(
    "select p.sku, s.onHand from Product p join p.stock s where s.onHand < 10", StockRow.class)
    .getResultList();
 
// 2. the JPA-standard spelling, any class with a matching constructor
List<StockRow> rows2 = em.createQuery(
    "select new com.acme.StockRow(p.sku, s.onHand) from Product p join p.stock s", StockRow.class)
    .getResultList();
 
// 3. untyped columns when the shape is ad hoc
List<Tuple> t = em.createQuery("select p.sku as sku, count(l) as lines from Product p join p.lines l group by p.sku", Tuple.class)
    .getResultList();
long lines = t.get(0).get("lines", Long.class);

A projection is the single biggest read optimisation available: fewer columns over the wire, no entity hydration, no snapshot, no dirty-check scan at flush, and nothing to accidentally lazy-load later. Report screens, lists and exports should almost never load entities.

// whole session: no snapshots are taken, flush has nothing to compare
em.unwrap(Session.class).setDefaultReadOnly(true);
 
// one query: the entities it returns are read-only
em.createQuery("select o from Order o", Order.class)
  .setHint("org.hibernate.readOnly", true)
  .getResultList();
 
// one entity, after the fact
em.unwrap(Session.class).setReadOnly(order, true);

Read-only entities are still managed — identity map, lazy loading, the lot — they just cannot be dirty. Hibernate skips the snapshot copy on load and the comparison on flush, which for a page that loads a thousand entities to render them is most of the flush cost. Changes you make are silently discarded; that is the contract, not a bug.

List<Order> page = em.createQuery("select o from Order o order by o.placed desc, o.id", Order.class)
    .setFirstResult(40)        // OFFSET
    .setMaxResults(20)         // LIMIT — Hibernate renders the dialect's syntax
    .getResultList();
 
// streaming a large result instead of materialising it
try (Stream<Order> s = em.createQuery("select o from Order o", Order.class)
        .setHint("org.hibernate.fetchSize", 500)
        .getResultStream()) {
    s.forEach(this::export);
}

Always order a paged query by something unique, or pages overlap. Offset paging degrades as the offset grows (the database still walks the skipped rows); keyset paging — where o.placed < :lastSeen — does not. fetchSize is a JDBC hint for how many rows the driver pulls per network read; PostgreSQL ignores it unless the connection is in a transaction with auto-commit off.

Caching: what it can and cannot do

Hibernate has three caches and they are routinely confused. The first-level cache is the persistence context itself (§3): per EntityManager, always on, guarantees one object per row and is the reason the same find twice in one context hits the database once. The second-level cache is shared across the whole EntityManagerFactory and caches entity rows by id (and collections by owner id) — not query results, and not the object graph. The query cache caches the ids returned by a particular query with particular parameters, and is invalidated the moment any table the query touches is written.

// configuration shape only — no cache provider is on this page's class path, so this block is not verified
.property("hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache", "true")
.property("hibernate.cache.region.factory_class", "jcache")       // hibernate-jcache + a provider such as Ehcache or Caffeine
.property("hibernate.javax.cache.uri", "classpath:ehcache.xml")
.property("hibernate.cache.use_query_cache", "true")              // only if you also set the hint per query
 
@Entity @Cacheable
@org.hibernate.annotations.Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_WRITE)
public class Product { ... }
 
@Entity @Immutable @Cacheable
@org.hibernate.annotations.Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_ONLY)   // the ideal cache citizen
public class Currency { ... }
 
em.createQuery("select p from Product p where p.category = :c", Product.class)
  .setHint("org.hibernate.cacheable", true)                         // opt in, per query
  .setParameter("c", Category.FASTENER).getResultList();
When a second-level cache is a win, and when it is a trap
  • Win: reference data read constantly and written rarely — categories, currencies, tax rates — especially @Immutable entities under READ_ONLY, which need no locking at all.
  • Win: find by id and the @NaturalId lookup (§11), which consult the cache before the database. JPQL never does, unless the query cache is on for that query.
  • Trap: entities written by anything other than this application. The cache does not know, and serves stale rows until the entry expires.
  • Trap: the query cache on a busy table. Every write to the table invalidates every cached query touching it, so the hit rate collapses while the bookkeeping cost stays.
  • Trap: caching to fix an N+1 problem. The queries are still issued; they are just served from memory. Fix the fetch plan (§5) first.

Measuring, and the pool underneath

Turn on hibernate.generate_statistics in any environment where you are investigating — it is cheap — and read getPrepareStatementCount, getEntityLoadCount, getCollectionFetchCount and getQueryExecutionCount around the operation you care about. getQueryExecutionMaxTime is also there; it was deliberately never printed in this module because a wall-clock number is not reproducible, and that is also why it is a poor thing to assert on in a test. For a running service, hibernate.session.events.log.LOG_QUERIES_SLOWER_THAN_MS=50 logs every statement that exceeds the threshold, with its SQL, which is usually how a slow page is first located.

Beneath all of it sits the connection pool. The warning you have seen on every run in this module — Using built-in connection pool (not intended for production use) — is Hibernate telling you its bundled pool is a toy. Production uses HikariCP (hibernate-hikaricp, hibernate.hikari.maximumPoolSize), sized small: a pool of ten connections outperforms a pool of a hundred on most databases, because connections beyond the core count mostly queue inside the database instead of outside it. A transaction that holds a connection while it calls a remote service is the classic way to exhaust even a well-sized pool.

Performance gotchas
  • show_sql cannot show batching. It logs each logical statement. Only Statistics or the driver's own logging (p6spy, datasource-proxy) reveal what was actually sent.
  • A bulk JPQL statement bypasses the context. Entities already loaded keep stale values and a later flush can overwrite the bulk change with them. Clear first, or run the bulk statement in its own transaction.
  • @DynamicUpdate is not free. It writes only changed columns, but Hibernate must then build and prepare a different statement per combination of changed columns, which defeats statement caching. Use it for wide tables with hot contention, not by default.
  • Loading to count. findAll().size() hydrates the table; select count(p) from Product p moves one number.
  • The pool is the real ceiling. Ten slow queries with a pool of ten freeze every other request. Measure pool wait time before adding threads.

Check yourself

1.You set hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50, insert 1,000 Order entities in one transaction, and Statistics still reports 1,000 prepared statements. Which is the most likely cause?

C. Exactly phase A of the worked example. An IDENTITY id exists only after the row is inserted, Hibernate needs the id to manage the entity, so persist cannot be deferred and there is never a queue to batch. Switch to SEQUENCE.

A is false: inserts, updates and deletes all batch. B is false: commit flushes, and the queued statements are batched then. D is false: H2 supports batching, and phase B proved it on this very database.

2.A report page lists 5,000 products with their SKU and price. It runs select p from Product p and maps each entity to a row. The query takes 40 ms; the page takes 900 ms. What is the first change to make?

B. The database is not the problem (40 ms); hydrating 5,000 managed entities, snapshotting each one and scanning them all at flush is. A projection hydrates nothing — the worked example showed entities hydrated = 0 — and the mapping step disappears too.

A and C keep the 5,000-entity hydration; they only skip the 40 ms query. D affects writes, and this page writes nothing.

3.Which statements about Hibernate's caches are true? Select all that apply.

A and D. The second-level cache is a map from id to row state; a query has to run to discover which ids match. The query cache keys on the query and its parameters and is dropped whenever a touched table changes, which is why it rarely pays on busy tables.

B describes the second-level cache; the first-level cache is the persistence context, one per EntityManager. C is wrong: the query cache stores ids (and scalar values) and then looks each entity up in the second-level cache, or in the database if it is not there — which can turn one cached query into N lookups.

Section 10

Schema generation, validation and migrations

Every program in this module has started with drop-and-create: Hibernate reads the mappings, derives DDL, and builds a fresh schema in an empty in-memory database. That is exactly right for a learning page and a test, and exactly wrong for a database with data in it. The question this section answers is who owns the schema once the data matters — and the answer is never "the application at startup".

Two vocabularies describe the same switch. JPA's is jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.database.action with the values none, create, drop, drop-and-create; Hibernate's older hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto adds the two values JPA does not have, update and validate. When both are set, the JPA property wins and the Hibernate one is ignored — a detail that bit the worked example below on its first draft.

Schema generation settings in JPA and Hibernate spelling
Hibernate hbm2ddl.autoJPA schema-generation.database.actionAt startupExisting data
createdrop-and-createdrop mapped tables, create themdestroyed
create-dropdrop-and-create (+ drop on close)as above, then drop on shutdowndestroyed
create-onlycreatecreate without dropping firstkept, but fails if tables exist
update—add missing tables and columnskept; drift accumulates
validate—compare, refuse to start on mismatchuntouched
nonenonenothinguntouched

Worked example: generate, export, validate, and refuse

One in-memory database, three bootstraps. The first generates the schema from the v1 mapping and also writes the DDL to a script file. The second starts with validate against the same mapping and is allowed through. The third validates a v2 mapping that gained a field nobody migrated — and the program ends there, in the exception the build expects.

javaSchemaValidate.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
 
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
 
public class SchemaValidate {
 
    /* Version 1 of the mapping: what the database was created from. */
    @Entity(name = "StockLevel")
    @Table(name = "stock_level")
    public static class StockLevel {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) private String sku;
        private int onHand;
        protected StockLevel() {}
        StockLevel(String sku, int onHand) { this.sku = sku; this.onHand = onHand; }
    }
 
    /* Version 2 of the mapping: a developer added a field — but nobody migrated the table. */
    @Entity(name = "StockLevelV2")
    @Table(name = "stock_level")
    public static class StockLevelV2 {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) private String sku;
        private int onHand;
        private int reorderPoint;          // new column, never added to the schema
        protected StockLevelV2() {}
    }
 
    static PersistenceConfiguration base(Class<?> entity) {
        return new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(entity)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:SchemaValidate;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "true");
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        System.out.println("-- 1. generate the schema from the v1 mapping, and export the DDL to a script --");
        Path script = Path.of("schema.sql");
        Files.deleteIfExists(script);
        var create = base(StockLevel.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_SCRIPTS_ACTION, "create")
            .property("jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.scripts.create-target", script.toString());
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = create.createEntityManagerFactory();
             EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
            em.getTransaction().begin();
            em.persist(new StockLevel("BOLT-7", 120));
            em.getTransaction().commit();
        }
        System.out.println("- schema.sql, the starting point for a hand-written migration -");
        for (String line : Files.readAllLines(script)) System.out.println("  " + line);
        Files.delete(script);
 
        System.out.println("-- 2. start again with 'none' + validate against the v1 mapping: fine --");
        var validateV1 = base(StockLevel.class)
            .property("hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto", "validate");
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = validateV1.createEntityManagerFactory();
             EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
            List<?> rows = em.createQuery("select s.sku from StockLevel s").getResultList();
            System.out.println("validated, rows = " + rows);
        }
 
        System.out.println("-- 3. the v2 mapping against the unmigrated table: bootstrap refuses --");
        var validateV2 = base(StockLevelV2.class)
            .property("hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto", "validate");
        EntityManagerFactory never = validateV2.createEntityManagerFactory();   // throws SchemaManagementException
        never.close();
        System.out.println("unreachable");
    }
}
Expected output
-- 1. generate the schema from the v1 mapping, and export the DDL to a script --
Hibernate: create global temporary table HTE_stock_level(onHand integer, rn_ integer not null, id bigint, sku varchar(16), primary key (rn_)) transactional
Hibernate: drop table if exists stock_level cascade
Hibernate: drop sequence if exists stock_level_SEQ
Hibernate: create sequence stock_level_SEQ start with 1 increment by 50
Hibernate: create table stock_level (onHand integer not null, id bigint not null, sku varchar(16) not null unique, primary key (id))
Hibernate: select next value for stock_level_SEQ
Hibernate: insert into stock_level (onHand,sku,id) values (?,?,?)
- schema.sql, the starting point for a hand-written migration -
  create sequence stock_level_SEQ start with 1 increment by 50;
  create table stock_level (onHand integer not null, id bigint not null, sku varchar(16) not null unique, primary key (id));
-- 2. start again with 'none' + validate against the v1 mapping: fine --
Hibernate: create global temporary table HTE_stock_level(onHand integer, rn_ integer not null, id bigint, sku varchar(16), primary key (rn_)) transactional
Hibernate: select sl1_0.sku from stock_level sl1_0
validated, rows = [BOLT-7]
-- 3. the v2 mapping against the unmigrated table: bootstrap refuses --
Hibernate: create global temporary table HTE_stock_level(onHand integer, reorderPoint integer, rn_ integer not null, id bigint, sku varchar(16), primary key (rn_)) transactional
Standard error (the build checks for this)
Exception in thread "main" jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException: Unable to build Hibernate SessionFactory  [persistence unit: warehouse]
Caused by: org.hibernate.tool.schema.spi.SchemaManagementException: Schema validation: missing column [reorderPoint] in table [stock_level]

Three things to take from the output. The schema.sql that step 1 wrote is almost the DDL that ran, and it is the right starting point for a migration: copy it into a versioned script, read every line, fix the names you do not like, add the index the mapping cannot express, and commit it. Step 2 shows validate costing one metadata query at startup and nothing else. Step 3 is the payoff: the deploy fails at bootstrap with the exact column named, instead of succeeding and then failing on the first request that touches reorderPoint. Notice also that validate left the HTE_stock_level temporary table alone in step 2 but recreated it in step 3 with the new column: that table is not part of your schema at all. Hibernate 7 declares it at every bootstrap for bulk-mutation queries, which is why it appears even under none, and why validate never complains about it.

Is this setting safe here?

Schema setting versus environment

Why update is not a migration

update looks like the grown-up option: it keeps the data and adds what is missing. The trouble is everything it cannot know. Rename a field from onHand to quantityOnHand and update adds a new nullable column and leaves the old one full of data, forever. Remove a field and the column stays. Narrow a String from 255 to 16 characters and nothing happens, because shrinking might fail. Add a nullable = false column to a populated table and the ALTER fails, or on some databases succeeds and leaves nulls in a not-null column. Add a unique constraint that existing data violates and startup fails in production at the worst possible moment. And in every case the DDL ran unreviewed, under the application's credentials, at the instant the pod started, possibly holding a table lock while traffic waited.

A migration tool fixes all of that by making schema change a versioned, reviewed, ordered artefact that runs once per environment and records that it ran.

src/main/resources/db/migration/
  V1__create_product_and_stock.sql      <- the hand-edited output of schema.sql
  V2__add_reorder_point.sql             <- alter table stock_level add column reorder_point integer not null default 0;
  V3__backfill_reorder_point.sql        <- update stock_level set reorder_point = 10 where ...;
  R__product_view.sql                   <- repeatable: re-run whenever its checksum changes
# Flyway and Liquibase are not on this page's class path — these are shown, not run
flyway -url=jdbc:postgresql://db/warehouse -user=deploy migrate     # applies V2, V3 in order, records each in flyway_schema_history
flyway info                                                          # which versions are applied, pending, or failed
flyway validate                                                      # checksums of applied scripts still match the files
flyway baseline -baselineVersion=1                                   # adopt an existing database without re-running V1

Plain SQL, one file per change, a version in the name, a checksum recorded on apply so an edited historical script is detected. Simple enough that the review is of the SQL itself, which is the point.

# db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml
databaseChangeLog:
  - changeSet:
      id: 2-add-reorder-point
      author: warehouse-team
      changes:
        - addColumn:
            tableName: stock_level
            columns:
              - column: { name: reorder_point, type: int, defaultValueNumeric: 0, constraints: { nullable: false } }
      rollback:
        - dropColumn: { tableName: stock_level, columnName: reorder_point }

Liquibase describes changes in a database-neutral form (YAML, XML, JSON or SQL) and renders them per dialect, tracks them in DATABASECHANGELOG, and supports declared rollbacks and preconditions. More machinery than Flyway; worth it when the same migrations must run on several database products.

  1. Change the mapping in the entity.
  2. Generate the DDL difference locally — schema-generation.scripts.action=create for a new table, or simply read what update would have done against a scratch database.
  3. Write the migration by hand from that output: real names, the index, the default value, the backfill, the constraint added after the backfill.
  4. Review it like code. Ask what happens to a 50-million-row table while this runs, and whether the previous version of the application can still run against the new schema during a rolling deploy.
  5. Run it in CI against a real database engine (Testcontainers), then run the tests with validate.
  6. Deploy with the migration step before the application starts, and the application on validate.

What validate checks, and what it does not

Validation compares, for every mapped entity: that the table exists, that each mapped column exists, and that each column's type is compatible with the mapping. It does not check indexes, foreign-key or unique-constraint names, column nullability, defaults, or column length on most dialects. So validate catches the missing column and the wrong type — the two failures that break at runtime — and ignores the ones that only affect performance or integrity. Those still need a migration review; validate is a tripwire, not an audit.

@Entity
@Table(name = "order_line",
       indexes = { @Index(name = "ix_order_line_order", columnList = "order_id"),
                   @Index(name = "ix_order_line_sku",   columnList = "sku") },
       uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(name = "uq_order_line_order_sku", columnNames = { "order_id", "sku" }))
public class OrderLine {
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
    @JoinColumn(name = "order_id", nullable = false, foreignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_order_line_order"))
    private Order order;
    ...
}

Naming is the other half. By default Hibernate derives column names from field names as written (priceInCents becomes a column called priceInCents, as every echoed statement in this module shows); most teams install a physical naming strategy that produces price_in_cents instead (hibernate.physical_naming_strategy, or the CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy that Spring Boot applies by default). Whichever you choose, choose it before the first migration is written, because renaming later is exactly the change update cannot make.

Schema gotchas
  • The JPA property silently wins. With schema-generation.database.action=none set, hbm2ddl.auto=validate is ignored and no validation happens. The first draft of the worked example printed "unreachable". Set one or the other.
  • H2 in tests, PostgreSQL in production. Types differ (timestamp(6) with time zone is not the same object in both), sequences differ, for update and on conflict differ, case-sensitivity of identifiers differs. A migration that passed on H2 can fail on PostgreSQL. Test on the engine you deploy to; Testcontainers makes that a one-line annotation.
  • create drops tables it does not own. Anything mapped is dropped, including a table another service shares with you.
  • Sequences are schema too. product_SEQ in the echoed DDL must exist in production with the same increment, or ids collide. A migration that creates the table but not the sequence passes validate (which does not check sequences) and fails on the first insert.
  • Rolling deploys need backward-compatible schemas. Add the column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, deploy code that reads the new column, drop the old one — five steps, two releases. A rename in one migration breaks the old pods still running.

Check yourself

1.A team renames the entity field onHand to quantity and deploys with hbm2ddl.auto=update. What happens to the production table?

C. update only adds. It cannot know a rename from an add-plus-remove, so it adds the new column and never drops anything. Every stock level now reads as null or zero, and nothing failed to tell you.

A would require intent the tool cannot infer. B is what validate does, not update. D is wrong because update never drops — which is sometimes presented as its safety feature, and is really why drift accumulates.

2.Production runs Flyway migrations in a deploy step and starts the application with hbm2ddl.auto=validate. A migration added a product table but forgot the product_SEQ sequence the mapping uses. When does this fail?

B. Validation checks tables and columns, not sequences. Startup passes; the first insert asks the sequence for a value and the database answers that it does not exist. This is the gap between a tripwire and an audit.

A overstates what validate checks. C is false under validate and none; only the generation modes create sequences. D is false: Flyway knows nothing about JPA mappings; it runs the SQL you wrote.

3.Which are sound reasons to run integration tests against the production database engine rather than H2? Select all that apply.

A, C and D. Each is a class of bug that only the real engine reveals: DDL and types, concurrency semantics, and dialect-specific native SQL. Testcontainers makes the real engine as convenient as H2 was.

B is false — every program in this module ran on H2. H2 is a fine learning and unit-test database; the argument is about fidelity, not capability.

Section 11

Designing entities: identity, equality and callbacks

An entity has three notions of "the same" and they do not agree. Database identity is the primary key: two rows are the same row if their ids match. Object identity is ==: inside one persistence context Hibernate guarantees one Java object per row (§3), so == works there and nowhere else — the same row loaded in two contexts is two objects. Equality is equals/hashCode, which you write, and which Set, Map and every contains call will trust completely.

The difficulty is that a generated id does not exist until the entity is persisted, and hashCode must never change while an object sits in a hash-based collection. Those two facts collide in a bug that is easy to write, invisible in tests that only use lists, and baffling in production.

Worked example: three ways to write equals, and the one that breaks

javaEntityDesign.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.annotations.Immutable;
import org.hibernate.annotations.NaturalId;
import org.hibernate.annotations.SQLDelete;
import org.hibernate.annotations.SQLRestriction;
 
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.Set;
 
public class EntityDesign {
 
    /* Option 1 — equals/hashCode on the generated id. Looks obvious, breaks in a Set. */
    @Entity(name = "IdHashProduct")
    @Table(name = "id_hash_product")
    public static class IdHashProduct {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 16) String sku;
        protected IdHashProduct() {}
        IdHashProduct(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof IdHashProduct p && Objects.equals(id, p.id); }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hashCode(id); }
    }
 
    /* Option 2 — a business key that never changes. */
    @Entity(name = "SkuProduct")
    @Table(name = "sku_product")
    public static class SkuProduct {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) String sku;
        protected SkuProduct() {}
        SkuProduct(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof SkuProduct p && sku.equals(p.sku); }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return sku.hashCode(); }
    }
 
    /* Option 3 — id equality once assigned, a constant hash so the bucket never moves. */
    @Entity(name = "SafeProduct")
    @Table(name = "safe_product")
    public static class SafeProduct {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 16) String sku;
        protected SafeProduct() {}
        SafeProduct(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
        @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof SafeProduct p && id != null && id.equals(p.id); }
        @Override public int hashCode() { return getClass().hashCode(); }
    }
 
    /* Auditing: callbacks on the entity plus an external listener. */
    public static class AuditListener {
        static int prePersist, preUpdate;
        @PrePersist void beforeInsert(Object e) { prePersist++; }
        @PreUpdate  void beforeUpdate(Object e) { preUpdate++; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "AuditedProduct")
    @Table(name = "audited_product")
    @EntityListeners(AuditListener.class)
    public static class AuditedProduct {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @NaturalId @Column(nullable = false, length = 16) String sku;
        int priceInCents;
        @Column(nullable = false, updatable = false) Instant createdAt;
        @Column(nullable = false) Instant updatedAt;
        protected AuditedProduct() {}
        AuditedProduct(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        @PrePersist void stamp() { createdAt = updatedAt = Instant.now(); }
        @PreUpdate  void touch() { updatedAt = Instant.now().plusSeconds(1); }   // +1s so the fact below cannot tie
    }
 
    /* Soft delete: DELETE becomes UPDATE, and every query gets a filter for free. */
    @Entity(name = "SoftProduct")
    @Table(name = "soft_product")
    @SQLDelete(sql = "update soft_product set deleted = true where id = ?")
    @SQLRestriction("deleted = false")
    public static class SoftProduct {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 16) String sku;
        boolean deleted;
        protected SoftProduct() {}
        SoftProduct(String sku) { this.sku = sku; }
    }
 
    /* Reference data that never changes: Hibernate skips dirty checking entirely. */
    @Entity(name = "Currency")
    @Table(name = "currency")
    @Immutable
    public static class Currency {
        @Id @Column(length = 3) String code;
        String name;
        protected Currency() {}
        Currency(String code, String name) { this.code = code; this.name = name; }
    }
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf(boolean showSql, Class<?>... entities) {
        var cfg = new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:EntityDesign;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", String.valueOf(showSql));
        for (Class<?> c : entities) cfg.managedClass(c);
        return cfg.createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("-- equality: add to a Set before persist, look it up after --");
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf(false, IdHashProduct.class, SkuProduct.class, SafeProduct.class)) {
            IdHashProduct a = new IdHashProduct("BOLT-7");
            SkuProduct b = new SkuProduct("BOLT-7");
            SafeProduct c = new SafeProduct("BOLT-7");
            Set<IdHashProduct> setA = new HashSet<>(Set.of(a));
            Set<SkuProduct> setB = new HashSet<>(Set.of(b));
            Set<SafeProduct> setC = new HashSet<>(Set.of(c));
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                em.persist(a); em.persist(b); em.persist(c);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
            System.out.println("id-based hashCode : id=" + a.id + ", set.contains = " + setA.contains(a));
            System.out.println("business key      : id=" + b.id + ", set.contains = " + setB.contains(b));
            System.out.println("id + constant hash: id=" + c.id + ", set.contains = " + setC.contains(c));
 
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {          // a second context: a different Java object
                SafeProduct reloaded = em.find(SafeProduct.class, c.id);
                System.out.println("reloaded == c: " + (reloaded == c) + ", reloaded.equals(c): " + reloaded.equals(c)
                        + ", set.contains(reloaded): " + setC.contains(reloaded));
            }
            System.out.println("two transient SafeProducts equal: " + new SafeProduct("X").equals(new SafeProduct("X")));
        }
 
        System.out.println("-- callbacks, soft delete, immutable, natural id --");
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf(true, AuditedProduct.class, SoftProduct.class, Currency.class)) {
            System.out.println("- @PrePersist / @PreUpdate -");
            Long auditedId;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                AuditedProduct p = new AuditedProduct("BOLT-7", 80);
                em.persist(p);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                auditedId = p.id;
                System.out.println("createdAt set: " + (p.createdAt != null) + ", createdAt equals updatedAt: " + p.createdAt.equals(p.updatedAt));
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                AuditedProduct p = em.find(AuditedProduct.class, auditedId);
                p.priceInCents = 90;
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                System.out.println("updatedAt moved after update: " + p.updatedAt.isAfter(p.createdAt));
            }
            System.out.println("listener calls: prePersist=" + AuditListener.prePersist + ", preUpdate=" + AuditListener.preUpdate);
 
            System.out.println("- @NaturalId lookup -");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                AuditedProduct p = em.unwrap(Session.class).byNaturalId(AuditedProduct.class).using("sku", "BOLT-7").load();
                System.out.println("by natural id: " + p.sku + " at " + p.priceInCents + "c");
            }
 
            System.out.println("- soft delete -");
            Long softId;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                SoftProduct s = new SoftProduct("NUT-3");
                em.persist(s);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                softId = s.id;
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                em.remove(em.find(SoftProduct.class, softId));
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                long jpql = em.createQuery("select count(s) from SoftProduct s", Long.class).getSingleResult();
                Number sql = (Number) em.createNativeQuery("select count(*) from soft_product").getSingleResult();
                System.out.println("JPQL count = " + jpql + ", native count = " + sql);
            }
 
            System.out.println("- @Immutable: a change is silently ignored -");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                em.persist(new Currency("GBP", "Pound sterling"));
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Currency gbp = em.find(Currency.class, "GBP");
                gbp.name = "changed";
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                System.out.println("GBP name = " + em.find(Currency.class, "GBP").name);
            }
        }
    }
}

The first block is the whole argument. All three products were put in a HashSet while transient, then persisted. Option 1 hashed null before persist (bucket 0) and hashes 1 after, so the set looks in the wrong bucket: contains is false for an object that is in the set. Nothing threw; the entity is simply stranded in a bucket it will never be found in, and remove will fail the same way, so the set can never be cleaned. Option 2 hashes the SKU, which was known from construction and never changes: correct, provided your entity has an immutable business key. Option 3 is the general answer when it does not: hashCode is a constant per class, so the bucket never moves, and equals compares ids once both are assigned — which the second context proves, where reloaded is a different object (== false) but equal to c and found in the set. The price is that every instance lands in one bucket, so a HashSet of these degrades to a list; for the handful of entities a @OneToMany typically holds, that is irrelevant. The last line is the one subtlety: two transient instances are never equal under option 3, because neither has an id yet — deliberate, since two unsaved products are two products.

The second block covers the supporting cast. @PrePersist stamped both timestamps before the INSERT (the output confirms they were set and equal) and @PreUpdate moved updatedAt before the UPDATE; the external listener counted one of each. The @NaturalId lookup went to the database by sku rather than by id, and would have consulted the natural-id cache first had one been configured. The soft delete turned remove into the UPDATE you wrote, and the @SQLRestriction was appended to the find, the count — every entity query — while the native query saw the row that is still physically there. And the @Immutable currency was changed and committed with no UPDATE at all: Hibernate takes no snapshot of an immutable entity, so there is nothing to dirty-check.

The three options, side by side

equals and hashCode strategies for entities

Immutable business key (sku, ISBN, natural id)yesyesa unique column you need anywaythe entity has a key that is assigned at construction and never changes
