Value objects, boundaries and the shape of an entity

// A value object has no identity: equal by value, immutable, embedded in the owning row.
// Hibernate 6.2+ maps a record directly as an embeddable.
@Embeddable
public record Money(long amountInCents, String currency) {
    public Money { if (amountInCents < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative"); }
}
 
@Entity
public class OrderLine {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) private Long id;
    @Embedded private Money unitPrice;              // columns unitPrice_amountInCents, unitPrice_currency
    @Embedded @AttributeOverride(name = "amountInCents", column = @Column(name = "discount_cents"))
              @AttributeOverride(name = "currency",      column = @Column(name = "discount_ccy"))
    private Money discount;
    ...
}
 
// At the boundary, the entity never leaves the service:
public record OrderSummary(Long id, String customer, long totalInCents) {}
public OrderSummary summary(long id) {
    Order o = em.find(Order.class, id);
    return new OrderSummary(o.getId(), o.getCustomer().getName(), o.total().amountInCents());
}

Three design pressures pull on an entity. First, push value semantics into value objects: money, a date range, an address, a quantity with its unit are not rows with identity; they are values, best modelled as records marked @Embeddable, equal by their fields and impossible to put into an inconsistent state. Second, keep entities inside the persistence boundary. An entity handed to a JSON serializer or a view template will trigger lazy loads outside the transaction (LazyInitializationException, §5), will serialize a bidirectional association forever (Order → lines → order → lines…), and will send every column to a client that wanted three. Map to a DTO at the service edge; the projection queries from §9 often make the entity unnecessary for reads altogether. Third, the rich-versus-anaemic argument: an entity that enforces its own invariants (order.addLine(...) checks stock and keeps both sides of the association in sync, §4) is easier to keep correct than a bag of getters and setters driven by a service, but entities that reach for repositories or external services from inside their methods become untestable. A reasonable line: invariants and state transitions live in the entity; coordination, transactions and I/O live in the service.

Callbacks, listeners and auditing

JPA lifecycle callbacks
CallbackFiresTypical useMust not
@PrePersistbefore the INSERT is queued (on persist, or on flush for cascades)stamp createdAt, assign a UUID, default a statuscall EntityManager methods
@PostPersistafter the INSERT ran (the generated id is available)publish a domain event by idassume the transaction committed
@PreUpdateat flush, only if the entity is dirtystamp updatedAt, recompute a derived columnchange other entities
@PostUpdate / @PreRemove / @PostRemovearound UPDATE / DELETEaudit trail, cleanup of external resourcesthrow to "cancel" (it rolls back everything)
@PostLoadafter the entity is hydrated from a row or refreshedcompute a transient field from loaded statetrigger lazy loads (N+1 by stealth)

Callbacks on the entity are fine for stamping; @EntityListeners moves the same logic into a reusable class — the worked example's AuditListener — that can be applied to every audited entity, usually through a @MappedSuperclass that carries createdAt/updatedAt/createdBy. Hibernate adds @CreationTimestamp and @UpdateTimestamp for the two commonest cases, and Envers (hibernate-envers, @Audited) for full history tables: every change to an audited entity is recorded in a _AUD table with a revision number, and you can query "what did this order look like at revision 17". Not on this page's class path, but the first thing to reach for when the requirement is "who changed what, when" rather than "when was it last changed".

Soft delete, honestly

Soft delete keeps the row and hides it, which auditors, undo features and foreign keys from other tables all like. It also costs more than the two annotations suggest. A unique constraint on sku now blocks re-creating a deleted product, so the constraint must become (sku, deleted) or a partial index. Every association to a soft-deletable entity needs the restriction too, or an Order will happily join to its deleted lines — and @SQLRestriction on the collection side is a separate declaration. Reports that must include deleted rows need native SQL or a second entity mapped without the restriction. And remove still fires @PreRemove, still cascades, still orphan-removes, exactly as if the row were gone. Hibernate 6.4 added @SoftDelete, which handles the column, the restriction and the collection cases together; prefer it to hand-rolled @SQLDelete when you are on a version that has it.

Entity design gotchas
  • Lombok @Data on an entity generates equals/hashCode over every field, including the generated id and lazy collections. That is option 1's bug plus a lazy-load (or a StackOverflowError through a bidirectional association) every time hashCode runs. Use @Getter/@Setter and write the two methods by hand.
  • final classes and final methods cannot be proxied, so lazy loading of a @ManyToOne to them silently becomes eager. Records cannot be entities for the same reason (and because they are immutable with no no-arg constructor); they are excellent embeddables and projections.
  • toString() that touches a collection loads it. A log statement at the wrong place becomes a query, or a LazyInitializationException.
  • Timestamps set in Java are the application's clock, not the database's. For ordering across servers prefer a database default or @CurrentTimestamp(source = SourceType.DB).
  • @DynamicInsert omits null columns so database defaults apply — and then the entity in memory still holds null until you refresh it.
  • A @NaturalId is immutable by default. Changing it throws unless you declare @NaturalId(mutable = true), and a mutable natural id is a poor hashCode ingredient for the reason this whole section is about.

Check yourself

1.An Order entity has @OneToMany Set<OrderLine> lines. OrderLine.hashCode() returns Objects.hash(id). A service creates a new line, adds it to order.getLines(), and calls em.persist(line). Later in the same transaction, order.getLines().remove(line) returns false and the line is still there. Why?

C. Exactly the stepper. The hash changed between add and remove, so the set looks in the wrong bucket. A business-key or constant hashCode would have kept the bucket stable.

A is false: Hibernate's PersistentSet supports removal. B is invented. D is a real rule (§4) but affects what is written, not whether a Java Set can find its own element.

2.With @SQLDelete and @SQLRestriction("deleted = false") on Product, which query can still return a soft-deleted product?

B. The restriction is appended to SQL that Hibernate generates. Native SQL is yours verbatim, which the worked example showed with its count(*) of 1 against a JPQL count of 0. Native queries that should respect soft delete must say so themselves.

A, C and D are all generated by Hibernate from the mapping and all carry the deleted = false predicate — the find in the output shows it in its where clause.

3.Which statements about lifecycle callbacks are true? Select all that apply.

A and D. Callbacks hang off the persistence context's own operations: dirty checking decides whether an UPDATE (and so @PreUpdate) happens, and listeners are plain classes attached by annotation to as many entities as you like.

B is false: the stateless session bypasses the persistence context and its events, which is part of why it is fast. C is false: a bulk statement is one SQL statement that never loads the entities, so no per-entity callback can run — the updatedAt column stays stale unless the statement sets it.

Section 12

Reading the SQL and the exceptions

An ORM fails in two ways: slowly, by issuing more SQL than you imagined, and loudly, with an exception whose name is three wrappers away from the thing that went wrong. Both are diagnosable in minutes once you know where Hibernate reports what it does. This section is the toolkit: what to switch on, how to read what comes out, and a map from each common exception to its cause and its fix.

The first rule applies to both kinds of failure: look at the SQL. Hibernate never does anything to the database that it cannot show you. If a page is slow, the statement count explains it; if a commit fails, the statement that failed is in the log one line above the stack trace.

Worked example: nine failures, nine cause chains

Every exception below is provoked on purpose, caught, and printed as its cause chain — outermost first, following getCause() to the end. Read the chains before the prose: the outermost type is what your catch sees, the innermost is what Hibernate actually detected.

javaExceptions.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
 
public class Exceptions {
 
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16)
        private String sku;
        private int priceInCents;
        @Version
        private int version;
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, int priceInCents) { this.sku = sku; this.priceInCents = priceInCents; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        void setPriceInCents(int p) { this.priceInCents = p; }
        int priceInCents() { return priceInCents; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "Order")
    @Table(name = "orders")                          // ORDER is a reserved word in SQL
    public static class Order {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)            // no cascade: the product must already be persistent
        private Product product;
        @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL)
        private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
        protected Order() {}
        Order(Product product) { this.product = product; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        List<OrderLine> lines() { return lines; }
        void addLine(int qty) { OrderLine l = new OrderLine(this, qty); lines.add(l); }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "OrderLine")
    @Table(name = "order_line")
    public static class OrderLine {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
        private Order order;
        private int qty;
        protected OrderLine() {}
        OrderLine(Order order, int qty) { this.order = order; this.qty = qty; }
    }
 
    static EntityManagerFactory emf() {
        return new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(Product.class).managedClass(Order.class).managedClass(OrderLine.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:Exceptions;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, "drop-and-create")
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "false")   // nine failure paths: the facts matter here, not the SQL
            .createEntityManagerFactory();
    }
 
    /* The exception you catch is rarely the one that explains the problem:
       JPA wraps Hibernate's, and commit wraps everything in RollbackException.
       Walk the cause chain and print every link, outermost first. */
    static String chain(Throwable t) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (Throwable c = t; c != null; c = c.getCause() == c ? null : c.getCause()) {
            if (sb.length() > 0) sb.append(" <- ");
            sb.append(c.getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
        return sb.toString();
    }
 
    interface Case { void run(EntityManager em) throws Exception; }
 
    static void attempt(EntityManagerFactory emf, String label, Case c) {
        EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager();
        try {
            em.getTransaction().begin();
            c.run(em);
            em.getTransaction().commit();
            System.out.println(label + ": no exception");
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.out.println(label + ": " + chain(e));
        } finally {
            if (em.isOpen()) {
                if (em.getTransaction().isActive()) em.getTransaction().rollback();
                em.close();
            }
        }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = emf()) {
            long boltId, orderId;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product bolt = new Product("BOLT-7", 80);
                em.persist(bolt);
                em.persist(new Product("NUT-3", 25));
                Order o = new Order(bolt);
                o.addLine(2);
                o.addLine(5);
                em.persist(o);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                boltId = bolt.id();
                orderId = o.id();
            }
 
            // 1. a lazy collection touched after the EntityManager is gone
            Order detachedOrder;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                detachedOrder = em.find(Order.class, orderId);
            }
            try {
                System.out.println("1 lines on a closed context: " + detachedOrder.lines().size());
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                System.out.println("1 lines on a closed context: " + chain(e));
            }
 
            // 2. an association to an object that was never persisted
            attempt(emf, "2 order -> unsaved product", em -> {
                Order o = new Order(new Product("CAM-9", 2300));   // CAM-9 is transient
                em.persist(o);
            });
 
            // 3. persist() on an entity that already has an identity
            attempt(emf, "3 persist a detached entity", em -> {
                Product bolt = em.find(Product.class, boltId);
                em.detach(bolt);
                em.persist(bolt);
            });
 
            // 4 & 5. getSingleResult expects exactly one row
            attempt(emf, "4 single result, two rows", em ->
                em.createQuery("select p from Product p", Product.class).getSingleResult());
            attempt(emf, "5 single result, no rows", em ->
                em.createQuery("select p from Product p where p.sku = 'NOPE'", Product.class).getSingleResult());
 
            // 6. two contexts edit the same row; the second commit is stale
            EntityManager em1 = emf.createEntityManager();
            EntityManager em2 = emf.createEntityManager();
            try {
                em1.getTransaction().begin();
                em2.getTransaction().begin();
                Product first = em1.find(Product.class, boltId);
                Product second = em2.find(Product.class, boltId);
                first.setPriceInCents(81);
                em1.getTransaction().commit();                  // version 0 -> 1
                second.setPriceInCents(82);
                try {
                    em2.getTransaction().commit();              // expects version 0: refused
                    System.out.println("6 stale update: no exception");
                } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                    System.out.println("6 stale update: " + chain(e));
                }
            } finally {
                if (em2.getTransaction().isActive()) em2.getTransaction().rollback();
                em1.close(); em2.close();
            }
 
            // 7. a unique constraint, discovered only at flush
            attempt(emf, "7 duplicate sku", em -> em.persist(new Product("BOLT-7", 1)));
 
            // 8. a JPQL path that does not exist, discovered at query creation
            attempt(emf, "8 unknown attribute in JPQL", em ->
                em.createQuery("select p from Product p where p.colour = 'red'", Product.class).getResultList());
 
            // 9. a transaction marked rollback-only: commit() quietly becomes rollback()
            attempt(emf, "9 commit after setRollbackOnly", em -> {
                em.find(Product.class, boltId).setPriceInCents(999);
                em.getTransaction().setRollbackOnly();
            });
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                System.out.println("  price after that commit: " + em.find(Product.class, boltId).priceInCents());
            }
 
            // the context survived all of it: the data is intact
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                System.out.println("products still in the database: " +
                    em.createQuery("select count(p) from Product p", Long.class).getSingleResult());
            }
        }
    }
}
Expected output
1 lines on a closed context: LazyInitializationException
2 order -> unsaved product: RollbackException <- IllegalStateException <- TransientPropertyValueException
3 persist a detached entity: EntityExistsException <- PersistentObjectException
4 single result, two rows: NonUniqueResultException <- NonUniqueResultException
5 single result, no rows: NoResultException
6 stale update: RollbackException <- OptimisticLockException <- StaleObjectStateException <- StaleStateException
7 duplicate sku: RollbackException <- ConstraintViolationException <- JdbcSQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException
8 unknown attribute in JPQL: IllegalArgumentException <- UnknownPathException <- PathElementException
9 commit after setRollbackOnly: no exception
  price after that commit: 81
products still in the database: 2

Nine lines, and each one teaches a rule about when Hibernate notices a problem:

  • 1 fails at access time, not at load time. The order loaded fine; the collection was left as a proxy, and the proxy's context was closed when it was first asked for its elements. Nothing in the stack trace points at the em.close() that caused it. §5 covers the fixes; the one that is not a fix is making the collection EAGER.
  • 2, 6 and 7 fail at flush, which happened inside commit(), which is why each chain starts with RollbackException. The real diagnosis is the innermost link: an unsaved reference, a stale version, a unique index. If you flushed explicitly you would see the inner exception directly and could still roll back on your own terms.
  • 3 fails immediately: persist refuses an object that already has an identifier. The JPA type is EntityExistsException; Hibernate's own message, one link in, is the famous detached entity passed to persist. The method you wanted was merge — or, more often, you wanted to keep the entity managed and never detach it.
  • 4 and 5 are query-contract failures. The doubled name in 4 is not a typo: Jakarta's NonUniqueResultException wraps Hibernate's class of the same simple name. Use getSingleResultOrNull() (JPA 3.2) or getResultStream().findFirst() when zero rows is a normal outcome.
  • 8 fails when the query is created, before any SQL exists: Hibernate parses JPQL against the mapped model, so a wrong attribute is caught as early as a compile error would be. Native SQL gives up that check.
  • 9 is the surprise: no exception at all. The JPA specification says commit() on a rollback-only transaction throws RollbackException; Hibernate, by default, silently rolls back instead and only throws if you set hibernate.jpa.compliance.transaction=true. The price check proves the write was discarded. If your code relies on commit failing to notice a problem, it never will.

What to switch on

.property("hibernate.show_sql", "true")        // print every statement to System.out — what this module uses
.property("hibernate.format_sql", "true")      // one clause per line; easier on a 40-join query, noisier on a page
.property("hibernate.highlight_sql", "true")   // ANSI colours; terminals only

show_sql writes to stdout, bypassing your logging framework entirely, which is why it is a development switch and not a production one. It also prints ? for every parameter; the bound values are a separate logging category (next tab). What it shows is exactly the statement text handed to JDBC, including Hibernate's generated aliases (p1_0) and column order.

Read a statement from its from clause outwards: which tables, joined how, then which columns, then the where. The things that should make you stop are a select inside a loop (the N+1 shape, §5), a select you did not expect before an update (a merge or a lazy load you forgot you triggered), and an update that writes every column when one changed (the default; @DynamicUpdate changes it, §9).

.property("hibernate.generate_statistics", "true")
 
Statistics st = emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
st.clear();
// … the code you are measuring …
st.getPrepareStatementCount();     // how many SQL statements were prepared
st.getEntityLoadCount();           // entities materialised from rows
st.getEntityFetchCount();          // of those, how many were lazy loads triggered by a proxy  ← the N+1 counter
st.getCollectionFetchCount();      // lazy collections initialised
st.getFlushCount();                // auto flushes forced by queries
st.getSecondLevelCacheHitCount();  // zero until you configure a cache (§9)
st.getQueryExecutionMaxTimeQueryString();   // the slowest JPQL since clear()

Statistics are the tool for a test: assert that listing twenty orders prepares one statement, and the N+1 regression can never come back silently. They are cheap enough to leave on in production behind a metrics endpoint; logSummary() prints the whole set on shutdown.

# logging.properties (java.util.logging; the same category names work in Log4j and Logback)
org.hibernate.SQL.level = FINE                # every statement, through the logging framework (no show_sql needed)
org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind.level = FINER     # the parameter values bound to each ?
org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.extract.level = FINER  # the values read back from each ResultSet column
org.hibernate.stat.level = FINE               # per-query timing and row counts as they happen
org.hibernate.SQL_SLOW.level = INFO           # with hibernate.log_slow_query=250: statements slower than 250 ms

Prefer the logger to show_sql as soon as the application has a logging framework: it goes where every other log line goes, carries timestamps and thread names, and can be turned on for one category in a running JVM. The bind category is the one that answers why did this query return nothing? — it shows the actual value, and the actual type, that was sent.

Two tools sit between Hibernate and the driver and see everything, including statements Hibernate did not issue (a migration tool, a second ORM, hand-written JDBC):

  • datasource-proxy wraps a DataSource and can log, count, or assert on statements — its QueryCountHolder is the basis of the test-time N+1 detectors in several libraries.
  • p6spy is a JDBC driver wrapper that logs every statement with its parameters inlined, timings included, with no code change beyond the JDBC URL.

For the database's own view, EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE) the statement text you copied out of the log, with the real parameter values from the bind category. Hibernate chose the statement; only the database can tell you whether it used an index.

The exception map

Common persistence exceptions, their cause and fix
Exception (innermost that matters)What it meansFix
LazyInitializationExceptionA proxy or lazy collection was touched after its context closedFetch what the use case needs inside the transaction: join fetch, an entity graph, or a DTO projection (§5)
TransientPropertyValueException / TransientObjectExceptionA managed entity references an object that was never persistedPersist the referenced entity first, or add cascade = PERSIST on that association deliberately
PersistentObjectException (detached entity passed to persist)persist called on an object that already has an idUse merge, or keep the entity managed instead of detaching it; check for an id set by hand
EntityExistsExceptionThe JPA wrapper for the previous row, or a second persist of the same id in one contextSame as above
NonUniqueObjectExceptionTwo instances with the same id in one context (typically a merge after a find)Work with the instance the context already holds; merge returns it
OptimisticLockException / StaleObjectStateExceptionThe row's @Version changed since this context read itCatch at the use-case boundary, reload, reapply, retry — or tell the user (§7)
PessimisticLockException / LockTimeoutExceptionA for update lock could not be obtained in timeShorter transactions, consistent lock order, a jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout hint
ConstraintViolationExceptionThe database rejected a row: unique, foreign key, not-null, checkValidate before persisting where the rule is yours; treat the SQL state 23505 (unique) as a normal business outcome where it is not
NonUniqueResultExceptiongetSingleResult saw more than one rowTighten the where, or use getResultList / setMaxResults(1)
NoResultExceptiongetSingleResult saw no rowsgetSingleResultOrNull() (JPA 3.2) or getResultStream().findFirst()
IllegalArgumentException wrapping UnknownPathException / SemanticExceptionJPQL refers to an attribute, entity or function that is not mappedRead the message — it names the path; check the entity name (not the table name) and the attribute spelling
QueryTimeoutExceptionThe statement exceeded jakarta.persistence.query.timeoutFix the query plan (EXPLAIN), add the index, or paginate
RollbackExceptioncommit() failed; the cause is one of the rows aboveAlways inspect getCause(); never catch this one on its own
SchemaManagementExceptionvalidate found a table or column that does not match the mappingRun the migration, or fix the mapping — never switch to update to make it go away (§10)
MappingException / AnnotationException at startupThe mapping itself is inconsistent (a mappedBy naming nothing, two owning sides, a missing no-arg constructor)The message names the entity and attribute; fix the annotation
JDBCConnectionExceptionThe driver could not reach the database, or the pool handed out a dead connectionInfrastructure: pool validation query, timeouts, and retry at the use-case boundary

A slow page: the six-step diagnosis

  1. Count the statements. Statistics or the proxy counter around the one request. A page that needs one query and runs sixty is not slow because of the database.
  2. Find the loop. Sixty near-identical select … where id=? lines are an N+1 (§5); getEntityFetchCount() names the entity being lazily loaded.
  3. Check the fetch plan. For each association the page touches: is it fetched by the query (join fetch, entity graph), batched (@BatchSize), or loaded one proxy at a time? Fix at the query, not the mapping.
  4. Check the flush count. A high getFlushCount() means queries kept forcing auto-flush of a dirty context — usually a long transaction that reads and writes alternately. Split it, or flush once at the end.
  5. Check the pool. If statements are few and fast but the request is slow, time is spent waiting for a connection: pool exhausted by long transactions, or a transaction held open across a remote call.
  6. EXPLAIN the worst statement. Only now is the database the suspect: a missing index, a cast that defeats an index (the bind category shows the type), or a select * of a table with a 4 MB blob column that a DTO projection would skip.

Mapping mistakes that cause most of the above

Common mapping mistakes and their consequences
MistakeWhat it causesInstead
FetchType.EAGER everywhere to avoid LazyInitializationExceptionEvery load drags the object graph along; a find of one order joins five tables; collections become Cartesian productsLAZY on every association (the default is already EAGER for @ManyToOne — override it), fetch per use case
List on both sides of a @ManyToManyRemoving one element deletes every join row and reinserts the restSet on the owning side
Lombok @Data (or any generated equals/hashCode/toString over all fields) on an entityhashCode changes when the id is assigned; toString walks lazy associations and throws; bidirectional links recurseBusiness-key or stable-id equality (§11), hand-written toString without associations
hashCode from the generated idAn entity put in a Set before persist is lost after it, because its hash moved bucketsNatural key, or a constant hash with id-based equals (§11)
cascade = ALL on @ManyToOneDeleting an order line deletes the product it pointed at — and fails on the foreign key from every other lineCascade only from parent to child, along the @OneToMany side
No transaction boundary around a use case (in Spring: a missing @Transactional, or one on a private method)Every statement auto-commits; dirty checking never runs; lazy loads fail outside the one statement's contextOne transaction per use case at the service boundary
spring.jpa.open-in-view=true left at its defaultLazy loads work in the view layer, so nobody notices the N+1 until production load; connections are held for the whole requestTurn it off and fetch what the view needs in the service

A word on Spring Data JPA, since most readers will meet Hibernate through it. It changes none of the above. @Transactional opens the transaction and the persistence context for you, and closes both when the method returns; JpaRepository methods such as findById and save are thin calls to find and persist-or-merge on an injected EntityManager; derived query methods are JPQL generated from the method name; @EntityGraph and @Query("… join fetch …") are how you fix N+1 there. The convenience hides the context's lifetime, which is exactly the thing this module has spent twelve sections making visible. When a Spring application misbehaves, the diagnosis is still the SQL and the statistics — and the exception map above is the same.

Debugging gotchas
  • The stack trace points at the commit, not the cause. A flush-time failure surfaces wherever the transaction ends. Flush explicitly in tests so the failing statement is next to the code that produced it.
  • An exception leaves the context unusable. After any PersistenceException the EntityManager may be inconsistent; roll back and discard it. Catching and carrying on inside the same context is how it fails only the second time bugs are born.
  • show_sql does not show parameter values. A query that returns nothing usually bound the wrong value or the wrong type; the bind log category shows both.
  • H2 is not your production database. It is excellent for this module and for fast tests, but it differs in locking, sequences, upsert syntax and type coercion. Run the integration suite against the real engine (Testcontainers makes that a one-line annotation).
  • Silence is not success. Case 9 above: Hibernate's default rollback-only behaviour never throws. A use case that ends without an exception has not necessarily written anything; read the outcome back when it matters.

Check yourself

1.A commit throws RollbackException. Where is the information that tells you what actually went wrong?

C. The worked example shows the shape: RollbackException <- ConstraintViolationException <- JdbcSQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException. The outer type only says commit failed; the inner ones say why.

A gives you a generic message. B is wrong — the chain is retained precisely so you can diagnose after rollback. D may also have it, but the JVM has it first and with the Java context.

2.A listing page runs 41 statements for 40 rows. Which statistic confirms the N+1 diagnosis most directly?

B. Fetch counts measure loads triggered by proxies — exactly the one-per-row pattern. Forty of them after one query is the fingerprint.

A measures auto-flushes forced by queries, a different problem. C is zero unless a cache is configured. D finds the slowest single query; an N+1 is forty fast queries.

3.Which of these are real consequences of putting Lombok's @Data on an entity with a bidirectional association? Select all that apply.

A, C and D. All-fields toString on both sides of a link is mutual recursion (A); walking an association to print or hash it initialises the proxy (C); and a hash that includes the generated id changes value when the id is assigned, so the Set looks in the wrong bucket (D, §11).

B is false: Hibernate maps the class happily, which is why the problems show up at runtime instead of at startup.

4.In the worked example, case 9 marks the transaction rollback-only and then calls commit(). Nothing is thrown. Why?

D. The specification mandates RollbackException; Hibernate chose leniency by default and gates the strict behaviour behind a compliance flag. The line price after that commit: 81 shows the work was indeed discarded.

A confuses the mechanism: a rollback discards the change whether or not it was flushed. B is wrong — attempt() prints any exception's chain, and would have. C is invented; rollback-only is a JPA-level flag, not a database feature.

Put it together

Hands-on lab: persisting the warehouse

Six steps that take the warehouse from in-memory collections to a real schema, with the three things a persistence layer must get right: a mapping that says what it means, stock that cannot be oversold, and reports that do not quietly run four hundred queries. Each step uses tools from one or two sections above and has a trap that the collections version never had. Write each one before opening its solution, and keep show_sql on while you do — the SQL is how you check your work.

Starter
mkdir warehouse-lab && cd warehouse-lab
# one file, WarehouseLab.java, grown step by step; LIB holds the jars from §1
javac -cp "$LIB/*" WarehouseLab.java && java -cp ".;$LIB/*" WarehouseLab      # on Linux/macOS the separator is :

Hibernate 7.4, JPA 3.2 and H2 as pinned in §1. The finished program below prints only facts and sorted data, so you can diff your run against it; it keeps show_sql off because six tables of DDL would bury the facts — the sections above have already shown you every statement shape it issues.

Step 1 — a product that knows what it is §2

Map Product with a SEQUENCE id, a sku that is both a unique column and Hibernate's @NaturalId, a Category enum stored as its name, and the price as an embedded Money value object (amount in cents plus currency). Then map StockLevel so that its primary key is the product's id, with a @Version column you will need in step 3.

Solution — step 1
@Embeddable
public record Money(long amountInCents, String currency) {}     // a record is a fine embeddable in Hibernate 6.2+
 
@Entity(name = "Product") @Table(name = "product")
public static class Product {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) private Long id;
    @NaturalId @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16) private String sku;
    @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING) @Column(nullable = false, length = 16) private Category category;
    @Embedded private Money price;
    …
}
 
@Entity(name = "StockLevel") @Table(name = "stock_level")
public static class StockLevel {
    @Id private Long id;                                     // not generated …
    @OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) @MapsId private Product product;   // … it is copied from the product
    private int onHand;
    @Version private int version;
}

@MapsId is the shared-primary-key one-to-one: no separate product_id column, no way to have a stock row for a product that does not exist, and a find(StockLevel.class, productId) that needs no join. EnumType.STRING costs a few bytes per row and survives reordering the enum; the default ORDINAL silently corrupts data the day someone inserts a constant in the middle.

Step 2 — orders, lines and suppliers §4

Order owns its OrderLines: bidirectional, cascade everything, orphan removal on, with addLine/removeLine helpers so the two sides can never disagree. The line copies the unit price at the time of the order. Supplier is many-to-many with Product through a join table — choose the collection type on the owning side deliberately. Remember that ORDER is a reserved word.

Solution — step 2
@Entity(name = "Order") @Table(name = "orders")
public static class Order {
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true) @OrderBy("id")
    private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
    void addLine(Product p, int qty) { lines.add(new OrderLine(this, p, qty, p.price().amountInCents())); }
    void removeLine(OrderLine l) { lines.remove(l); l.order = null; }
}
 
@Entity(name = "OrderLine") @Table(name = "order_line")
public static class OrderLine {
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false) private Order order;     // the owning side: this column is the FK
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false) private Product product;
    private long unitPriceInCents;                                            // history must not change when the price does
}
 
@Entity(name = "Supplier") @Table(name = "supplier")
public static class Supplier {
    @ManyToMany @JoinTable(name = "supplier_product",
        joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "supplier_id"), inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "product_id"))
    private Set<Product> products = new HashSet<>();
}

The constructor of OrderLine sets order, and addLine adds to the list: both sides, always, in one place. Cascade lives on the parent-to-child side only; a @ManyToOne with cascade = ALL would delete the product when a line is removed. The Set matters: with a List, removing one product from a supplier deletes every join row and reinserts the survivors.

Step 3 — stock that cannot be oversold §3, §7

Write reserve(sku, qty) twice. The pessimistic version loads the StockLevel with PESSIMISTIC_WRITE — a select … for update — so a second reservation waits. The optimistic version loads it normally and relies on @Version: if someone else committed first, the commit fails with OptimisticLockException, and you retry once in a fresh context. Prove the retry by having another transaction change the row between your read and your commit.

Solution — step 3
StockLevel s = em.find(StockLevel.class, productId, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE);   // pessimistic: nobody else may read-for-update until commit
s.take(qty);
 
while (true) {                                                                       // optimistic: read, change, let the version decide
    attempts++;
    try {
        if (!em.getTransaction().isActive()) em.getTransaction().begin();
        em.find(StockLevel.class, productId).take(qty);
        em.getTransaction().commit();                                                // update … where id=? and version=?
        return attempts;
    } catch (RollbackException e) {
        if (!(e.getCause() instanceof OptimisticLockException)) throw e;
        em.close(); em = emf.createEntityManager();                                  // the stale context is useless now
    }
}

Both are correct; they fail differently. Pessimistic serialises the two reservations in the database and costs a lock held for the transaction. Optimistic lets both proceed and refuses the loser at commit — cheaper when conflicts are rare, and the retry must start from a new context, because the old one still holds the stale row. After the second failure, the version check is the only thing standing between you and an oversold warehouse.

Step 4 — reports without an N+1 §5, §6

Three queries: revenue per category as a DTO (select new into a record, grouped and summed in the database); the two most expensive products with pagination; and every order with its lines and their products, listed in one statement. Prove the last claim with Statistics.getPrepareStatementCount().

Solution — step 4
select new WarehouseLab$CategoryRevenue(p.category, sum(l.qty * l.unitPriceInCents))   // a nested record: use its binary name
from OrderLine l join l.product p group by p.category order by p.category
 
select p from Product p order by p.price.amountInCents desc, p.sku        // then setFirstResult(0).setMaxResults(2)
 
select distinct o from Order o join fetch o.lines l join fetch l.product order by o.placed

The projection never materialises an entity: no persistence context entry, no dirty checking, exactly the columns the report needs. The ordered-and-limited query is the only correct pagination — getResultList().subList(…) loads the whole table. The double join fetch brings lines and products in the same result set, so touching them later costs nothing; without it the loop would run one query per order for the lines and one per line for the product. distinct keeps Hibernate from handing you the same order once per line.

Step 5 — importing five hundred products §9

Insert 500 products in one transaction without the context growing to 500 managed entities and without 500 round trips. Use a second EntityManagerFactory configured for writes — JDBC batching at 50, ordered inserts — flush and clear every 50, and report how many statements Hibernate actually prepared.

Solution — step 5
EntityManagerFactory bulk = base("none")                       // same database, no schema action this time
    .property("hibernate.jdbc.batch_size", "50")
    .property("hibernate.order_inserts", "true")
    .createEntityManagerFactory();
 
for (int i = 1; i <= 500; i++) {
    em.persist(new Product("IMP-" + i, …));
    if (i % 50 == 0) { em.flush(); em.clear(); }               // one batch out, context emptied
}

Twenty statements for five hundred rows: ten batched inserts of fifty, and ten select next value calls, because the sequence hands out fifty ids per call (§2). An IDENTITY id would have made batching impossible — Hibernate must insert each row to learn its key. The flush-and-clear keeps dirty checking cheap: a context holding ten thousand entities checks ten thousand snapshots at every flush.

Step 6 — auditing and soft delete §10, §11

Give Product createdAt/updatedAt timestamps and a revision counter maintained by lifecycle callbacks, not by every caller. Then make em.remove(product) a soft delete: the row stays, flagged, and disappears from every JPQL query — while a native count still sees it.

Solution — step 6
@Entity(name = "Product") @Table(name = "product")
@SQLDelete(sql = "update product set deleted = true where id = ?")     // what remove() issues instead of DELETE
@SQLRestriction("deleted = false")                                     // appended to every query and find
public static class Product {
    private boolean deleted;
    private Instant createdAt, updatedAt;
    private int revision;
    @PrePersist void onCreate() { createdAt = updatedAt = Instant.now(); }
    @PreUpdate  void onUpdate() { updatedAt = Instant.now(); revision++; }
}

Callbacks run inside the flush, so no caller can forget them, and @PreUpdate fires only when dirty checking found a real change. The two Hibernate annotations make soft delete a mapping concern rather than a where deleted = false that every query must remember. The native count is the reminder that the restriction is Hibernate's, not the database's: reports written in SQL, and other applications, still see the row.

The finished thing

All six steps assembled. This program is compiled and run against the pinned Hibernate and H2 during the build of this page, so every number below is what it really printed.

javaWarehouseLab.java
import jakarta.persistence.*;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.annotations.NaturalId;
import org.hibernate.annotations.SQLDelete;
import org.hibernate.annotations.SQLRestriction;
import org.hibernate.stat.Statistics;
 
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.*;
 
public class WarehouseLab {
 
    public enum Category { FASTENER, STRUCTURAL, TOOLING }
 
    @Embeddable
    public record Money(long amountInCents, String currency) {}
 
    // ── step 1: products and stock ───────────────────────────────────────────
    @Entity(name = "Product")
    @Table(name = "product")
    @SQLDelete(sql = "update product set deleted = true where id = ?")   // step 6: soft delete
    @SQLRestriction("deleted = false")
    public static class Product {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @NaturalId
        @Column(nullable = false, unique = true, length = 16)
        private String sku;
        @Column(nullable = false)
        private String name;
        @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)
        @Column(nullable = false, length = 16)
        private Category category;
        @Embedded
        private Money price;
        private boolean deleted;
        private Instant createdAt;
        private Instant updatedAt;
        private int revision;
 
        protected Product() {}
        Product(String sku, String name, Category category, long priceInCents) {
            this.sku = sku; this.name = name; this.category = category;
            this.price = new Money(priceInCents, "EUR");
        }
        @PrePersist void onCreate() { createdAt = updatedAt = Instant.now(); }
        @PreUpdate  void onUpdate() { updatedAt = Instant.now(); revision++; }
 
        Long id() { return id; }
        String sku() { return sku; }
        Category category() { return category; }
        Money price() { return price; }
        void rename(String n) { this.name = n; }
        boolean hasTimestamps() { return createdAt != null && updatedAt != null; }
        int revision() { return revision; }
        @Override public String toString() { return sku + " " + price.amountInCents() + "c"; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "StockLevel")
    @Table(name = "stock_level")
    public static class StockLevel {
        @Id
        private Long id;                                  // shares the product's id …
        @OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY) @MapsId          // … because this is the product's stock
        private Product product;
        private int onHand;
        @Version
        private int version;
 
        protected StockLevel() {}
        StockLevel(Product product, int onHand) { this.product = product; this.onHand = onHand; }
        int onHand() { return onHand; }
        int version() { return version; }
        void take(int qty) {
            if (qty > onHand) throw new IllegalStateException("only " + onHand + " on hand");
            onHand -= qty;
        }
    }
 
    // ── step 2: orders, lines, suppliers ────────────────────────────────────
    @Entity(name = "Order")
    @Table(name = "orders")                               // ORDER is a reserved word
    public static class Order {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        private LocalDate placed;
        @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
        @OrderBy("id")
        private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
 
        protected Order() {}
        Order(LocalDate placed) { this.placed = placed; }
        Long id() { return id; }
        LocalDate placed() { return placed; }
        List<OrderLine> lines() { return Collections.unmodifiableList(lines); }
        void addLine(Product p, int qty) {                // keeps both sides in step
            OrderLine l = new OrderLine(this, p, qty, p.price().amountInCents());
            lines.add(l);
        }
        void removeLine(OrderLine l) { lines.remove(l); l.order = null; }
        long totalInCents() { return lines.stream().mapToLong(OrderLine::subtotal).sum(); }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "OrderLine")
    @Table(name = "order_line")
    public static class OrderLine {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
        private Order order;
        @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
        private Product product;
        private int qty;
        private long unitPriceInCents;                    // copied: a later price change must not rewrite history
 
        protected OrderLine() {}
        OrderLine(Order order, Product product, int qty, long unitPriceInCents) {
            this.order = order; this.product = product; this.qty = qty; this.unitPriceInCents = unitPriceInCents;
        }
        Product product() { return product; }
        int qty() { return qty; }
        long subtotal() { return qty * unitPriceInCents; }
    }
 
    @Entity(name = "Supplier")
    @Table(name = "supplier")
    public static class Supplier {
        @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)
        private Long id;
        private String name;
        @ManyToMany
        @JoinTable(name = "supplier_product",
                   joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "supplier_id"),
                   inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "product_id"))
        private Set<Product> products = new HashSet<>();   // a Set: a List here makes every removal rewrite the join table
 
        protected Supplier() {}
        Supplier(String name) { this.name = name; }
        void supplies(Product p) { products.add(p); }
        Set<Product> products() { return products; }
    }
 
    // ── step 4: a projection that is not an entity ──────────────────────────
    public record CategoryRevenue(Category category, Long revenueInCents) {}
 
    // ── bootstrap ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    static PersistenceConfiguration base(String schemaAction) {
        return new PersistenceConfiguration("warehouse")
            .managedClass(Product.class).managedClass(StockLevel.class)
            .managedClass(Order.class).managedClass(OrderLine.class).managedClass(Supplier.class)
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_URL, "jdbc:h2:mem:WarehouseLab;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_USER, "sa")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.JDBC_PASSWORD, "")
            .property(PersistenceConfiguration.SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTION, schemaAction)
            .property("hibernate.show_sql", "false")
            .property("hibernate.generate_statistics", "true");
    }
 
    static Product bySku(EntityManager em, String sku) {         // the natural key is how the business names a product
        return em.createQuery("select p from Product p where p.sku = :sku", Product.class)
                 .setParameter("sku", sku).getSingleResult();
    }
 
    static Statistics stats(EntityManagerFactory emf) {
        return emf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
    }
 
    // ── step 3: reserve stock ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    static void reservePessimistic(EntityManagerFactory emf, String sku, int qty) {
        try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
            em.getTransaction().begin();
            Product p = bySku(em, sku);
            StockLevel s = em.find(StockLevel.class, p.id(), LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE);  // select … for update
            s.take(qty);
            em.getTransaction().commit();
        }
    }
 
    static int reserveOptimistic(EntityManagerFactory emf, EntityManager stale, long productId, int qty) {
        // 'stale' already holds a StockLevel read before someone else changed it
        int attempts = 0;
        EntityManager em = stale;
        while (true) {
            attempts++;
            try {
                if (!em.getTransaction().isActive()) em.getTransaction().begin();
                StockLevel s = em.find(StockLevel.class, productId);
                s.take(qty);
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                em.close();
                return attempts;
            } catch (RollbackException e) {
                if (!(e.getCause() instanceof OptimisticLockException)) throw e;
                em.close();
                em = emf.createEntityManager();           // a fresh context: re-read, re-apply
            }
        }
    }
 
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (EntityManagerFactory emf = base("drop-and-create").createEntityManagerFactory()) {
            Statistics st = stats(emf);
 
            // ── seed ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
            long boltId;
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product bolt = new Product("BOLT-7", "M8 bolt", Category.FASTENER, 80);
                Product nut  = new Product("NUT-3", "M8 nut", Category.FASTENER, 25);
                Product gird = new Product("GIRD-1", "Steel girder", Category.STRUCTURAL, 120_000);
                Product cam  = new Product("CAM-9", "Cam follower", Category.TOOLING, 2_300);
                for (Product p : List.of(bolt, nut, gird, cam)) em.persist(p);
                em.persist(new StockLevel(bolt, 500));
                em.persist(new StockLevel(nut, 1_000));
                em.persist(new StockLevel(gird, 3));
                em.persist(new StockLevel(cam, 40));
 
                Supplier acme = new Supplier("Acme Fasteners");
                acme.supplies(bolt); acme.supplies(nut);
                em.persist(acme);
 
                Order o1 = new Order(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 1));
                o1.addLine(bolt, 100); o1.addLine(nut, 100);
                Order o2 = new Order(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 3));
                o2.addLine(gird, 1); o2.addLine(cam, 2);
                Order o3 = new Order(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 9));
                o3.addLine(bolt, 20);
                for (Order o : List.of(o1, o2, o3)) em.persist(o);       // cascades to the lines
                em.getTransaction().commit();
                boltId = bolt.id();
            }
            System.out.println("-- step 1+2: mapped and seeded --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                Product bolt = em.find(Product.class, boltId);
                System.out.println("product     = " + bolt + " (" + bolt.category() + ")");
                System.out.println("stock id    = " + em.find(StockLevel.class, boltId).onHand() + " on hand, shares id " + boltId);
                Supplier s = em.createQuery("select s from Supplier s", Supplier.class).getSingleResult();
                System.out.println("supplier    = " + s.products().stream().map(Product::sku).sorted().toList());
                System.out.println("orders      = " + em.createQuery("select count(o) from Order o", Long.class).getSingleResult()
                    + ", lines = " + em.createQuery("select count(l) from OrderLine l", Long.class).getSingleResult());
            }
 
            // ── step 3 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
            System.out.println("-- step 3: reserving stock --");
            reservePessimistic(emf, "BOLT-7", 120);
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                System.out.println("after pessimistic reserve: " + em.find(StockLevel.class, boltId).onHand());
            }
            EntityManager stale = emf.createEntityManager();
            stale.getTransaction().begin();
            stale.find(StockLevel.class, boltId);                           // version 0 is now in this context
            reservePessimistic(emf, "BOLT-7", 30);                          // someone else commits first: version 1
            int attempts = reserveOptimistic(emf, stale, boltId, 50);
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                StockLevel s = em.find(StockLevel.class, boltId);
                System.out.println("optimistic reserve took " + attempts + " attempts; on hand " + s.onHand() + ", version " + s.version());
            }
 
            // ── step 4 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
            System.out.println("-- step 4: reports --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                List<CategoryRevenue> rev = em.createQuery(
                    "select new WarehouseLab$CategoryRevenue(p.category, sum(l.qty * l.unitPriceInCents)) " +
                    "from OrderLine l join l.product p group by p.category order by p.category", CategoryRevenue.class)
                    .getResultList();
                for (CategoryRevenue r : rev) System.out.println("revenue " + r.category() + " = " + r.revenueInCents());
 
                List<Product> top = em.createQuery(
                    "select p from Product p order by p.price.amountInCents desc, p.sku", Product.class)
                    .setFirstResult(0).setMaxResults(2).getResultList();
                System.out.println("top 2 by price = " + top);
 
                st.clear();
                List<Order> orders = em.createQuery(
                    "select distinct o from Order o join fetch o.lines l join fetch l.product order by o.placed", Order.class)
                    .getResultList();
                for (Order o : orders) {
                    System.out.println("order " + o.placed() + " total " + o.totalInCents() + "c, " + o.lines().size() + " lines, first " + o.lines().get(0).product().sku());
                }
                System.out.println("statements for " + orders.size() + " orders with lines and products: " + st.getPrepareStatementCount());
            }
 
            // ── step 6 (part a): callbacks ──────────────────────────────────
            System.out.println("-- step 6: callbacks and soft delete --");
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product bolt = em.find(Product.class, boltId);
                System.out.println("timestamps set on persist: " + bolt.hasTimestamps() + ", revision " + bolt.revision());
                bolt.rename("M8 bolt, zinc");
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                Product bolt = em.find(Product.class, boltId);
                System.out.println("revision after one update: " + bolt.revision());
                Product cam = bySku(em, "CAM-9");
                em.remove(cam);                                              // runs the @SQLDelete update instead
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
            try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
                long visible = em.createQuery("select count(p) from Product p", Long.class).getSingleResult();
                Number rows = (Number) em.createNativeQuery("select count(*) from product").getSingleResult();
                System.out.println("products via JPQL: " + visible + ", rows in the table: " + rows);
            }
        }
 
        // ── step 5: bulk import on a second factory tuned for writes ────────
        System.out.println("-- step 5: bulk import --");
        try (EntityManagerFactory bulk = base("none")
                .property("hibernate.jdbc.batch_size", "50")
                .property("hibernate.order_inserts", "true")
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {
            Statistics st = stats(bulk);
            st.clear();
            try (EntityManager em = bulk.createEntityManager()) {
                em.getTransaction().begin();
                for (int i = 1; i <= 500; i++) {
                    em.persist(new Product("IMP-" + i, "Imported part " + i, Category.TOOLING, 100 + i));
                    if (i % 50 == 0) { em.flush(); em.clear(); }           // keep the context small
                }
                em.getTransaction().commit();
            }
            System.out.println("entities inserted     : " + st.getEntityInsertCount());
            System.out.println("statements prepared   : " + st.getPrepareStatementCount());
            try (EntityManager em = bulk.createEntityManager()) {
                System.out.println("imported rows visible : " +
                    em.createQuery("select count(p) from Product p where p.sku like 'IMP-%'", Long.class).getSingleResult());
            }
        }
    }
}
Expected output
-- step 1+2: mapped and seeded --
product     = BOLT-7 80c (FASTENER)
stock id    = 500 on hand, shares id 1
supplier    = [BOLT-7, NUT-3]
orders      = 3, lines = 5
-- step 3: reserving stock --
after pessimistic reserve: 380
optimistic reserve took 2 attempts; on hand 300, version 3
-- step 4: reports --
revenue FASTENER = 12100
revenue STRUCTURAL = 120000
revenue TOOLING = 4600
top 2 by price = [GIRD-1 120000c, CAM-9 2300c]
order 2026-10-01 total 10500c, 2 lines, first BOLT-7
order 2026-10-03 total 124600c, 2 lines, first GIRD-1
order 2026-10-09 total 1600c, 1 lines, first BOLT-7
statements for 3 orders with lines and products: 1
-- step 6: callbacks and soft delete --
timestamps set on persist: true, revision 0
revision after one update: 1
products via JPQL: 3, rows in the table: 4
-- step 5: bulk import --
entities inserted     : 500
statements prepared   : 20
imported rows visible : 500

Why each number is what it is. The stock row shares id 1 because @MapsId copied the bolt's generated key. After the pessimistic reserve of 120, 380 remain; the optimistic attempt read the row at version 0, another transaction took 30 and committed (version 1, 350 on hand), so the first commit was refused, the retry read 350 at version 1 and committed 300 at version 2 — the printed 3 is one more because the pessimistic path also bumps the version. Revenue sums qty × unitPriceInCents per line: 100 × 80 + 100 × 25 + 20 × 80 = 12100 for fasteners. The three orders with all their lines and products took 1 statement because of the two join fetches. Revision 1 after the rename shows @PreUpdate fired exactly once. JPQL sees 3 products after the soft delete; the native count sees the row still there, 4. And the import prepared 20 statements for 500 rows: ten batches of fifty inserts and ten sequence calls.

Extensions worth attempting
  • Turn show_sql back on and read the step 3 statements: find the for update, and the update … where id=? and version=?. Then change StockLevel to IDENTITY ids and watch the step 5 statement count explode.
  • Add a Warehouse entity and make StockLevel keyed by (product, warehouse) with an @EmbeddedId. What does reserve need to change, and which query in step 4 now has to say which warehouse it means?
  • Make the soft delete visible to one report: write a native query that lists deleted products, then a JPQL equivalent — and discover why the JPQL one cannot be written without @FilterDef/@Filter, which can be switched off per session where @SQLRestriction cannot.

Reference

Cheat sheet

Everything worth having in front of you while a persistence layer is misbehaving. This section is laid out to print cleanly — controls and navigation are hidden, and tables are kept whole across page breaks. Each block names the section it condenses. Where a fact is specific to the pinned stack (Hibernate 7.4, JPA 3.2, H2), it says so.

Bootstrap without persistence.xml §1

PersistenceConfiguration keys and their Hibernate equivalents
JPA 3.2 constantPropertyHibernate equivalent / note
JDBC_URL, JDBC_USER, JDBC_PASSWORDjakarta.persistence.jdbc.url …hibernate.connection.url …; the built-in pool is not for production — use HikariCP
SCHEMAGEN_DATABASE_ACTIONjakarta.persistence.schema-generation.database.actionnone / create / drop-and-create / drop; if set, it overrides hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto (§10)
—hibernate.hbm2ddl.autovalidate is Hibernate-only; set this and not the JPA key when you want validation
—hibernate.show_sqlEcho each logical statement to stdout; format_sql pretty-prints; cannot show batching
—hibernate.generate_statisticsemf.unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics(): prepared statements, entity loads, flushes
—hibernate.jdbc.batch_size, hibernate.order_inserts, hibernate.order_updatesJDBC batching (§9); useless with IDENTITY ids
—hibernate.physical_naming_strategyCamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy → price_in_cents (Spring Boot's default)
—hibernate.jpa.compliance.transactiontrue makes commit() on a rollback-only transaction throw RollbackException; by default Hibernate rolls back quietly (§7)
.managedClass(X.class)—Register every entity, embeddable and auto-applied converter; a nested entity needs @Entity(name = "X") or JPQL must say Outer$X

Architecture: one EntityManagerFactory per application (expensive, thread-safe); one EntityManager per unit of work (cheap, not thread-safe); one transaction per unit of work. The first Hibernate: line of every program here, create global temporary table HTE_…, is Hibernate 7's scratch table for bulk HQL on H2 — harmless.

Mapping annotations by purpose §2

Mapping annotations grouped by what they control
PurposeAnnotationsRemember
The class@Entity(name), @Table(name, indexes, uniqueConstraints), @Access(FIELD)no-arg constructor, not final, not a record, static if nested
The key@Id, @GeneratedValue(strategy), @SequenceGenerator(allocationSize), @EmbeddedId, @NaturalId (Hibernate)default SEQUENCE allocation is 50; IDENTITY inserts at persist
A column@Column(name, nullable, unique, length, precision, scale, updatable), @Basic(optional), @Lob, @Transientunannotated String is varchar(255); hints become constraints only via schema generation
A type@Enumerated(STRING), @Convert / @Converter(autoApply = true), java.time types need nothingnever ORDINAL; @Temporal is for java.util.Date only
A value object@Embeddable + @Embedded + @AttributeOverride; an @Embeddable record works in Hibernate 6.2+columns live in the owner's table; no identity
Concurrency@VersionHibernate owns the field: no setter
Hibernate extras@Formula, @DynamicUpdate, @Immutable, @SQLDelete, @SQLRestriction, @BatchSize, @Fetch(SUBSELECT)portable only between Hibernate versions

Id strategies and what they cost §2 §9

Identifier generation strategies compared
StrategyId known atInsert runs atBatchingRound trips for 100 rows
SEQUENCE, allocationSize 50 (default)persistflushyes2 sequence calls + 100 inserts, or 5 batches of 20
SEQUENCE, allocationSize 1persistflushyes100 sequence calls + the inserts
IDENTITYafter insertpersist — and it flushes earlier queued inserts firstno100, always
TABLEpersistflushyesselect + update on the generator table per block; slow, portable, avoid
UUIDpersist (in the JVM)flushyesno database call; random v4 scatters the primary-key index — prefer time-ordered at scale

MySQL has no sequences: SEQUENCE silently becomes a table generator there — read the DDL.

Entity states × operations §3

What each EntityManager operation does to an entity's state
OperationFrom → toSQL at call timeSQL at flushGotcha
persist(e)transient → managedselect next value (SEQUENCE) / the insert (IDENTITY)insertdetached argument → PersistentObjectException
find(C, id)row → managed, or identity-map hitselect unless already in the context—second find in one context never re-reads: repeatable read, stale if another transaction wrote
getReference(C, id)→ managed proxynone—first non-id getter loads; getClass() is a subclass
a setter on a managed entitymanaged → managed (dirty)noneupdate of every column (unless @DynamicUpdate)no "save" call exists or is needed
merge(e)argument stays detached; returns a managed copyselect if not in the contextupdate (or insert for a transient argument)copies all fields: a half-filled form overwrites the rest
detach(e) / clear()managed → detachednonenothing for that entityclear() also discards un-flushed changes
refresh(e)managed → managed, memory overwrittenselect—the opposite of flush
remove(e)managed → removed (leaves the context now)nonedeletecascades REMOVE; a later find goes to the database
flush()—the whole queue: inserts, updates, collection changes, deletes — in that order, not call order—remove + persist of the same unique key fails: the insert runs first

FlushModeType.AUTO (default) flushes before a JPQL/Criteria query over a table with pending changes and before every native query; COMMIT flushes only at commit. Rollback evicts every managed entity: after rollback() they are detached.

Associations: owning side, fetch default, collection type §4

Association types and their defaults
AssociationOwning side (what is written)Default fetchCollection
@ManyToOnethis side: the foreign-key column (@JoinColumn(name = …) — name it)EAGER — set LAZY—
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "…")the many side; this side is inverse and ignored for writesLAZYList = bag (remove re-inserts), Set needs a correct equals, @OrderColumn for a real list
@OneToMany unidirectional, no mappedBythis side, via a join table you did not ask for (unless @JoinColumn)LAZYas above
@ManyToManythe side declaring @JoinTable; the other says mappedByLAZYSet; never cascade REMOVE
@OneToOnethe side with @JoinColumn, or @MapsId to share the parent's keyEAGER; the inverse (mappedBy) side cannot be lazy — Hibernate must query to know if it is null—

Cascade and orphan removal §4

When to cascade and when not to
SituationUseNever
Parent owns children that cannot exist alone (order → lines)cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true on the parent's collection—
Reference to a shared entity (line → product, product ↔ supplier)no cascade; persist the target yourself or getReference itREMOVE on @ManyToOne or @ManyToMany — deletes the shared row
Remove a child from the parent's collection and delete its roworphanRemoval = truerelying on cascade = REMOVE (that only fires when the parent is removed)
Keep both sides of a bidirectional pair consistenta sync helper: lines.add(l); l.order = this;setting only the inverse side — the FK is written as null
 
// Bidirectional one-to-many, done the way that writes the foreign key
@Entity(name = "Order") @Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) private Long id;
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();
 
    public void addLine(OrderLine line)    { lines.add(line);    line.setOrder(this); }   // both sides, always
    public void removeLine(OrderLine line) { lines.remove(line); line.setOrder(null); }   // orphanRemoval deletes the row
}
 
@Entity(name = "OrderLine") @Table(name = "order_line")
public class OrderLine {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE) private Long id;
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)      // LAZY: never let a line drag its order in
    @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")                            // name the column; the default follows the field name
    private Order order;
    void setOrder(Order order) { this.order = order; }
}

Fetch strategies and statement counts §5

Fetch strategies with the number of statements each costs
StrategyStatements for N parents, one collectionDeclared inTrap
Lazy (default), touched in a loop1 + Nthe mappingthe N+1 problem; invisible locally, ruinous over a network
fetch = EAGER on the mapping1 + N for JPQL (one join only for find)the mapping — for every load, foreverdoes not fix N+1 for queries; mark everything LAZY instead
join fetch (inner) / left join fetch1the querytwo Lists → MultipleBagFetchException; two Sets → cartesian product; with setMaxResults → in-memory paging, warning HHH90003004
Entity graph (jakarta.persistence.fetchgraph / loadgraph)1 (a left join)a hint or @NamedEntityGraphfetchgraph makes everything not listed lazy
@BatchSize(size = k) / session.setFetchBatchSize(k)1 + ⌈N / k⌉mapping, class or sessionin (?, …) lists are padded to the batch size
@Fetch(SUBSELECT)2the mapping (Hibernate)loads every collection of the original result at the first touch
DTO projection (select new)1the querynone — no entities, no lazy anything; the right default for read screens

LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy / collection of role … (no session) = the entity outlived its context. Fix the fetch plan or return a DTO; open-session-in-view only hides it.

JPQL constructs and the SQL Hibernate generates for them
JPQLBecomesNote

// Criteria API skeleton: predicates added only for the filters that were supplied
CriteriaBuilder cb = em.getCriteriaBuilder();
CriteriaQuery<Product> cq = cb.createQuery(Product.class);
Root<Product> p = cq.from(Product.class);
List<Predicate> where = new ArrayList<>();
if (category != null) where.add(cb.equal(p.get("category"), category));
if (minPrice != null) where.add(cb.ge(p.get("priceInCents"), minPrice));
cq.select(p).where(where.toArray(new Predicate[0])).orderBy(cb.asc(p.get("sku")));
List<Product> result = em.createQuery(cq).getResultList();
// projection: cb.construct(SkuRevenue.class, p.get("sku"), cb.sum(...)) with .groupBy(...)

Flush modes and lock modes §7

Flush modes, lock modes and the SQL each produces
SettingEffectSQL you will see
FlushModeType.AUTOflush before a query that could see pending changes, and at commitan insert/update just before your select
FlushModeType.COMMITflush only at commit; queries may contradict pending writesthe query first, the writes at commit()
@Version (optimistic)every update carries the version it read; 0 rows updated → OptimisticLockException (wrapped in RollbackException at commit)update … set …, version=? where id=? and version=?
LockModeType.OPTIMISTICre-check the version at commit even without changesa select version at commit
OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENTbump the version on a read — version the aggregate through its parentupdate … set version=? where id=? and version=?
PESSIMISTIC_WRITEexclusive row lock until commit; waiters block, then PessimisticLockException / LockTimeoutException after jakarta.persistence.lock.timeoutselect … for update
PESSIMISTIC_READshared lock: others may read, none may writefor share where the dialect has it
setRollbackOnly()commit rolls back instead; no exception with Hibernate's defaultsnothing — unless hibernate.jpa.compliance.transaction=true

Isolation is the connection's default (READ_COMMITTED on PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, H2; REPEATABLE_READ on MySQL/InnoDB); JPA sets none. Inside one context you have repeatable reads anyway, via the identity map.

// Optimistic retry: re-read and re-apply, never reuse the failed EntityManager
int attempts = 0;
while (true) {
    attempts++;
    try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) {
        em.getTransaction().begin();
        StockLevel s = em.find(StockLevel.class, id);     // fresh copy, current version
        s.pick(qty);                                      // the business change
        em.getTransaction().commit();                     // update … where id=? and version=?
        return attempts;
    } catch (RollbackException e) {
        if (!(e.getCause() instanceof OptimisticLockException) || attempts >= 3) throw e;
        // someone else committed first: loop, with a fresh context
    }
}

Inheritance strategies, their DDL and their query shapes
StrategyTablesPolymorphic querySubclass NOT NULL?IdsDefault choice
SINGLE_TABLEone, with a discriminator column (and a check constraint on its values)one select filtered by the discriminatorno — subclass columns must be nullableanyyes, unless subclass fields are many and mandatory
JOINEDparent + one per subclass sharing the primary keyparent left join every subclass table, with a case to decide the typeyesanywhen constraints and normalisation matter

Writes and reads that scale §9

Performance levers and what each changes
LeverSetting / APIMeasured effect in the worked example
JDBC batchinghibernate.jdbc.batch_size=20 + order_inserts + order_updates, SEQUENCE ids100 inserts: 100 statements with IDENTITY → 8 with SEQUENCE and batching (3 sequence calls + 5 batches)
Bounded context in loopsem.flush(); em.clear(); every batch, or a StatelessSessionmemory stays flat; dirty checking stays cheap
Read without hydratingselect new Dto(…), Tuple, select count(p)entities hydrated: 3 → 0
Read without dirty checkingsession.setDefaultReadOnly(true) / hint org.hibernate.readOnlyentity updates after a change: 0
Change many rowsbulk JPQL update / deleteone statement; clear the context afterwards
Narrow updates@DynamicUpdateonly changed columns, at the cost of statement-cache misses
Second-level cache@Cacheable + a JCache/Infinispan provider (not on this class path)caches entities by id (and natural ids, collections if asked); not queries
Query cachehibernate.cache.use_query_cache + the hint per querycaches id lists; invalidated by any write to the tables involved — rarely a win

Measure with Statistics (getPrepareStatementCount, getEntityLoadCount, getFlushCount), never with show_sql alone: it prints one line per logical statement whether or not it was batched.

Schema settings per environment §10

Which schema setting is acceptable where
SettingDoesLocal devCI testsStaging / production
drop-and-create / create-dropdrops everything mapped, recreates itfinefinenever
createdrops and creates, keeps the schema at exitfinefinenever
updateadds missing tables/columns; cannot rename, narrow, drop or move data; no reviewtolerableriskynever — it is not a migration
validate (hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto only)compares mapping to tables and columns; refuses to start on a mismatch; ignores indexes, sequences and FK names—yesyes, with a migration tool owning the DDL
nonenothing — and it disables validate if both are set——with Flyway/Liquibase and without validate

Workflow: generate DDL from the entities once (jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.scripts.action=create) as a starting point, hand-edit it into V1__init.sql, let Flyway or Liquibase apply it, run validate at startup. Rolling deploys need backward-compatible migrations: add, write both, backfill, switch reads, drop.

Entity identity and equality §11

equals/hashCode options for entities
OptionBehaviour in a HashSet across persistUse when
equals/hashCode on the generated idbreaks: hash changes when the id is assigned; contains returns false after persistnever with generated ids
Immutable business key (sku)correcta natural key exists and never changes
equals on id (null-safe), hashCode returns a constantcorrect; all entities share one bucket per set — fine for the small sets entities live inno business key; the usual recommendation
No override (identity)correct within one context, wrong across contextsentities never compared across contexts

Never put a lazy @ManyToOne in equals or toString. Lombok @Data on an entity generates all of the above wrongly at once. Callbacks: @PrePersist/@PreUpdate (and @EntityListeners) for audit fields; @SQLDelete + @SQLRestriction for soft delete — JPQL and find no longer see the row, native SQL still does; @Immutable for reference data (changes are silently ignored).

Exceptions → cause → fix §12

Common persistence exceptions with cause and fix
Exception (as thrown by Hibernate 7.4)CauseFix
LazyInitializationExceptionlazy proxy or collection touched after the context closedfetch in the query, entity graph, batch size, or return a DTO
RollbackException ← IllegalStateException ← TransientPropertyValueExceptionflushed an entity referencing an unsaved one, no cascadepersist the target first, or cascade PERSIST
EntityExistsException ← PersistentObjectException "detached entity passed to persist"persist on an object that has an idmerge, or load and modify the managed instance
