RollbackException ← ConstraintViolationException ← the driver's integrity exceptionunique / FK / not-null / check violated at flushvalidate before the write; read the constraint name
IllegalArgumentException ← UnknownPathExceptiona JPQL attribute that does not existJPQL names fields, not columns; use the metamodel

Rehearsal

Interview questions

Twelve questions that actually get asked about JPA and Hibernate, with the answer a strong candidate gives. Say your answer out loud before opening the reveal — recognising an answer and being able to produce one are different skills.

Easy  1. What is the persistence context?

It is the set of entities an EntityManager currently manages, implemented as two things: an identity map and a snapshot store. The identity map guarantees one Java instance per primary key inside one context — a second find for the same id returns the same object without touching the database, which is why it is also called the first-level cache. The snapshot store holds each managed entity's state as loaded; at flush time Hibernate compares the current state with the snapshot and emits an update for every row that differs. That is dirty checking, and it is why there is no update method on the API. The context is write-behind: operations are queued and flushed at commit, before a query that could see them, or on an explicit flush(). It is scoped to one EntityManager, which is cheap, single-threaded and meant to live for one unit of work.

Easy  2. What is the difference between persist and merge?

persist takes a transient object and makes that instance managed; it returns nothing, and passing a detached instance throws PersistentObjectException ("detached entity passed to persist"). With a SEQUENCE id it only asks the sequence for a value and queues the insert; with IDENTITY it must insert at once to learn the id. merge takes a detached (or transient) object, loads the current row if it is not already in the context, copies the argument's state onto the managed instance and returns that instance — the argument stays detached, so a setter called on it afterwards is lost. Because it copies every field, merging a half-populated object overwrites the columns it did not carry. The habit to recommend: load, modify the managed instance, commit; reach for merge only for a genuinely detached object, and always use its return value.

Easy  3. What does "owning side" mean, and what does mappedBy do?

A relational database stores a relationship in one place — a foreign-key column or a join-table row — while an object graph can hold it on both ends. JPA resolves that by declaring one side the owner: the side whose field maps to the column. For @ManyToOne/@OneToMany that is always the many side, because the foreign key lives in its table; for @ManyToMany it is the side that declares @JoinTable; for @OneToOne it is the side with @JoinColumn or @MapsId. mappedBy marks the other side as the inverse: Hibernate loads it, iterates it and cascades through it, but ignores it when deciding what to write. Add a line to order.getLines() without setting line.setOrder(order) and the row is inserted with a null foreign key. The fix is a sync helper that sets both sides, and the rule is that only the owning side's state reaches the database.

Easy  4. What causes the N+1 problem and how do you fix it?

Lazy associations load on first access, one query per instance. Query fifty orders and loop over order.getLines() and you run one query for the orders and fifty more for the lines — fifty-one round trips for a page that needed one. It is invisible in the code and in local tests because each query is tiny; it shows up as latency under network round-trip cost. You detect it by counting statements, with hibernate.generate_statistics or a proxy driver, never by reading the code. Three fixes, chosen per query: join fetch (or an entity graph) to bring the collection in the same statement; @BatchSize to load collections for several parents at once with an in (…) list; or a DTO projection that reads only the columns the screen needs and hydrates no entities. The non-fix is fetch = EAGER: it changes every load forever and does not even reduce the statement count for JPQL queries.

Medium  5. What is LazyInitializationException, and is open-session-in-view the answer?

It is thrown when a lazy proxy or collection is touched after the persistence context that owned it has closed — typically an entity returned from a service method and then rendered in a view, or serialised to JSON. The message names the collection role and the key: "no session". Open-session-in-view keeps the EntityManager open until the response is written, so the lazy loads succeed; I argue against it. It hides the exception while leaving every lazy load in place, now running N+1 from the template; it pins a database connection for the whole request including the rendering time; and it moves data access out of the layer that is supposed to own transactions. The right answers are to fetch what the view needs inside the service — join fetch, an entity graph, batch fetching — or to return a DTO that already contains it. Spring Boot's spring.jpa.open-in-view defaults to true, which is why so many teams meet this question late.

Medium  6. How does @Version work, and what exactly fails?

It is optimistic locking: a numeric (or timestamp) column that Hibernate includes in every update's where clause and increments in its set clause — update … set …, version=? where id=? and version=?. Two transactions read the row at version 0; the first commits and the row becomes version 1; the second's update still says where version=0, matches zero rows, and Hibernate turns that unexpected count into OptimisticLockException, wrapped in RollbackException because it happened at commit. Nothing was overwritten — the lost update was detected rather than prevented. The caller must close that context, re-read and retry, or report the conflict; the context after the exception is undefined. The field belongs to Hibernate: no setter, never copied from a DTO. The same version carried through a detached entity or a hidden form field makes the check work across an hour and two transactions, which is how long edit forms stay correct without holding a connection.

Medium  7. Why does GenerationType.IDENTITY hurt insert performance?

With an identity column the database assigns the key during the insert, and Hibernate must know the key to register the entity in the persistence context. So persist cannot queue the insert; it executes it immediately, reads the generated id back, and — to keep statement order — flushes any earlier queued inserts first. Write-behind is gone for that entity, and with it JDBC batching: a hundred persists are a hundred round trips whatever hibernate.jdbc.batch_size says, and the statistics prove it. With SEQUENCE the id comes from a select next value call, one per allocation block of fifty by default, the inserts wait for the flush, and with batching and ordered inserts a hundred rows become a handful of statements. IDENTITY is the right choice only when the database offers nothing else or writes are rare; on MySQL be aware that SEQUENCE falls back to a table generator.

Medium  8. What goes wrong when you paginate a query that uses join fetch?

A fetched collection multiplies the result rows: an order with three lines is three rows in the joined result. A SQL LIMIT 10 would therefore cut through the middle of some order's lines and return a partially initialised collection, which Hibernate refuses to do. Instead it drops the limit from the SQL, loads the whole result, and applies setFirstResult/setMaxResults in memory, logging HHH90003004: firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory. For a large table that is the full table through the network on every page. The fix is two steps: page the parent entities with a plain query, then load their collections for that page with batch fetching or a second join fetch query restricted to those ids, or project a DTO. Related traps: two List collections cannot be join-fetched together (MultipleBagFetchException), and two Sets can, but produce a cartesian product.

Medium  9. SINGLE_TABLE or JOINED — how do you choose?

SINGLE_TABLE puts the whole hierarchy in one table with a discriminator column: a polymorphic query is one select, a subtype query is the same select with a discriminator predicate, inserts touch one table. The cost is that every subclass-specific column must be nullable, because rows of other subtypes have nothing to put there, so the database cannot enforce "a card payment always has a last-four". JOINED gives each subclass its own table sharing the parent's primary key: subclass columns can be NOT NULL, the schema is normalised, but a polymorphic query left-joins every subclass table and uses a case expression to decide the type, and inserts write two rows. My default is SINGLE_TABLE while the subclass-specific fields are few; I move to JOINED when they are many or must be constrained. TABLE_PER_CLASS — a union over every concrete table and no identity ids — almost never. A @MappedSuperclass is not inheritance mapping at all: it copies shared columns into each table and cannot be queried.

Hard  10. Why is hbm2ddl.auto=update not a migration strategy?

Because it only adds. It compares the mapping to the schema and creates missing tables and columns; it cannot rename a column, narrow a type, drop anything, move data between columns or add the not-null constraint to a column that already has nulls. Rename a field and you get a new empty column beside the old full one, silently. Nothing is reviewed, nothing is versioned, nothing can be rolled back, and the DDL it runs differs by dialect, so what worked on H2 in tests is not what runs on PostgreSQL. The alternative is boring and right: generate the DDL from the entities once as a starting point, hand-edit it into a versioned script, let Flyway or Liquibase apply scripts in order with checksums, and run validate at startup so the application refuses to boot against a schema it does not match. Two details people miss: validate checks tables and columns but not sequences or indexes, and setting the JPA property schema-generation.database.action=none alongside it silently disables the validation.

Hard  11. How should an entity implement equals and hashCode?

The constraint is that hashCode must not change while the object is in a hash-based collection, and a generated id does not exist until persist. So the obvious implementation — equals and hashCode on the id — breaks: add the entity to a HashSet, persist it, and contains returns false because it now hashes to a different bucket; the worked example prints exactly that. Three correct options. If there is an immutable business key, such as a SKU, use it for both. Otherwise use the id for equals (null-safe, so two transient instances are never equal) and return a constant from hashCode; every entity of that type shares a bucket, which is fine for the small sets entities live in, and the hash never moves. Or do not override at all and compare only within one context, where the identity map makes == correct. Never include a lazy @ManyToOne in either method, and never let Lombok's @Data generate them for an entity.

Hard  12. What does the second-level cache cache, and what does it not?

It caches entity state by primary key, shared across persistence contexts and backed by a provider such as JCache or Infinispan, for entities marked @Cacheable. A find or a lazy proxy resolution for a cached id skips the database; natural-id lookups and collections can be cached too if asked. It does not cache queries: select p from Product p where … still hits the database, and if you enable the separate query cache it stores only the matching ids, with a timestamp region that invalidates every cached result the moment any table in the query is written — which in a system that writes regularly makes it a cost, not a saving. Concurrency strategies matter: READ_ONLY for reference data, READ_WRITE or TRANSACTIONAL for data that changes, and any write outside Hibernate (a bulk JPQL statement, a migration, another service) leaves the cache stale. My rule: cache immutable reference entities, measure with statistics, and treat the query cache as a last resort.

Assessment

Self-assessment quiz

Sixteen questions covering all twelve learning objectives. Answer every one, then submit — nothing is marked until you do, and the explanations stay hidden until then. Your answers are saved locally, so you can leave and come back. Each question about runtime behaviour was checked against this module's verified programs on Hibernate 7.4 and H2.

1.An entity uses GenerationType.SEQUENCE with the default allocation size. Inside a transaction you call em.persist(product) and stop there. Which SQL has executed so far?

B. The identity map needs a key, so the sequence is consulted at persist (once per block of fifty); the insert waits for the flush. FirstEntity printed two sequence calls, then two inserts at commit. A and D describe IDENTITY, where the row must be inserted to obtain the key. C is contradicted by the id being printable before commit.

2.Product has SEQUENCE ids, Warehouse has IDENTITY ids. In one transaction the code persists a product, then a warehouse, then prints a line, then commits. Which inserts have run when the line is printed?

C. The Mapping program's output shows the product insert, then insert into warehouse … values (?,default), and only then the printed line. A ignores that an identity column is assigned by the database during the insert. B misses the ordering rule: Hibernate does not let a later insert overtake an earlier queued one. D has the forced insert on the wrong entity.

3.sku has a unique constraint. One transaction calls em.remove(oldBolt), then persists a new product with the same SKU, then commits. Result?

B. The action queue is sorted at flush: inserts, updates, collection changes, deletes. An explicit flush() between the two calls fixes it. A is the assumption behind the bug. C concerns a duplicate id in the context; the new entity has a fresh one. D: two different entities are never folded into one statement.

4.Order.lines is @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true) and OrderLine.order is the @ManyToOne with the @JoinColumn. Which are true? Select all that apply.

A and C. Both were printed by the Relationships program: a line with order_id null in block 1, and a delete from order_line after removeLine in block 3. B is reversed — the side holding the foreign key owns the association, and mappedBy marks Order.lines as inverse. D: cascade = ALL includes REMOVE, so the lines are deleted before the order.

5.Fifty orders with a lazy lines collection are loaded with select o from Order o, and a loop reads getLines().size() on each. Statement count with the default mapping, and with @BatchSize(size = 25) on the collection?

C. One query for the orders plus one per collection: 51. Batch fetching groups the collection loads into in (…) chunks: 1 + ⌈50 / 25⌉ = 3, the same arithmetic as phase D of NPlusOne. A would need join fetch or an entity graph. B drops the orders query. D halves the loads instead of chunking them.

6.A template reads order.getLines() after the service's EntityManager closed and gets LazyInitializationException. Which fix removes both the exception and the hidden extra queries?

D. The exception means the entity outlived its context; deciding what the view needs inside the service fixes the cause in one statement. A is open-session-in-view: the lazy loads now succeed from the template, one query each, with a connection held for the whole request. B changes every load forever and, for JPQL, still issues the extra selects. C renders wrong data.

7.What SQL shape does select o.customer from PurchaseOrder o where o.lines is empty become?

B. The Queries program printed exactly that not exists subquery; size(o.lines) = 2 likewise became a correlated count(*) subquery. A is a valid hand-written alternative but not what Hibernate emits. C describes lazy loading, which a predicate never triggers. D: collection predicates are part of JPQL.

8.bolt is a managed Product at 80 cents. The same transaction runs the bulk statement update Product p set p.priceInCents = p.priceInCents + 5 where p.category = :c, which affects that row. What does bolt.priceInCents() return right after executeUpdate()?

C. The output reads managed copy still says 80c and then after refresh 85c. Bulk statements go straight to the database; managed copies keep their snapshot, and a later flush could even overwrite the bulk change with stale values. A and B invent synchronisation that does not exist. D: versions are checked when this context writes, not when it reads.

9.In an empty table, inside one transaction, the code persists a product and then runs select count(p) from Product p. What is the count with the default flush mode, and with FlushModeType.COMMIT?

A. FlushModeType.AUTO flushes the pending insert before a query that could see it, so the count is 1; COMMIT defers the insert to commit and the query counts 0. Both numbers are printed by Flushing. B and C deny that the mode changes anything. D has the two modes swapped.

10.Which statements about committing are true on Hibernate 7.4 with default settings? Select all that apply.

B and D. OptimisticLock printed RollbackException caused by OptimisticLockException; Flushing printed that commit() returned normally after setRollbackOnly() and no row was written. A forgets the wrapping at commit time. C is the JPA-specified behaviour, which Hibernate adopts only with hibernate.jpa.compliance.transaction=true.

11.CardPayment extends Payment must store last4 as NOT NULL, and Payment ids come from an identity column. Which strategy satisfies both?

B. A subclass table of its own can carry last4 varchar(4) not null, as the InheritanceMapping DDL showed, and identity ids are fine because the parent row is inserted first. A forces subclass columns to be nullable. C cannot use identity ids — keys must be unique across tables, so a sequence is required. D makes Payment unqueryable and gives no polymorphism.

12.A loop persists 100 products with hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=20 and order_inserts=true. Prepared-statement count with IDENTITY ids, and with SEQUENCE ids (default allocation) plus flush()/clear() every 20?

C. These are the numbers Batching measured: every IDENTITY insert is its own statement, while SEQUENCE lets the inserts queue and batch — five batches of twenty plus the sequence round trips. A gives IDENTITY a batching ability it does not have. B is false; inserts batch when deferred. D: an identity insert cannot be grouped at all.

13.Production configuration sets jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.database.action=none and hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto=validate. A migration was forgotten and a mapped column is missing. What happens at startup?

C. The §10 worked example hit this: with the JPA key set, validate is ignored. Set only hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto=validate to get A, which is the behaviour you want. B is what update would do, and why update is not a deployment strategy. D is invented; Hibernate never silently drops a mapped column.

14.An entity's equals and hashCode use its generated id. The code adds a new instance to a HashSet, persists it, then calls set.contains(instance). Result?

B. EntityDesign printed id-based hashCode : id=1, set.contains = false; a business-key hash or a constant hash with an id-based equals printed true. A confuses identity with hashing — HashSet finds the bucket first. C needs iteration during modification, which did not happen. D: flushing writes the row; it does not move the object between buckets.

15.An entity carries @SQLDelete(sql = "update soft_product set deleted = true where id = ?") and @SQLRestriction("deleted = false"). After em.remove(p) and commit, what do select count(p) from SoftProduct p (JPQL) and select count(*) from soft_product (native) return for a table that held only that row?

C. remove became an update … set deleted = true, the restriction hides the row from JPQL and find, and native SQL still sees it — JPQL count = 0, native count = 1 in the worked example. A would need a real delete. B ignores the restriction. D reverses which API sees the filter.

16.Which of these were demonstrated by this module's verified programs? Select all that apply.

A, B and D. A is why Batching switched the echo off and counted with statistics. B was visible in Relationships block 4: find(Product) also selected product_details, because Hibernate cannot proxy a field that may be null. D is the JPQL in Queries. C is false: for JPQL an eager collection is loaded by secondary selects after the query — the statement count does not drop, which is one more reason to keep every mapping lazy.

Reference

Glossary

Thirty terms, each linked back to the section that introduces it. The same entries drive the flashcard deck below — one list, two ways to use it.

Flashcards

Bag
Hibernate's name for a List collection mapping without an @OrderColumn: unordered, duplicates allowed. Removing one element can delete and re-insert the rest, and two bags cannot be fetch-joined in one query (MultipleBagFetchException). §4
Batch fetching
Loading lazy collections or proxies for several parents at once with where id in (?, …), via @BatchSize or session.setFetchBatchSize. Turns 1 + N statements into 1 + ⌈N / size⌉ with no change to the query. §5
Cascade
Propagating an EntityManager operation along an association: cascade = PERSIST persists the children with the parent, REMOVE deletes them with it. Right for owned children; wrong — and destructive — on references to shared entities. §4
Criteria API
Building a JPQL-equivalent query from Java objects (CriteriaBuilder, Root, Predicate) instead of a string. The right tool when the query's shape depends on which filters the caller supplied; verbose for anything static. §6
Dirty checking
At flush, Hibernate compares every managed entity with the snapshot taken when it was loaded and emits an update for each one that differs — all columns by default. It is why a plain setter on a managed entity reaches the database without any "save" call. §3
Discriminator
The column in a SINGLE_TABLE hierarchy that records which subclass a row is (@DiscriminatorColumn / @DiscriminatorValue). Hibernate 7 adds a check constraint on its values and filters by it for subtype queries. §8
Entity graph
A declared fetch plan — which attributes to load with the root — applied to a query or a find as the jakarta.persistence.fetchgraph or loadgraph hint. The same SQL join as join fetch, kept out of the query text so one query can serve several screens. §5
Entity states
Transient: a new object with no row. Managed: tracked by a context, dirty-checked at flush. Detached: has a row, no context watching it. Removed: scheduled for deletion. Every EntityManager method is a transition between them. §3
EntityManagerFactory
Hibernate's SessionFactory: the thread-safe, expensive, application-scoped object holding the metamodel, dialect, connection pool and second-level cache. Build one per application; create a cheap EntityManager from it per unit of work. §1
First-level cache
The persistence context's identity map: within one EntityManager, a second find for the same id returns the same instance with no SQL. Gives repeatable reads for free — and stale ones if another transaction wrote in between. §3
Flush
Turning the queued inserts, updates and deletes into SQL — at commit, before a query that could see them (FlushModeType.AUTO), or on flush(). Statements run in a fixed order (inserts, updates, collection changes, deletes), not the order you called the methods. §7
Impedance mismatch
The five ways objects and rows disagree — identity, associations, granularity, inheritance, navigation — that an object-relational mapper exists to translate across, and that every later section is a consequence of. §1
JDBC batching
Sending many parameter sets for one statement in a single round trip (hibernate.jdbc.batch_size, with order_inserts/order_updates). Needs write-behind, so it is impossible with IDENTITY ids; invisible to show_sql, visible in Statistics. §9
Join fetch
select o from Order o join fetch o.lines: load the association in the same statement as the root. One query instead of N+1; inner join unless written left join fetch; cannot be combined with database-side pagination. §5
JPQL
The Jakarta Persistence Query Language: SQL-like syntax over entities and their attributes rather than tables and columns, translated per dialect by Hibernate (whose superset is HQL). Paths become joins, collection predicates become subqueries, select new becomes a DTO. §6
Mapped superclass
A class whose mapped fields are copied into every entity table that extends it (@MappedSuperclass). Not an entity: no table, no queries against it, no associations to it. The tool for shared audit columns, not for polymorphism. §8
mappedBy
Marks the inverse side of a bidirectional association, naming the owning field on the other entity. Hibernate reads and cascades through it but never writes from it — set only this side and the foreign key stays null. §4
Merge
em.merge(detached) copies the argument's state onto a managed instance (loading it first if needed) and returns that instance; the argument stays detached. Copies every field, so a partially filled object overwrites the rest of the row. §3
Migration
A versioned, reviewed, checksummed DDL script applied in order by a tool such as Flyway or Liquibase. The only safe way to change a production schema; hbm2ddl.auto=update is not one, because it can only add. §10
N+1 problem
One query for N parents and then one more per parent as each lazy association is touched. The most common JPA performance bug; detected by counting statements, fixed per query with join fetch, an entity graph, batch fetching or a DTO — never with EAGER. §5
Natural id
A unique, immutable business key such as a SKU, marked @NaturalId (Hibernate). Gets its own lookup API and cache region, and is the best candidate for equals/hashCode when one exists. §2
Optimistic locking
Detecting rather than preventing concurrent updates: a @Version column goes into every update's where clause, a stale version matches zero rows, and Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException. No locks, no waiting; the loser retries. §7
Orphan removal
orphanRemoval = true: removing a child from the parent's collection deletes its row at flush. For children that cannot exist without their parent; distinct from cascade = REMOVE, which fires only when the parent itself is removed. §4
Owning side
The side of an association whose field maps to the foreign-key column or join table — the many side of one-to-many, the @JoinTable side of many-to-many, the @JoinColumn side of one-to-one. Only its state is written to the database. §4
Persistence context
What an EntityManager owns: an identity map (one instance per id) plus a snapshot of each managed entity's loaded state, and a queue of pending writes. The source of the identity guarantee, dirty checking and write-behind. §3
Pessimistic locking
LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE → select … for update: the database locks the row until commit and other lockers wait, then time out. Prevents conflicts instead of detecting them; needs a timeout and a consistent lock order to avoid deadlocks. §7
Projection
A query that returns scalars, a Tuple or a DTO (select new …) instead of entities. Nothing is hydrated or dirty-checked and nothing can lazy-load later — the right shape for read-only screens and reports. §6
Proxy
A runtime subclass (ByteBuddy) standing in for an entity or collection that has not been loaded; the first access to anything but the id runs the select. Why entities cannot be final, why getClass() lies, and what LazyInitializationException is thrown by. §5
Second-level cache
An optional, provider-backed cache of entity state by primary key, shared across persistence contexts for @Cacheable entities. Does not cache queries; is left stale by writes that bypass Hibernate. Worth it for immutable reference data, measured with statistics. §9
Soft delete
Marking a row deleted instead of removing it: @SQLDelete turns remove into an update, @SQLRestriction hides the row from find and JPQL. Native SQL still sees it, and unique constraints and joins need thought. §11

Further reading

Primary sources only — the specification, the Hibernate guide that documents the version this module runs, the tools, and the few books and articles that are worth the time. These are links, but nothing on this page loads them; the module remains fully offline.

Specifications and reference guides

  • Jakarta Persistence 3.2 Specification — the contract behind every annotation, the EntityManager lifecycle rules (chapter 3), the JPQL grammar (chapter 4), the Criteria API (chapter 6) and the exception hierarchy. Chapter 3's state transitions are §3 of this module, stated formally.
    https://jakarta.ee/specifications/persistence/3.2/
  • Hibernate ORM 7.4 documentation — the User Guide's chapters on the domain model (§2, §4, §8), the persistence context (§3), fetching (§5), HQL (§6), locking (§7), batching and caching (§9) and schema generation (§10). The HQL chapter documents the superset Hibernate accepts beyond JPQL.
    https://hibernate.org/orm/documentation/7.4/
  • Hibernate ORM migration guide — what changed between 6.x and 7.x: JPA 3.2, the PersistenceConfiguration bootstrap used in every program here, deprecated APIs such as byNaturalId, and changed defaults.
    https://github.com/hibernate/hibernate-orm/blob/main/migration-guide.adoc
  • H2 Database documentation — the SQL grammar and the jdbc:h2:mem: URL options (DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1 keeps an in-memory database alive between connections) behind the verified programs.
    https://h2database.com/html/main.html
  • Flyway documentation and Liquibase documentation — versioned migrations, checksums, baselining an existing schema, and the naming conventions (V1__init.sql) that §10 recommends over hbm2ddl.auto=update.
    https://documentation.red-gate.com/flyway · https://docs.liquibase.com/

  • Vlad Mihalcea, "How to implement equals and hashCode using the JPA entity identifier" — the constant-hashCode idiom §11 uses, with the test that proves the id-based version breaks.
    https://vladmihalcea.com/how-to-implement-equals-and-hashcode-using-the-jpa-entity-identifier/
  • Vlad Mihalcea, "How to batch INSERT and UPDATE statements with Hibernate" — batch_size, ordered inserts, why IDENTITY defeats it, and how to verify with a proxy driver (§9).
    https://vladmihalcea.com/how-to-batch-insert-and-update-statements-with-hibernate/
  • Thorben Janssen's Hibernate tips — short, current answers to the questions that come up in code review: lazy one-to-one, @DynamicUpdate, entity graphs, natural ids.
    https://thorben-janssen.com/

Books

  • High-Performance Java Persistence, Vlad Mihalcea — the book behind §5, §7 and §9: how JDBC, the database and Hibernate interact, with measurements. Read it when you have shipped one Hibernate application and want to know why it behaves as it does.
  • Java Persistence with Spring Data and Hibernate, Cătălin Tudose — the long-form treatment of mapping, the persistence context, conversations and caching, and the bridge to Spring Data that this module deliberately left out.
  • Effective Java, Joshua Bloch, 3rd edition — items 10 and 11 are the equals/hashCode contract that §11 has to satisfy under the extra constraint of a generated id.

Tools worth knowing now

Tools for diagnosing a persistence layer
ToolUse it to
hibernate.generate_statistics + StatisticsCount prepared statements, entity loads, flushes and cache hits per unit of work; assert on them in tests so an N+1 regression fails the build.
datasource-proxyWrap the DataSource to log every statement with its bound parameters and batch sizes — what show_sql cannot show.
p6spyThe same at the JDBC-driver level, with timing per statement, for applications you cannot change.
EXPLAIN ANALYZETake the slowest statement from the log to the database and read the plan; a missing index is a database fix, not a Hibernate one.
TestcontainersRun the integration tests against the real database engine in a container, so that H2's dialect differences never reach production.
Schema export (schema-generation.scripts.action=create)Generate the DDL for the current mapping as the starting point of a migration script, as §10's worked example does.
jOOQThe type-safe SQL builder for the reports and bulk jobs that should not go through entities at all.
Where to go from here

This is the last module of the course. Three things will teach you more than any further reading.

  • Add Spring Data JPA on top, deliberately. A JpaRepository is an EntityManager with the boilerplate generated and @Transactional drawing the unit-of-work boundary for you. Every mechanism here — the context, flush timing, lazy loading, @Version — behaves identically underneath; the first thing to do in a new Spring Boot project is set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false and read the SQL.
  • Run the lab against PostgreSQL in Testcontainers. Watch which Hibernate: lines change (types, sequences, for update), move the generated DDL into a Flyway script, and start the application with validate. That is the production shape.
  • Finish the lab's extensions. The @EmbeddedId stock key, the filterable soft delete and the IDENTITY experiment each force a design decision this module only described — and the statistics will tell you whether you got it right.
